This lesson gives you the number system that quantum computing is written in. Every amplitude in every state you will meet in this degree is a complex number, and every phase gate, every interference pattern and the whole Quantum Fourier Transform are statements about multiplying complex numbers. By the end you can add, multiply and divide complex numbers by hand, switch between Cartesian and polar form, use Euler's formula without looking it up, list the N-th roots of unity, and explain with numbers why a global phase is invisible while a relative phase is not. This is the first section of the Mathematical Foundations chapter; everything after it assumes these skills.

The idea in plain words

A classical probability is a single non-negative number. A quantum amplitude is a number with a size and a direction (an angle). The size squared gives a probability; the angle decides whether two routes to the same outcome reinforce each other or cancel. Real numbers only have two directions (plus and minus), so they can only cancel in one way. Complex numbers have a full circle of directions, and that is exactly the freedom quantum mechanics needs. Picture every amplitude as an arrow in a plane: adding amplitudes is adding arrows tip to tail, and multiplying amplitudes multiplies lengths and adds angles.

The definition

📘 DEFINITION

A complex number is z = a + bi, where a and b are real numbers and i is defined by i² = −1. The real part is Re(z) = a and the imaginary part is Im(z) = b (note: b itself is real). The set of all complex numbers is written ℂ.

The complex conjugate is z̄ = a − bi (physicists also write z*). The modulus is |z| = √(a² + b²), the length of the arrow from 0 to the point (a, b) in the complex plane. The argument arg(z) is the angle that arrow makes with the positive real axis.

The complex plane (also called the Argand diagram) puts Re(z) on the horizontal axis and Im(z) on the vertical axis. So 1 is one step right, i is one step up, −1 is one step left and −i is one step down. Powers of i cycle with period 4: i¹ = i, i² = −1, i³ = −i, i⁴ = 1. To find i2023, reduce the exponent mod 4: 2023 = 4·505 + 3, so i2023 = i³ = −i.

Arithmetic: add, multiply, divide

  • Add component by component: (a + bi) + (c + di) = (a + c) + (b + d)i.
  • Multiply by expanding and replacing i² by −1: (a + bi)(c + di) = (ac − bd) + (ad + bc)i.
  • Divide by multiplying top and bottom by the conjugate of the bottom, which turns the denominator into a real number: z/w = z·w̄ / |w|².
🧮 KEY EQUATION

|z|² = z·z̄ = a² + b² and 1/z = z̄ / |z|²

Here z = a + bi is any non-zero complex number, z̄ = a − bi is its conjugate and |z| is its modulus. The first identity is the one you will use most in this degree: the probability of an outcome is |amplitude|² = amplitude × conjugate(amplitude), which is always a real number ≥ 0.

Polar form and Euler's formula

Any non-zero complex number can be written by its length r = |z| and angle θ = arg(z): z = r(cos θ + i sin θ). Euler's formula compresses the bracket into an exponential.

📊 FIGURE — Euler's formula on the unit circle, and multiplying 3 + 4i by 1 − 2i
Left: e^{iθ} is the point at angle θ on the unit circle (here θ = 53.13°, the angle of 3 + 4i). Right: zw has length 5 × 2.236 = 11.18 and angle 53.13° − 63.43° = −10.30°.
🧮 KEY EQUATION

eiθ = cos θ + i sin θ, so z = r eiθ

θ is a real angle in radians, e ≈ 2.71828 is the base of natural logarithms, r ≥ 0 is the modulus. Because cos²θ + sin²θ = 1, every number eiθ has modulus exactly 1: it lies on the unit circle. Such a number is called a phase.

Polar form makes multiplication easy: (r₁eiθ₁)(r₂eiθ₂) = r₁r₂ ei(θ₁+θ₂). Lengths multiply, angles add. This is why a phase gate that multiplies an amplitude by eiφ rotates the arrow by φ without changing its length. Values you should know on sight:

θeiθwhere you will meet it
01ei0 = 1
π/4(1 + i)/√2 ≈ 0.7071 + 0.7071ithe T-gate phase
π/2ithe S-gate phase
π−1the Z-gate phase (Euler's identity eiπ + 1 = 0)
3π/2 (or −π/2)−ii³
2π1a full turn

The argument is only defined up to multiples of 2π, and the quadrant matters. For −1 − i the arrow points down-left, so arg = −3π/4 (−135°), not the +π/4 (45°) you get from arctan(b/a) = arctan(1). Use the two-argument arctangent (numpy: np.angle or np.arctan2(b, a)).

Roots of unity

The N-th roots of unity are the N solutions of zN = 1. They sit equally spaced around the unit circle: ωk for k = 0, 1, …, N − 1, where ω = e2πi/N. For N = 4 they are 1, i, −1, −i. For N = 3 they are 1, −0.5 + 0.8660i and −0.5 − 0.8660i. For any N ≥ 2 they add up to zero, because they are arrows spread evenly around a circle and cancel in pairs or triangles. That cancellation is the engine of the Quantum Fourier Transform, where amplitudes of the form ωjk interfere destructively everywhere except at the \"right\" answer.

ω = e2πi/N, 1 + ω + ω² + … + ωN−1 = 0 (N ≥ 2)

Global versus relative phase, as numbers

A qubit state is a pair of amplitudes (α, β) with |α|² + |β|² = 1. Two kinds of phase change look similar on paper and behave completely differently.

  • Global phase: multiply both amplitudes by the same eiγ. Every modulus is unchanged, and so is every inner-product modulus |⟨φ|ψ⟩| (the next lesson defines these), so every measurement probability in every basis is unchanged. Physically it is the same state.
  • Relative phase: multiply only one amplitude, e.g. (α, β) → (α, eiφβ). The probabilities of 0 and 1 are unchanged, but the arrows now combine differently when a later gate adds them, so probabilities in other bases change.

Here is the check, computed in numpy, comparing |+⟩ = (1, 1)/√2 with (1, i)/√2 (relative phase i = eiπ/2 on the second amplitude) and with e0.7i(1, 1)/√2 (a global phase). \"X-basis\" means measuring in the basis |+⟩, |−⟩; the probability of + is |(α + β)/√2|².

stateP(0)P(1)P(+)P(−)
(1, 1)/√20.50.51.00.0
(1, i)/√20.50.50.50.5
e0.7i(1, 1)/√20.50.51.00.0

The global phase row is identical to the first row in every column; the relative phase row differs in the X basis. For P(+) of (1, i)/√2: (α + β)/√2 = (1 + i)/2, and |(1 + i)/2|² = (1 + 1)/4 = 0.5.

Worked example

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Let z = 3 + 4i and w = 1 − 2i. Compute z + w, zw, z/w, |z|, arg(z), and verify that |zw| = |z||w|. All results were checked with Python complex numbers (z = 3+4j; w = 1-2j).

  1. Sum. Add parts: (3 + 1) + (4 − 2)i = 4 + 2i.
  2. Product. Expand: 3·1 + 3·(−2i) + 4i·1 + 4i·(−2i) = 3 − 6i + 4i − 8i². Since i² = −1, −8i² = +8. Collect: (3 + 8) + (−6 + 4)i = 11 − 2i.
  3. Quotient. Multiply top and bottom by w̄ = 1 + 2i. Bottom: |w|² = 1² + 2² = 5. Top: (3 + 4i)(1 + 2i) = 3 + 6i + 4i + 8i² = −5 + 10i. Divide: (−5 + 10i)/5 = −1 + 2i.
  4. Modulus. |z| = √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5. Check with the conjugate: z·z̄ = (3 + 4i)(3 − 4i) = 9 + 16 = 25 = |z|².
  5. Argument. The point (3, 4) is in the first quadrant, so arg(z) = arctan(4/3) = 0.9273 rad = 53.13°. Polar form: z = 5e0.9273i.
  6. Modulus of the product. |w| = √5 = 2.2361, so |z||w| = 5 × 2.2361 = 11.1803. Directly: |11 − 2i| = √(121 + 4) = √125 = 11.1803. They agree, as polar form predicts.
  7. Argument of the product. arg(w) = −1.1071 rad, so arg(z) + arg(w) = 0.9273 − 1.1071 ≈ −0.1799 rad (−0.17985 from the unrounded angles), and numpy gives np.angle(11-2j) = −0.1799. Angles add.

Answer: z + w = 4 + 2i, zw = 11 − 2i, z/w = −1 + 2i, |z| = 5, arg z ≈ 0.9273 rad. Sanity check: w·(z/w) = (1 − 2i)(−1 + 2i) = −1 + 2i + 2i − 4i² = 3 + 4i = z.

The same computation in Python, which you can paste into any notebook:

import numpy as np
z, w = 3+4j, 1-2j
print(z+w, z*w, z/w) # (4+2j) (11-2j) (-1+2j)
print(abs(z), np.angle(z)) # 5.0 0.9273
print(z*np.conj(z)) # (25+0j)

The traps

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Squaring instead of taking modulus squared. For z = 1 + i, z² = 2i (a complex number), but |z|² = z·z̄ = 2 (a real probability weight). Probabilities always use |z|², never z².

Quadrant errors in the argument. arctan(b/a) only returns angles between −π/2 and π/2. For −1 − i it says 45°; the true argument is −135°. Always look at the signs of a and b, or use np.angle.

Treating a relative phase as global. (1, −1)/√2 is not \"the same as\" (1, 1)/√2 just because the moduli match: the minus sign sits on one amplitude only, so it is a relative phase and the two states are perfectly distinguishable in the X basis.

📊 YOUR DATA EDGE

Python has complex numbers built in (1j is i), and numpy arrays accept dtype=complex. Use abs(z)**2 for probabilities, np.angle for arguments and np.isclose rather than == when comparing: np.exp(1j*np.pi) prints −1 + 1.2e-16i because of floating-point rounding, exactly the kind of tiny residue you already know to ignore in numerical data work.

What the exam asks

★ ON THE EXAM

Expect: (1) arithmetic with conjugates, especially division; (2) converting between a + bi and reiθ with the correct quadrant; (3) evaluating eiθ at multiples of π/4; (4) listing or summing roots of unity; (5) deciding whether two amplitude vectors differ by a global phase (one common factor on every entry) or a relative phase, and saying which measurement would tell them apart.

A fast test for global phase: divide the two vectors entry by entry. If every non-zero ratio is the same unit-modulus number, the difference is global.

This lesson teaches the notation that the rest of the degree is written in. A qubit state is a unit vector of complex numbers, and Dirac's bra-ket notation is simply a compact way of writing column vectors, conjugated row vectors and their products. After it you can compute inner and outer products by hand, turn an amplitude vector into measurement probabilities in any orthonormal basis, build an orthonormal basis with Gram-Schmidt, and change basis using the completeness relation. It builds on the complex arithmetic of the previous section and feeds directly into the next one on Hermitian and unitary matrices.

The idea in plain words

A single qubit lives in a two-dimensional complex vector space: its state is a column of two complex numbers, the amplitudes of |0⟩ and |1⟩. A \"bra\" is the same list written as a row with every entry conjugated. Put a bra in front of a ket and you get one complex number that measures how much the two states overlap (the inner product). Put a ket in front of a bra and you get a matrix (the outer product). Almost every formula in quantum computing is one of these two moves.

The definitions

📘 DEFINITION

A ket |ψ⟩ is a column vector in ℂⁿ. For a qubit (n = 2) the standard basis is |0⟩ = (1, 0)ᵀ and |1⟩ = (0, 1)ᵀ, so |ψ⟩ = α|0⟩ + β|1⟩ = (α, β)ᵀ. The bra ⟨ψ| is its conjugate transpose, the row (ᾱ, β̄); in general ⟨ψ| = (|ψ⟩)†, where † (\"dagger\") means transpose and conjugate every entry.

The norm is ‖ψ‖ = √⟨ψ|ψ⟩. A state is normalised when ‖ψ‖ = 1. Two vectors are orthogonal when ⟨φ|ψ⟩ = 0. An orthonormal basis is a set of n mutually orthogonal unit vectors in ℂⁿ; the computational basis {|0⟩, |1⟩} and the Hadamard basis {|+⟩, |−⟩}, with |±⟩ = (|0⟩ ± |1⟩)/√2, are the two you will use most.

Inner products and the Born rule

🧮 KEY EQUATION

⟨φ|ψ⟩ = φ̄₁ψ₁ + φ̄₂ψ₂ + … + φ̄ₙψₙ P(φ) = |⟨φ|ψ⟩|²

φᵢ and ψᵢ are the i-th entries of the two column vectors, the bar is complex conjugation, and ⟨φ|ψ⟩ is a single complex number. The second formula is the Born rule: if |ψ⟩ is measured in an orthonormal basis that contains |φ⟩, the probability of the outcome φ is the squared modulus of the overlap.

Three properties are used constantly:

  • Conjugate symmetry: ⟨ψ|φ⟩ is the complex conjugate of ⟨φ|ψ⟩. Swapping the order conjugates the answer, it does not leave it unchanged.
  • Linearity in the ket: ⟨φ|(a|ψ⟩ + b|χ⟩) = a⟨φ|ψ⟩ + b⟨φ|χ⟩, but a scalar pulled out of the bra comes out conjugated.
  • Cauchy-Schwarz: |⟨φ|ψ⟩|² ≤ ⟨φ|φ⟩⟨ψ|ψ⟩, so for two unit vectors every Born-rule probability is between 0 and 1.

Outer products, projectors and completeness

The outer product |ψ⟩⟨φ| is a column times a row: an n × n matrix whose (i, j) entry is ψᵢφ̄ⱼ. Acting on a ket it does (|ψ⟩⟨φ|)|χ⟩ = |ψ⟩ ⟨φ|χ⟩: take the overlap with φ, then point along ψ. For example |0⟩⟨+| has first row (0.7071, 0.7071) and second row (0, 0). When φ = ψ is a unit vector, P = |ψ⟩⟨ψ| is the projector onto ψ.

📊 FIGURE — Bra times ket gives a number, ket times bra gives a matrix
Top: the order of bra and ket decides the shape of the answer. Bottom: the two Hadamard-basis projectors add up to the identity, which is how a change of basis is done.

The two Hadamard-basis projectors, computed in numpy, are:

|+⟩⟨+| =1/21/2
1/21/2
|−⟩⟨−| =1/2−1/2
−1/21/2

Their sum is the 2 × 2 identity. That is a special case of the most useful identity in the subject.

🧮 KEY EQUATION

∑ᵢ |eᵢ⟩⟨eᵢ| = I (completeness relation)

The sum runs over any orthonormal basis {|eᵢ⟩} of the space and I is the identity matrix. Inserting I between anything lets you expand a state in that basis: |ψ⟩ = I|ψ⟩ = ∑ᵢ |eᵢ⟩⟨eᵢ|ψ⟩, so the new coordinates are cᵢ = ⟨eᵢ|ψ⟩. That is change of basis in one line.

Gram-Schmidt: building an orthonormal basis

Given linearly independent vectors v₁, v₂, …, Gram-Schmidt produces an orthonormal basis for the same span: normalise v₁ to get e₁; subtract from v₂ its component along e₁, u₂ = v₂ − e₁⟨e₁|v₂⟩, then normalise; continue, subtracting components along every earlier eᵢ. The only complex-number subtlety is the order in ⟨e₁|v₂⟩: the already-built vector goes in the bra.

Example (checked in numpy): v₁ = (1, 1), v₂ = (1, i).

  1. e₁ = v₁/‖v₁‖ = (1, 1)/√2 = |+⟩.
  2. ⟨e₁|v₂⟩ = (1·1 + 1·i)/√2 = (1 + i)/√2.
  3. u₂ = v₂ − e₁⟨e₁|v₂⟩ = (1, i) − ((1 + i)/2)(1, 1) = ((1 − i)/2, (−1 + i)/2) = ((1 − i)/2)(1, −1).
  4. ‖u₂‖² = |1 − i|²/4 × 2 = (2/4) × 2 = 1, so e₂ = u₂ = (0.5 − 0.5i, −0.5 + 0.5i).
  5. Check: ⟨e₁|e₂⟩ = 0 (numpy gives about 1e-16). Note e₂ = e−iπ/4|−⟩: Gram-Schmidt returned |−⟩ up to a global phase, which is physically the same basis vector.

Worked example: probabilities in a new basis

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Let |ψ⟩ = (1/√3)(|0⟩ + (1 + i)|1⟩). Check it is normalised, find its coordinates in the Hadamard basis, give the probabilities of measuring + and −, and rebuild |ψ⟩ from those coordinates. Convention: |0⟩ = (1, 0)ᵀ, |1⟩ = (0, 1)ᵀ, |±⟩ = (1, ±1)ᵀ/√2. Every number below was printed by numpy (np.vdot conjugates its first argument, so np.vdot(phi, psi) is ⟨φ|ψ⟩).

  1. Normalisation. ⟨ψ|ψ⟩ = (1/3)(|1|² + |1 + i|²) = (1/3)(1 + 2) = 1. Normalised.
  2. Coordinate along |+⟩. ⟨+| = (1, 1)/√2 (real, so conjugation changes nothing). ⟨+|ψ⟩ = (1/√2)(1/√3)(1 + 1 + i) = (2 + i)/√6 ≈ 0.8165 + 0.4082i.
  3. Coordinate along |−⟩. ⟨−|ψ⟩ = (1/√6)(1 − (1 + i)) = −i/√6 ≈ −0.4082i.
  4. Probabilities. P(+) = |2 + i|²/6 = (4 + 1)/6 = 5/6 ≈ 0.8333. P(−) = |−i|²/6 = 1/6 ≈ 0.1667.
  5. Rebuild. ((2 + i)/√6)|+⟩ + (−i/√6)|−⟩ = (1/√12)((2 + i − i), (2 + i + i)) = (1/√12)(2, 2 + 2i) = (1/√3)(1, 1 + i). This is |ψ⟩ again, as completeness promises.

Answer: |ψ⟩ = ((2 + i)/√6)|+⟩ − (i/√6)|−⟩, so P(+) = 5/6 and P(−) = 1/6. Sanity check: 5/6 + 1/6 = 1. Note that in the computational basis the same state gives P(0) = 1/3 and P(1) = 2/3: same state, different basis, different probabilities.

In numpy: psi = np.array([1, 1+1j])/np.sqrt(3); plus = np.array([1, 1])/np.sqrt(2) then abs(np.vdot(plus, psi))**2 prints 0.8333.

The traps

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Forgetting to conjugate the bra. In numpy, psi @ psi for the state above gives 0.3333 + 0.6667i, a complex \"norm\" that is nonsense. The correct np.vdot(psi, psi) gives 1. With real vectors the two agree, which is why this bug survives in code until the first complex amplitude appears.

Reading ⟨φ|ψ⟩ as a probability. The overlap is an amplitude; the probability is its modulus squared. For ⟨+|ψ⟩ = (2 + i)/√6, the probability is 5/6, not \"(2 + i)/√6\" and not its real part.

Mixing inner and outer products. ⟨φ|ψ⟩ is a number, |ψ⟩⟨φ| is a matrix. If a result that should be a probability comes out as a 2 × 2 array, the bra and ket are in the wrong order.

What the exam asks

★ ON THE EXAM

Typical tasks: normalise a vector with complex entries; compute ⟨φ|ψ⟩ and the probability of an outcome in the X basis {|+⟩, |−⟩} or the Y basis {|+i⟩, |−i⟩} with |±i⟩ = (|0⟩ ± i|1⟩)/√2; write an outer product as a matrix; show that a set of vectors is orthonormal; run one or two steps of Gram-Schmidt; prove ∑|eᵢ⟩⟨eᵢ| = I for a given basis; express a state in a new basis using cᵢ = ⟨eᵢ|ψ⟩.

Show the conjugation step explicitly. Markers look for it, and it is where most lost marks come from.

This lesson is about the three kinds of matrix that do all the work in quantum computing: unitary matrices (gates and time evolution), Hermitian matrices (observables such as energy or the Z measurement) and projectors (the outcomes of a measurement). After it you can take the adjoint of any matrix, test whether it is Hermitian, unitary or a projector, find eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a 2 × 2 matrix by hand, write a Hermitian matrix in spectral form, compute traces and commutators, and evaluate functions such as e−iθX/2 that define rotation gates. It uses the kets, bras and outer products of the previous section.

The idea in plain words

A square matrix acting on a state vector is an operation on the qubit. Quantum mechanics only allows two kinds of thing to happen to a closed system: it evolves by a transformation that preserves lengths (so probabilities keep summing to 1) and it is measured. Length-preserving transformations are unitary matrices. Measurable quantities are Hermitian matrices, because Hermitian matrices are exactly the ones guaranteed to have real eigenvalues (the numbers a meter can show) and an orthonormal set of eigenvectors (the distinguishable outcomes). A projector picks out one outcome.

The definitions

📘 DEFINITION

The adjoint (dagger) of a matrix A is A† = Āᵀ: transpose it and conjugate every entry. It satisfies (AB)† = B†A† (order reverses) and (A|ψ⟩)† = ⟨ψ|A†.

  • Hermitian (self-adjoint): A† = A. Real eigenvalues, orthogonal eigenvectors.
  • Unitary: U†U = UU† = I, so U−1 = U†. Preserves inner products, so ⟨Uφ|Uψ⟩ = ⟨φ|ψ⟩ and norms; every eigenvalue has modulus 1 (it is a phase eiθ).
  • Projector: P² = P and P† = P. Eigenvalues are only 0 and 1; tr P is the dimension of the subspace it projects onto.
  • Normal: A†A = AA†. Hermitian and unitary matrices are both normal, and normal matrices are exactly the ones the spectral theorem covers.

The Pauli matrices are the most important examples; each is both Hermitian and unitary, and each squares to the identity I.

X01Y0−iZ10
10i00−1

Check Y by hand: Yᵀ has rows (0, i) and (−i, 0); conjugating every entry gives rows (0, −i) and (i, 0), which is Y again, so Y is Hermitian. And Y·Y: row 1 times column 1 is 0·0 + (−i)(i) = 1, so Y² = I and Y is unitary too. By contrast the matrix with rows (0, 1) and (−1, 0) is unitary (it is a real rotation by −90°) but not Hermitian, since its adjoint has rows (0, −1) and (1, 0); its eigenvalues are ±i, which have modulus 1 but are not real.

Eigenvalues and the spectral theorem

An eigenvector of A is a non-zero |v⟩ with A|v⟩ = λ|v⟩; the number λ is its eigenvalue. For a 2 × 2 matrix solve the characteristic equation det(A − λI) = 0, which is λ² − (tr A)λ + det A = 0, then for each λ solve (A − λI)|v⟩ = 0 and normalise.

🧮 KEY EQUATION

A = ∑ᵢ λᵢ |vᵢ⟩⟨vᵢ| (spectral theorem, for normal A)

The λᵢ are the eigenvalues, the |vᵢ⟩ form an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors, and each |vᵢ⟩⟨vᵢ| is the projector onto one eigenvector. A Hermitian matrix is a weighted sum of projectors with real weights. This is the maths behind measurement: the projectors are the outcomes, the λᵢ are the values you record.

Two more tools. The trace tr A is the sum of the diagonal entries; it equals the sum of the eigenvalues, and tr(AB) = tr(BA) (the cyclic property). The commutator is [A, B] = AB − BA. It is zero exactly when the order of A and B does not matter; for Pauli matrices [X, Y] = 2iZ, [Y, Z] = 2iX and [Z, X] = 2iY, which is why X-, Y- and Z-measurements disturb one another.

Functions of a matrix

To apply a function f to a normal matrix, apply it to the eigenvalues and keep the projectors: f(A) = ∑ f(λᵢ)|vᵢ⟩⟨vᵢ|. For a Pauli matrix P, which satisfies P² = I, the power series of the exponential splits into even terms (I) and odd terms (P), giving the rotation-gate formula.

🧮 KEY EQUATION

e−iθP/2 = cos(θ/2) I − i sin(θ/2) P for P ∈ {X, Y, Z}

θ is the rotation angle in radians and I is the 2 × 2 identity. These are the gates RX(θ), RY(θ), RZ(θ). For θ = π/2 and P = X, scipy.linalg.expm gives the matrix with rows (0.7071, −0.7071i) and (−0.7071i, 0.7071), exactly cos(π/4)I − i sin(π/4)X. The exponential of −i times a Hermitian matrix is always unitary.

Worked example: diagonalising a Hermitian matrix

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Take A with rows (2, 1 − i) and (1 + i, 3). Show it is Hermitian, find its eigenvalues and orthonormal eigenvectors, write its spectral decomposition and use it to compute A³. Every number was checked with np.linalg.eigh and matrix products.

📊 FIGURE — A Hermitian matrix as a weighted sum of eigen-projectors
A splits into projectors onto its two eigenvectors, weighted by the eigenvalues 1 and 4. Cubing A only cubes the weights: A³ = P₁ + 64P₄.
  1. Hermitian? Transpose: rows (2, 1 + i) and (1 − i, 3). Conjugate: rows (2, 1 − i) and (1 + i, 3). That is A, so A† = A. The diagonal is real, as it must be.
  2. Characteristic equation. tr A = 2 + 3 = 5. det A = 2·3 − (1 − i)(1 + i) = 6 − 2 = 4. So λ² − 5λ + 4 = 0, i.e. (λ − 1)(λ − 4) = 0: λ = 1 and λ = 4. Both real, as the theorem promises.
  3. Eigenvector for λ = 1. A − I has rows (1, 1 − i) and (1 + i, 2). The first row says v₁ + (1 − i)v₂ = 0; choose v₂ = −1, so v₁ = 1 − i. Check row 2: (1 + i)(1 − i) + 2(−1) = 2 − 2 = 0. Norm² = |1 − i|² + 1 = 3, so |v₁⟩ = (1 − i, −1)/√3.
  4. Eigenvector for λ = 4. A − 4I has rows (−2, 1 − i) and (1 + i, −1). Choose v₂ = 2, then −2v₁ + 2(1 − i) = 0 gives v₁ = 1 − i. Norm² = 2 + 4 = 6, so |v₄⟩ = (1 − i, 2)/√6.
  5. Orthogonal? ⟨v₁|v₄⟩ = [(1 + i)(1 − i) + (−1)(2)]/√18 = (2 − 2)/√18 = 0.
  6. Projectors. P₁ = |v₁⟩⟨v₁| has rows (2/3, (−1 + i)/3) and ((−1 − i)/3, 1/3). P₄ = |v₄⟩⟨v₄| has rows (1/3, (1 − i)/3) and ((1 + i)/3, 2/3). Each has trace 1, and P₁ + P₄ = I (completeness).
  7. Spectral form. 1·P₁ + 4·P₄: top-left 2/3 + 4/3 = 2; top-right (−1 + i)/3 + 4(1 − i)/3 = (3 − 3i)/3 = 1 − i; bottom-right 1/3 + 8/3 = 3. That is A.
  8. A³ the easy way. A³ = 1³P₁ + 4³P₄ = P₁ + 64P₄. Top-left 2/3 + 64/3 = 22; top-right (−1 + i)/3 + 64(1 − i)/3 = 21 − 21i; bottom-right 1/3 + 128/3 = 43.

Answer: eigenvalues 1 and 4 with eigenvectors (1 − i, −1)/√3 and (1 − i, 2)/√6; A = P₁ + 4P₄; A³ has rows (22, 21 − 21i) and (21 + 21i, 43). Sanity check: eigenvalues sum to tr A = 5 and multiply to det A = 4; np.linalg.matrix_power(A, 3) gives the same A³.

In numpy: A = np.array([[2, 1-1j], [1+1j, 3]]); w, V = np.linalg.eigh(A) returns w = [1, 4]. The columns of V may differ from the hand answer by a phase (numpy printed (−0.8165, 0.4082 + 0.4082i) for λ = 1, which is ei5π/4 times the hand vector). Eigenvectors are only defined up to such a factor.

The traps

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Transposing without conjugating. A matrix with rows (0, i) and (i, 0) is symmetric but not Hermitian: its adjoint has rows (0, −i) and (−i, 0). \"Symmetric\" and \"Hermitian\" only coincide for real matrices.

Reversing the order wrongly. (AB)† = B†A†, not A†B†. The same rule makes a circuit of gates U₁ then U₂ equal to the product U₂U₁, and its inverse U₁†U₂†.

Assuming Hermitian implies unitary. The Paulis are both, but A above is Hermitian with eigenvalue 4, which a unitary cannot have. Test each property separately.

Using np.linalg.eig on a Hermitian matrix. It works, but it can return eigenvalues with tiny imaginary parts and eigenvectors that are not orthonormal when eigenvalues repeat. Use np.linalg.eigh for Hermitian matrices.

What the exam asks

★ ON THE EXAM

Expect to: compute A† and classify a matrix as Hermitian, unitary, a projector, several or none; find eigenvalues and normalised eigenvectors of a 2 × 2 Hermitian matrix; write the spectral decomposition and use it to compute a power, a square root or an exponential; compute commutators of Paulis; evaluate e−iθP/2 for a specific angle; compute an expectation value ⟨ψ|A|ψ⟩; use the cyclic property of the trace.

A fast exam check: for a 2 × 2 matrix the eigenvalues must add to the trace and multiply to the determinant. For a Hermitian matrix both must be real; for a unitary both must have modulus 1.

This lesson shows how to describe more than one qubit. The tool is the tensor product (in numpy, the Kronecker product np.kron), and it is the reason a quantum computer's state space grows exponentially with the number of qubits. After it you can build multi-qubit basis states and product states, compute A⊗B for 2 × 2 matrices by hand, apply a gate to one qubit of a register, test whether a two-qubit state is a product state or entangled, and read Qiskit's bit ordering without being caught out. It completes the Mathematical Foundations chapter and leads straight into multi-qubit gates and entanglement.

The idea in plain words

If you have two independent coins, the probability of \"first heads, second tails\" is the product of the two probabilities, and you need 2 × 2 = 4 numbers to list the joint distribution. Qubits work the same way with amplitudes: the joint state of two independent qubits has four amplitudes, each the product of one amplitude from each qubit. The tensor product is the bookkeeping that lays those products out in a fixed order. The twist, which makes quantum computing interesting, is that most vectors in the joint space cannot be written as such a product at all. Those are the entangled states.

The definitions

📘 DEFINITION

The tensor product of a = (a₀, a₁) and b = (b₀, b₁) is the 4-vector a⊗b = (a₀b₀, a₀b₁, a₁b₀, a₁b₁): every entry of a multiplies the whole of b, in order. For matrices, the Kronecker product A⊗B is the block matrix whose (i, j) block is aᵢⱼB; if A is m × m and B is n × n, then A⊗B is mn × mn.

📊 FIGURE — The Kronecker product H ⊗ Z laid out as four blocks of Z
Block (i, j) of H ⊗ Z is H’s entry (i, j) times the whole matrix Z; only the bottom-right block is −Z. Rows and columns run |00⟩, |01⟩, |10⟩, |11⟩ (divide by √2).

Convention in this course (textbook, big-endian): |q₀q₁⟩ = |q₀⟩⊗|q₁⟩, qubit 0 is the leftmost label. The two-qubit basis is |00⟩, |01⟩, |10⟩, |11⟩, which are the vectors with a single 1 in position 0, 1, 2, 3 (read the label as a binary number). A state of n qubits is a unit vector in ℂ2ⁿ. A product state can be written |a⟩⊗|b⟩; a state that cannot is entangled.

A gate that acts on the first qubit only is U⊗I; on the second qubit only, I⊗U. Here is H⊗Z written out as a 4 × 4 table (every entry multiplied by √2, so divide by √2 to get the matrix). The top-left 2 × 2 block is 1·Z, the top-right is 1·Z and the bottom-right is −1·Z, because H has entries (1, 1; 1, −1)/√2. Computed with np.kron(H, Z).

|00⟩|01⟩|10⟩|11⟩
1010
0−10−1
10−10
0−101

(Columns and rows are in the order |00⟩, |01⟩, |10⟩, |11⟩.)

The rules that make it computable

🧮 KEY EQUATION

(A⊗B)(|a⟩⊗|b⟩) = (A|a⟩)⊗(B|b⟩) (A⊗B)(C⊗D) = (AC)⊗(BD)

A, B, C, D are matrices (A and C act on the first system, B and D on the second) and |a⟩, |b⟩ are kets of matching size. The first rule says a gate on each qubit of a product state just acts on each factor separately. The second is the mixed-product rule. Also: (A⊗B)† = A†⊗B†, tr(A⊗B) = (tr A)(tr B), and the tensor product of unitaries is unitary. Order matters: A⊗B ≠ B⊗A in general.

🧮 KEY EQUATION

dim(n qubits) = 2 × 2 × … × 2 = 2ⁿ

n is the number of qubits and dim is the number of complex amplitudes needed to write a general state. Dimensions multiply under ⊗, they do not add: two qubits need 4 amplitudes, not 2 + 2.

What 2ⁿ means for classical simulation: stored as numpy complex128 (16 bytes per amplitude), a 30-qubit state vector needs 2³⁰ × 16 bytes = 16 GiB (about 17.2 GB), 40 qubits need 16 TiB, and 50 qubits need 16 PiB (16,777,216 GiB). These are pure arithmetic, not records. Two cautions. First, cleverer simulators (tensor networks, stabiliser methods) avoid storing the full vector for many circuits, so 2ⁿ is a worst case, not a law. Second, 2ⁿ amplitudes do not mean 2ⁿ numbers you can read out: measuring n qubits yields only n bits, and Holevo's theorem limits the classical information retrievable from n qubits to n bits. Quantum speed-ups have to come from interference, not from \"storing\" 2ⁿ values.

Product or entangled? A two-line test

For a two-qubit state with amplitudes (a, b, c, d) on |00⟩, |01⟩, |10⟩, |11⟩, arrange them as a 2 × 2 grid with rows (a, b) and (c, d). A product state (α₀, α₁)⊗(β₀, β₁) gives rows (α₀β₀, α₀β₁) and (α₁β₀, α₁β₁); the second row is a multiple of the first, so the determinant is zero. Conversely, if the determinant is zero, the grid factorises. So:

two-qubit state is a product state ⇔ ad − bc = 0

statead − bcverdict
(|00⟩ + |01⟩ + |10⟩ + |11⟩)/21/4 − 1/4 = 0product: |+⟩⊗|+⟩
(|00⟩ + i|01⟩ + |10⟩ + i|11⟩)/2i/4 − i/4 = 0product: |+⟩⊗|+i⟩
(|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√21/2 − 0 = 1/2entangled (Bell state Φ⁺)
(|00⟩ + |01⟩ + |10⟩ − |11⟩)/2−1/4 − 1/4 = −1/2entangled

This test only works for exactly two qubits. For more qubits you check every way of splitting the register, which is the subject of the entanglement chapter.

Worked example

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Let |a⟩ = (|0⟩ + i|1⟩)/√2 and |b⟩ = (√3/2)|0⟩ + (1/2)|1⟩. (i) Compute |a⟩⊗|b⟩ and its measurement probabilities. (ii) Compute (H⊗X)|00⟩ two ways. (iii) Confirm the answer to (i) passes the product test. Convention: big-endian |q₀q₁⟩. Checked with np.kron.

  1. Multiply out. a = (1, i)/√2, b = (√3/2, 1/2). Entries: a₀b₀ = √3/(2√2), a₀b₁ = 1/(2√2), a₁b₀ = i√3/(2√2), a₁b₁ = i/(2√2).
  2. Decimals. √3/(2√2) = 0.6124 and 1/(2√2) = 0.3536, so |a⟩⊗|b⟩ = (0.6124, 0.3536, 0.6124i, 0.3536i).
  3. Probabilities. |0.6124|² = 0.375 = 3/8 and |0.3536|² = 0.125 = 1/8, so P(00) = 0.375, P(01) = 0.125, P(10) = 0.375, P(11) = 0.125. These equal P(q₀)·P(q₁): 1/2 × 3/4 = 3/8 and 1/2 × 1/4 = 1/8, as independence requires.
  4. (ii) by factors. (H⊗X)(|0⟩⊗|0⟩) = (H|0⟩)⊗(X|0⟩) = |+⟩⊗|1⟩ = (1, 1)/√2 ⊗ (0, 1) = (0, 1, 0, 1)/√2 ≈ (0, 0.7071, 0, 0.7071).
  5. (ii) by the 4 × 4 matrix. H⊗X has blocks (X, X; X, −X)/√2. Multiplying it by |00⟩ = (1, 0, 0, 0) picks out its first column, (0, 1, 0, 1)/√2. Same answer.
  6. (iii) product test on (i): ad − bc = (0.6124)(0.3536i) − (0.3536)(0.6124i) = 0.2165i − 0.2165i = 0. Product state, as it must be.

Answer: |a⟩⊗|b⟩ = (0.6124, 0.3536, 0.6124i, 0.3536i) with probabilities (0.375, 0.125, 0.375, 0.125); (H⊗X)|00⟩ = (|01⟩ + |11⟩)/√2. Sanity check: 0.375 + 0.125 + 0.375 + 0.125 = 1.

Reading Qiskit without being fooled

Qiskit labels qubits the other way round when it prints bitstrings and matrices: qubit 0 is the rightmost bit (little-endian). This runs as written with Qiskit 2.x:

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from qiskit.quantum_info import Statevector, Operator
qc = QuantumCircuit(2)
qc.x(0)
print(Statevector(qc).probabilities_dict()) # key '01' with probability 1.0

In our textbook convention, X on qubit 0 gives |10⟩; Qiskit prints '01'. Likewise, a circuit with just qc.h(0) on two qubits has Operator(qc) equal to np.kron(I, H), not np.kron(H, I) (checked with np.allclose). Neither is wrong; they are two orderings of the same tensor product. Decide which one you are using before you compare numbers.

The traps

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Swapping the factors. |0⟩⊗|1⟩ = (0, 1, 0, 0) = |01⟩ but |1⟩⊗|0⟩ = (0, 0, 1, 0) = |10⟩. Similarly H⊗I (H on qubit 0) and I⊗H (H on qubit 1) are different matrices.

Adding instead of multiplying dimensions. A 3-qubit register is described by 2³ = 8 amplitudes, not 6.

Assuming every multi-qubit state factorises. (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2 has no single-qubit description at all; trying to find α, β with α₀β₀ = α₁β₁ = 1/√2 and α₀β₁ = α₁β₀ = 0 is impossible.

Mixing conventions. Comparing a hand calculation (big-endian) with Qiskit output (little-endian) and \"finding a bug\" that is only the bit order.

What the exam asks

★ ON THE EXAM

Expect: write a product state such as |+⟩⊗|−⟩ as a 4-vector; compute A⊗B for two named 2 × 2 gates; apply U⊗I or I⊗U to a basis state; decide whether a given two-qubit state is entangled using ad − bc; use the mixed-product rule to simplify (A⊗B)(C⊗D); state how many amplitudes n qubits need; translate between big-endian and Qiskit little-endian labels.

Write the basis order (|00⟩, |01⟩, |10⟩, |11⟩) at the top of any 4-vector answer. It costs one line and prevents the most common lost marks.

A quantum computer never hands you its state. You run the same circuit many times (each run is a shot), read out a bitstring each time, and turn the counts into numbers. This lesson gives you the probability you need to do that honestly: distributions, expectation and variance, the error bar on a probability estimated from shots, and Bayes' rule for correcting noisy readout. It sits right after the linear-algebra chapter and before the postulates, because the Born rule (next chapter) produces exactly the kind of random variable you will learn to handle here.

The idea in plain words: a quantum program ends in a sampling experiment

Think of each shot as one draw from a hidden probability distribution over bitstrings. For one qubit the distribution is just two numbers, P(0) and P(1). For n qubits there are 2n possible bitstrings, so the full distribution can be enormous, and you only ever see a finite sample of it. Everything you report from a quantum experiment (a probability, an expectation value, an energy in a chemistry calculation) is therefore an estimate with statistical error, even on a perfect, noise-free machine. That error is called shot noise.

Two further ideas return throughout the degree. First, conditioning: once you know one qubit's result, the probabilities for the others can change, and Bayes' rule tells you how. Second, marginals: to get the distribution of one qubit out of an n-qubit histogram you add up all the rows that agree on that qubit, exactly like a GROUP BY.

Definitions: random variables, distributions, expectation, variance

📘 DEFINITION

A discrete random variable X takes values x with probabilities p(x) ≥ 0 that satisfy ∑x p(x) = 1. The list of pairs (x, p(x)) is its distribution.

The expectation (mean) is E[X] = ∑x x·p(x). The variance is Var(X) = E[(X − E[X])2] = E[X2] − (E[X])2, and the standard deviation is √Var(X).

A Bernoulli variable takes the value 1 with probability p and 0 with probability 1 − p: mean p, variance p(1 − p). The number of 1s in N independent Bernoulli trials is Binomial(N, p): mean Np, variance Np(1 − p).

A quick check with a fair six-sided die: E[X] = (1+2+3+4+5+6)/6 = 3.5 and Var(X) = 35/12 ≈ 2.9167. A qubit measured in the computational basis is a Bernoulli variable: outcome 1 with probability p = P(1). Two random variables X and Y are independent when P(X = x, Y = y) = P(X = x)·P(Y = y) for every x and y. Much of this degree is about states whose two-qubit outcome tables are not products of their marginals; a correlation on its own is not proof of anything quantum, but the pattern of correlations across several measurement settings can be (the Bell-test chapter).

The key equations: estimating a probability from shots

Run N shots and count k outcomes equal to 0. The natural estimate and its standard error are:

p̂ = k / N

SE(p̂) = √( p̂ (1 − p̂) / N )

95% confidence interval ≈ p̂ ± 1.96 · SE(p̂)

🧮 KEY EQUATION

p̂ is the estimated probability, k the count of the outcome of interest, N the number of shots, SE the standard error (the standard deviation of the estimator p̂ across imagined repeats of the whole N-shot experiment), and 1.96 is the two-sided 95% point of the standard normal distribution.

Because SE ∝ 1/√N, halving the error bar costs four times the shots. The worst case is p = ½, where p(1 − p) = ¼; the shots needed for a 95% half-width of ε are then N = (1.96 · 0.5 / ε)2, which is 9,604 for ε = 0.01.

For the Pauli-Z expectation of a qubit, ⟨Z⟩ = (+1)·P(0) + (−1)·P(1) = 2P(0) − 1, so its estimate is 2p̂ − 1 and its standard error is 2·SE(p̂): an expectation on the scale −1 to +1 carries twice the error bar of the probability it is built from.

These formulas use the normal approximation to the binomial. It is fine when Np̂ and N(1 − p̂) are both comfortably above about 10. Near p = 0 or p = 1 (say 0 errors in 200 shots) it gives a zero-width interval, which is nonsense; there you should use a Wilson or Clopper–Pearson interval instead.

Worked example: an error bar from 1,000 shots

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Convention: |0⟩ = (1,0)ᵀ, |1⟩ = (0,1)ᵀ. A qubit is prepared with Qiskit's Ry(π/4) gate acting on |0⟩, giving |ψ⟩ = cos(π/8)|0⟩ + sin(π/8)|1⟩. You are told the exact probabilities only after the experiment, to check your estimate. We ran 1,000 shots and saw 853 zeros. Every number below was computed in Python.

📊 FIGURE — An estimated probability and its 95% error bar from 1,000 shots
The bar splits the 1,000 shots by outcome. Below, the 95% interval around p̂ = 0.853 contains the true value 0.8536; quadrupling the shots would halve its width.
  1. Estimate: p̂ = k/N = 853/1000 = 0.8530.
  2. Variance factor: p̂(1 − p̂) = 0.853 × 0.147 = 0.125391.
  3. Standard error: SE = √(0.125391/1000) = √0.000125391 = 0.0112.
  4. 95% interval: 0.8530 ± 1.96 × 0.0112 = 0.8530 ± 0.0219, i.e. [0.8311, 0.8749].
  5. Expectation of Z: 2p̂ − 1 = 2(0.853) − 1 = 0.7060, with SE 2 × 0.0112 = 0.0224.
  6. Now the truth: amplitudes are cos(π/8) = 0.9239 and sin(π/8) = 0.3827, so P(0) = 0.92392 = 0.8536 and P(1) = 0.1464. Exact ⟨Z⟩ = cos(π/4) = 0.7071.
  7. Sanity check: 0.8536 + 0.1464 = 1, and the true P(0) = 0.8536 lies inside [0.8311, 0.8749]; the estimate is off by 0.0006, well under one SE.
  8. Planning question: how many shots give a 95% half-width of 0.01 for this state? Here p(1 − p) = 0.8536 × 0.1464 = 0.125 exactly, so N = 1.962 × 0.125 / 0.012 = 4,802 shots (half the 9,604 needed at p = ½).

You can reproduce the exact probabilities with Qiskit (these lines run as written):

from math import pi
from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from qiskit.quantum_info import Statevector
qc = QuantumCircuit(1); qc.ry(pi/4, 0)
print(Statevector(qc).probabilities()) # [0.85355339 0.14644661]

And you can simulate the shot noise with numpy: numpy.random.default_rng(7).binomial(1000, 0.8536, size=5) returned 851, 862, 871, 848 and 849 zeros in five repeats of the whole 1,000-shot experiment. That spread of roughly ±11 around 854 is the standard error you just computed, now visible.

Bayes' rule and noisy readout

Real qubits misreport. Suppose a qubit that is truly in 1 is read as 1 with probability 0.95, and a qubit truly in 0 is wrongly read as 1 with probability 0.03. If your prior belief is P(true 1) = 0.5, what is the chance the qubit was really 1 given that you read 1?

P(A | B) = P(B | A) · P(A) / P(B)

P(B) = P(B | A) P(A) + P(B | not A) P(not A)

Here A = \"truly 1\", B = \"read 1\". The numerator is 0.95 × 0.5 = 0.475. The law of total probability gives P(read 1) = 0.475 + 0.03 × 0.5 = 0.490. So P(truly 1 | read 1) = 0.475/0.490 = 0.9694. With a prior of 0.2 instead, the same readout gives 0.19/0.214 = 0.8879: the prior matters. Readout-error mitigation, which you will meet in the NISQ chapter, is this calculation done for every bitstring at once with a matrix of P(read | true).

📊 YOUR DATA EDGE

You already know this material from A/B tests: a count out of N trials, a standard error, a confidence interval, and the rule that precision grows only as √N. Treat a quantum benchmark exactly like a dashboard metric: ask for N, ask for the error bar, and ask whether a quoted improvement is larger than twice the combined standard error. A Qiskit counts dictionary is a GROUP BY bitstring with COUNT(*); a marginal on one qubit is a second GROUP BY on one character of that string.

The traps

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Confusing the standard deviation of one shot, √(p(1 − p)), which does not shrink, with the standard error of p̂, which shrinks as 1/√N.

Reading a count of zero as a probability of zero. Zero errors in 200 shots is consistent with an error rate of a percent or so; the normal formula breaks down there.

Treating amplitudes as probabilities. An amplitude can be negative or complex; the probability is its squared magnitude. In the worked example the amplitude 0.9239 gives probability 0.8536, not 0.9239.

Reading Qiskit bitstrings left to right as qubit 0, 1, 2. Qiskit prints little-endian: qubit 0 is the rightmost character. When you compute a marginal from Qiskit counts, pick the character from the right.

What the exam asks

★ ON THE EXAM

Expect: compute a mean and variance from a small table; turn counts into p̂, SE and a 95% interval; say how many shots a target precision needs (and that halving the error needs four times the shots); convert P(0) to ⟨Z⟩ and back; and apply Bayes' rule to a readout-error story. Always state N and the error bar, and finish with a sanity check that probabilities sum to 1.

Before you can say what a quantum computer does differently, you need a precise picture of what an ordinary computer does. This lesson builds the circuit model of classical computation from Boolean logic, shows which small gate sets can build everything, and then makes the step that quantum computing depends on: rewriting computation so that it is reversible. By the end you can turn any classical function into a reversible circuit, write Toffoli as a matrix, compute Landauer's bound, and explain why every quantum gate before measurement has to be reversible.

The idea in plain words: circuits of gates acting on bits

A bit takes the value 0 or 1. A computation on n input bits producing m output bits is a function f: {0,1}n → {0,1}m. A circuit computes f by wiring together small gates (AND, OR, NOT, and so on) in an acyclic network: bits flow along wires from left to right and never loop back. Two numbers measure a circuit's cost: its size (the number of gates) and its depth (the number of gates on the longest input-to-output path, roughly its running time if every gate in a layer fires in parallel). Quantum circuits in this degree use the same vocabulary.

abANDORXOR (a ⊕ b)NAND
000001
010111
100111
111100

There are 22n different Boolean functions of n input bits (each of the 2n rows of the truth table can independently output 0 or 1): 16 for n = 2 and 256 for n = 3.

Definitions: universality and reversibility

📘 DEFINITION

A gate set is universal if every Boolean function can be computed by a circuit built only from those gates (allowing wires to be copied, which classical physics permits). {AND, OR, NOT} is universal: write the function as an OR of one AND-term for each input row that outputs 1. NAND alone is universal, because NOT a = NAND(a, a), AND = NOT(NAND), and OR(a, b) = NAND(NOT a, NOT b).

A gate is reversible if its inputs can always be recovered from its outputs, i.e. it is a bijection (a one-to-one, onto map) from {0,1}n to itself. Reversible gates therefore have as many outputs as inputs. NOT is reversible; AND is not, since three different inputs (00, 01, 10) all give output 0.

Universality is cheap, but efficiency is not guaranteed. Shannon's counting argument (1949) proves that almost every Boolean function of n bits needs a circuit whose size grows exponentially in n; there are simply too many functions for small circuits to cover. The famous open problems of the next lesson are about which specific, natural functions have small circuits.

The standard reversible gates, written as maps on bits (⊕ is XOR, i.e. addition mod 2):

NOT: a → a ⊕ 1

CNOT: (a, b) → (a, b ⊕ a)

Toffoli (CCNOT): (a, b, c) → (a, b, c ⊕ a·b)

Fredkin (CSWAP): (a, b, c) → (a, b, c) if a = 0; (a, c, b) if a = 1

Here a and b are the control bits and the last bit of CNOT or Toffoli is the target. Toffoli flips the target only when both controls are 1. Fredkin swaps the last two bits only when the control is 1; it never changes the number of 1s, which makes it a \"conservative\" gate. Toffoli alone, and Fredkin alone, are each universal for reversible computation provided you may supply constant input bits (ancillas).

The key equation: a reversible gate is a permutation matrix

Label the 2n bitstrings as basis vectors. In the textbook big-endian convention the 3-bit string abc is basis vector number 4a + 2b + c, so |110⟩ is vector 6 and |111⟩ is vector 7. A reversible gate sends each basis vector to exactly one other, so its matrix has a single 1 in every row and column: a permutation matrix. For Toffoli it is the 8 × 8 identity with the last two rows swapped:

000001010011100101110111
10000000
01000000
00100000
00010000
00001000
00000100
00000001
00000010
🧮 KEY EQUATION

PT P = I for every permutation matrix P, so P is orthogonal and, being real, also unitary: P†P = I.

P is the gate's matrix, PT its transpose, P† its conjugate transpose (equal to PT for real matrices), and I the identity. Columns are inputs and rows are outputs; the column headed 110 has its 1 in row 111. Toffoli is also its own inverse, P2 = I: applying it twice restores the input.

Worked example: a reversible half adder and NAND from Toffoli

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Goal: add two bits a and b reversibly, producing sum s = a ⊕ b and carry c = a·b, then check the Toffoli matrix. Convention: big-endian bit order (a, b, c); c starts as an ancilla set to 0. Circuit, in time order: step 1 Toffoli with controls a, b and target c; step 2 CNOT with control a and target b. All results were computed in Python with numpy and checked in Qiskit.

📊 FIGURE — A reversible half adder built from a Toffoli and a CNOT
Bits flow left to right: the Toffoli writes the carry a·b into the ancilla c, then the CNOT turns b into the sum a ⊕ b. The table lists all four inputs.
  1. Input (a, b, c) = (0, 0, 0). Step 1: c = 0 ⊕ 0·0 = 0. Step 2: b = 0 ⊕ 0 = 0. Output (0, 0, 0): sum 0, carry 0.
  2. Input (0, 1, 0). Step 1: c = 0 ⊕ 0 = 0. Step 2: b = 1 ⊕ 0 = 1. Output (0, 1, 0): sum 1, carry 0.
  3. Input (1, 0, 0). Step 1: c = 0 ⊕ 0 = 0. Step 2: b = 0 ⊕ 1 = 1. Output (1, 1, 0): sum 1, carry 0.
  4. Input (1, 1, 0). Step 1: c = 0 ⊕ 1 = 1. Step 2: b = 1 ⊕ 1 = 0. Output (1, 0, 1): sum 0, carry 1. The order matters: Toffoli must read b before the CNOT overwrites it.
  5. NAND from Toffoli: set the target to c = 1. It becomes 1 ⊕ a·b, which is 1, 1, 1, 0 for ab = 00, 01, 10, 11: exactly NAND. Because NAND is universal, Toffoli with ancillas can compute any Boolean function reversibly.
  6. Copying (FANOUT) from Toffoli: input (1, b, 0) gives (1, b, 0 ⊕ b) = (1, b, b).
  7. Matrix check in numpy: building P as above and computing P.T @ P gave the 8 × 8 identity, P @ P gave the identity, and P applied to basis vector 6 (|110⟩) returned basis vector 7 (|111⟩).
  8. Sanity check: the four half-adder outputs 000, 010, 110, 101 are all different, as they must be for a reversible map, and a + b = s + 2c holds in every row.

The same check in Qiskit, which runs as written:

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from qiskit.quantum_info import Statevector
qc = QuantumCircuit(3); qc.x(0); qc.x(1); qc.ccx(0, 1, 2)
print(Statevector(qc).probabilities_dict()) # {'111': 1.0}

Warning on bit order: Qiskit prints little-endian, so qubit 0 is the rightmost character. Statevector.from_label('011') means qubit 2 = 0, qubit 1 = 1, qubit 0 = 1; evolving it through ccx(0, 1, 2) gives '111' because the two controls (qubits 0 and 1) are the two rightmost 1s.

Landauer's principle: erasing costs heat, computing need not

Why care about reversibility at all? Rolf Landauer argued in 1961 that logically irreversible operations have a thermodynamic price. Erasing one bit (resetting it to 0 whatever it held) reduces the number of possible logical states by a factor of 2, and that entropy must go somewhere, as heat.

Q ≥ kB T ln 2 per erased bit

Q is the heat released to the environment, kB = 1.380649 × 10−23 J/K is Boltzmann's constant, T the temperature in kelvin, and ln 2 ≈ 0.6931. At T = 300 K this is 2.871 × 10−21 J ≈ 0.0179 eV; at 77 K it is 7.369 × 10−22 J. Today's chips dissipate far more than this per operation, so the bound is a floor in principle, not today's engineering limit. Charles Bennett showed in 1973 that any computation can be made logically reversible: compute the answer while keeping all intermediate \"garbage\" bits, copy the answer out with CNOTs, then run the computation backwards to uncompute the garbage. The uncompute trick reappears in every quantum oracle you will build.

✅ VERIFIED

Landauer's bound was confirmed experimentally by A. Bérut et al., \"Experimental verification of Landauer's principle linking information and thermodynamics\", Nature 483, 187–189 (2012), using a single colloidal particle in a modulated double-well potential; the mean dissipated heat approached kBT ln 2 for slow erasure cycles. Source: nature.com/articles/nature10872, checked 28 Sep 2026.

Why quantum gates must be reversible

In the postulates chapter you will see that a closed quantum system evolves by a unitary matrix U, one with U†U = I. A unitary always has an inverse (U†), so every quantum gate is reversible: no information is destroyed until you measure. That has three consequences you will use constantly:

  • Every classical reversible gate is a permutation matrix, hence unitary, hence a legal quantum gate. Toffoli is a quantum gate, so a quantum computer can run any classical computation, with only polynomial overhead in ancillas and gates. This is why a quantum computer is at least as powerful as a classical one.
  • An irreversible function f is loaded into a quantum computer as the reversible oracle Uf|x⟩|y⟩ = |x⟩|y ⊕ f(x)⟩, where x is the input register, y a target register and ⊕ bitwise XOR. It is its own inverse, like Toffoli.
  • Measurement is the one irreversible step. Garbage left entangled with your answer spoils interference, which is why Bennett's uncompute step is not optional in quantum algorithms.
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Thinking CNOT \"copies\" a qubit. It copies basis states (|a⟩|0⟩ → |a⟩|a⟩ for a = 0 or 1) but not superpositions; the no-cloning theorem forbids a general quantum copier. Classical FANOUT has no quantum equivalent.

Reading Landauer's principle as \"all computation costs at least kBT ln 2 per gate\". Only logically irreversible steps, such as erasure, carry the bound; reversible gates in principle do not.

Assuming a reversible gate needs fewer bits. It needs at least as many outputs as inputs, and reversible versions of AND or OR need an ancilla bit; the extra output is the price of keeping the inputs recoverable.

Mixing up bit orders: textbook |abc⟩ has a on the left; Qiskit's printed 'abc' has qubit 0 on the right.

What the exam asks

★ ON THE EXAM

Expect: fill in a truth table; build NOT, AND or OR from NAND; decide whether a gate is reversible by checking whether any two inputs share an output; apply Toffoli, Fredkin or CNOT to a given input; write a reversible gate as a permutation matrix and check PTP = I; compute kBT ln 2 at a given temperature; and explain in two sentences why unitarity forces quantum gates to be reversible and how an irreversible f becomes Uf.

Every claim of \"quantum advantage\" is a claim about complexity: that some problem needs far fewer steps on a quantum computer than on any classical one. This lesson gives you the vocabulary to read such claims precisely: Big-O notation, the classes P, NP, NP-complete, BPP and (in outline) BQP, the real status of factoring, and the query model in which most quantum speed-ups are actually proven. Its main skill is separating three kinds of statement: proven, widely believed, and open. The complexity chapter near the end of the degree returns to BQP in depth.

The idea in plain words: count steps as the input grows

We do not ask how many seconds an algorithm takes on one machine; we ask how its step count grows with the size of the input, n, measured in bits. An algorithm is efficient if its step count is bounded by a polynomial in n, such as n2 or n3. Exponential growth, such as 2n, eventually defeats any hardware improvement:

nn2n32n
101001,0001,024
204008,0001,048,576
502,500125,000≈ 1.126 × 1015
10010,0001,000,000≈ 1.268 × 1030

The crucial subtlety for quantum computing: the input size of a number N is its bit length n ≈ log2 N, not N itself. Trying every divisor up to √N sounds modest, but √N = 2n/2, which is exponential in n.

Definitions: Big-O and the main complexity classes

📘 DEFINITION

f(n) = O(g(n)) means there are constants c > 0 and n0 with f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n0 (an upper bound on growth). Ω(g) is the matching lower bound and Θ(g) means both.

A decision problem has a yes/no answer. P: decidable by a deterministic algorithm in polynomial time. NP: every yes-instance has a polynomial-length certificate that a polynomial-time verifier accepts (e.g. a satisfying assignment for a formula). coNP: the same for no-instances. NP-hard: every NP problem reduces to it in polynomial time; NP-complete: NP-hard and in NP. SAT was the first (Cook, 1971; Karp listed 21 more in 1972).

BPP: solvable in polynomial time by a randomised algorithm that answers correctly with probability at least 2/3 on every input. BQP: the same with a quantum computer (defined properly in the postulates and complexity chapters). PSPACE: solvable with polynomial memory and unlimited time. EXP: solvable in time 2poly(n).

The 2/3 in BPP is arbitrary: repeat the algorithm k times and take the majority vote, and the error falls exponentially in k. That is why a randomised (or quantum) algorithm with a bounded error is treated as \"solving\" a problem.

🧮 KEY EQUATION

P(majority wrong) = ∑j > k/2 C(k, j) εj (1 − ε)k − j

k is the (odd) number of independent repeats, ε ≤ 1/3 the error of one run, and C(k, j) the binomial coefficient. With ε = 1/3, computed in Python: k = 1 gives 0.3333, k = 3 gives 7/27 = 0.2593, k = 11 gives 0.1221, k = 51 gives 0.00689, and k = 101 gives 0.000272. The Chernoff bound guarantees exponential decay in k for any fixed ε < 1/2.

Proven, believed, open: the scorecard

Get this table right and you will avoid most of the exaggerations in popular writing about quantum computers.

📊 FIGURE — Complexity classes nested, with proven and believed facts marked
Each class sits inside the ones around it, and those containments are proven. The strict gaps (NP outside BQP, P smaller than NP) are beliefs; only P ≠ EXP is proven.
StatementStatus
P ⊆ NP ⊆ PSPACE ⊆ EXPProven
P ⊆ BPP ⊆ BQP ⊆ PP ⊆ PSPACEProven (BQP ⊆ PSPACE: Bernstein–Vazirani 1997; BQP ⊆ PP: Adleman–DeMarrais–Huang 1997)
P ≠ EXPProven (time hierarchy theorem), so at least one inclusion in the first row is strict
P ≠ NPOpen; widely believed
P = BPPOpen; widely believed (follows from plausible circuit lower bounds, Impagliazzo–Wigderson 1997)
BPP ≠ BQPOpen; believed, mainly because of Shor's algorithm
NP ⊆ BQPOpen; believed false
PRIMES ∈ PProven (Agrawal–Kayal–Saxena)
Factoring ∈ BQPProven (Shor, 1994)
Factoring ∈ POpen; no polynomial classical algorithm known
Factoring is NP-completeNot known; believed false

Note what the table implies. Because BQP ⊆ PSPACE, a proof that BPP ≠ BQP would also prove P ≠ PSPACE, itself a famous open problem. So nobody can currently prove that quantum computers are faster than classical ones for any decision problem in the ordinary (non-oracle) setting; every such claim is conditional on an unproven belief about classical hardness.

✅ VERIFIED

P versus NP is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute's seven Millennium Prize Problems (set in 2000, US$1,000,000 each) and remains unsolved: claymath.org/millennium-problems. Agrawal, Kayal and Saxena, \"PRIMES is in P\", Annals of Mathematics 160 (2004) 781–793, gives an unconditional deterministic polynomial-time primality test: microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/primes-is-in-p. RSA-250 (250 decimal digits, 829 bits) was factored in February 2020 with the number field sieve (CADO-NFS) in about 2,700 core-years by Boudot, Gaudry, Guillevic, Heninger, Thomé and Zimmermann: caramba.loria.fr/rsa250.txt. All checked 28 Sep 2026.

The status of factoring

Take the decision version: \"does N have a nontrivial factor ≤ k?\". A yes-certificate is the factor itself. A no-certificate is the full prime factorisation, whose primality can be checked in polynomial time since PRIMES ∈ P. So factoring lies in NP ∩ coNP. If any NP ∩ coNP problem were NP-complete, NP would equal coNP, which almost nobody believes; so factoring is believed not to be NP-complete. It is a problem of intermediate apparent difficulty: hard enough to protect RSA, structured enough (through periodicity) for Shor's algorithm.

The best known classical method, the general number field sieve (GNFS), has a heuristic running time (it relies on unproven but well-tested assumptions):

L(N) = exp( (64/9)1/3 (ln N)1/3 (ln ln N)2/3 (1 + o(1)) )

Here N is the number to factor, ln the natural logarithm, (64/9)1/3 ≈ 1.9230, and o(1) a term that tends to 0 as N grows. This is sub-exponential: faster than 2cn for any c, slower than any polynomial in n. No classical lower bound for factoring is known, so a fast classical algorithm has not been ruled out.

Worked example: three ways to price factoring a 2048-bit number

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Compare how trial division, the GNFS formula and Shor's algorithm scale for n = 2048 bits (a common RSA key size), using RSA-250 (n = 829) as a calibration point. Every number was computed in Python; o(1) is dropped, so the GNFS values show growth, not real operation counts.

  1. Input size: n = 2048 bits, so ln N = 2048 × ln 2 = 1419.57.
  2. Trial division tests divisors up to √N = 2n/2 = 21024: exponential in n and hopeless.
  3. GNFS exponent: (ln N)1/3 = 1419.571/3 = 11.2388; ln ln N = 7.2581, so (ln ln N)2/3 = 3.7487; product with 1.9230 gives 81.02. So L ≈ e81.02 ≈ 2116.9.
  4. Same for 829 bits: 574.621/3 = 8.3137, (ln 574.62)2/3 = 6.35372/3 = 3.4305, exponent 54.84, so L ≈ 279.1.
  5. Ratio: 2116.9 − 79.1 = 237.8 ≈ 2.4 × 1011. RSA-250 took about 2,700 core-years, so naive extrapolation puts 2048-bit keys far out of classical reach.
  6. Shor's algorithm uses a number of gates polynomial in n; textbook arithmetic gives roughly n3 = 20483 ≈ 8.6 × 109 ≈ 233 elementary operations in scaling terms (before error-correction overhead, covered in the Shor and error-correction chapters).
  7. Conclusion: quantum factoring is exponentially faster than the best known classical algorithm, not than every possible one. Sanity check: the GNFS exponent (2117) sits between the polynomial (233) and the exponential (21024), as a sub-exponential function should.

Query complexity: where speed-ups are actually proven

In the query model the input is hidden inside a black box (an oracle) and cost is the number of times you call it. Because this model is simpler, lower bounds can be proven in it, and it is where most rigorous quantum separations live.

  • Unstructured search among N items with one marked item: a classical randomised algorithm needs about N/2 queries on average (N − 1 in the deterministic worst case); Grover's algorithm needs about (π/4)√N. For N = 220 = 1,048,576 that is 524,288 expected classical queries against ⌊(π/4) × 1024⌋ = 804 quantum ones. Bennett, Bernstein, Brassard and Vazirani (1997) proved Ω(√N) queries are necessary, so the speed-up is exactly quadratic, no more.
  • Deutsch–Jozsa: 1 quantum query against 2n−1 + 1 for a deterministic classical algorithm, but a randomised algorithm succeeds with high probability after a few queries, so there is no separation from BPP.
  • Simon's problem: an exponential separation between quantum and randomised classical query complexity, proven. It is the direct ancestor of Shor's period finding.
  • For total Boolean functions (defined on every input, no promise) deterministic and quantum query complexities are polynomially related: Beals et al. (2001) proved D(f) = O(Q(f)6). Exponential query speed-ups therefore need a promise or hidden structure in the input.

So why are exponential speed-ups rare? They need structure that interference can exploit, such as a hidden period. Brute-force search over unstructured possibilities, the heart of NP-complete problems, gets at most Grover's quadratic gain in the black-box setting, and BBBV showed that relative to a random oracle NP is not contained in BQP. Even known quantum speed-ups can shrink when a clever classical algorithm is found (so-called dequantisation), which is why every advantage claim deserves a check of the best classical competitor.

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

\"A quantum computer tries all answers in parallel, so it solves NP-complete problems.\" Measurement returns one outcome; useful algorithms need interference, and NP ⊆ BQP is believed false.

\"Factoring is NP-complete\" or \"Shor proves quantum computers are exponentially faster.\" Factoring is not known (or believed) to be NP-complete, and Shor beats the best known classical algorithm, not a proven lower bound.

Measuring cost in N instead of in bits n = log2 N. An O(√N) algorithm for a number N is exponential.

Treating an oracle separation as a real-world speed-up. Query separations count oracle calls; implementing the oracle has its own cost.

What the exam asks

★ ON THE EXAM

Expect: state P, NP, NP-complete, BPP and BQP precisely; place factoring in the class diagram and justify NP ∩ coNP; say which relations are proven, believed or open (the scorecard table); compute Grover versus classical query counts; convert a cost in N to a cost in bits; and critique a claim such as \"quantum computers make every hard problem easy\" in three sentences using the words proven, believed and open.

This lesson lets you write down the state of a qubit, check that it is a legal state, turn it into measurement probabilities, and say exactly which phases change the physics and which do not. It is the first postulate of quantum mechanics, and it sits directly on top of the Dirac notation and complex numbers from the Foundations chapter; every gate, circuit and algorithm later in the degree is built on the three rules you meet here.

The idea in plain words

A classical bit is 0 or 1. A probabilistic bit (a coin you have not looked at) is described by two non-negative numbers, p0 and p1, that add to 1. A qubit is described by two complex numbers, called amplitudes, one for each classical outcome. Amplitudes are not probabilities: they can be negative or complex, and when two paths lead to the same outcome their amplitudes add, so they can cancel. That cancellation (interference) is the whole engine of quantum computing. You only ever see probabilities, and you get them by taking the squared magnitude of an amplitude.

Superposition simply means that the state is a linear combination of basis states. It does not mean the qubit is secretly 0 or secretly 1 and we are ignorant of which; the worked example below shows an experiment that tells a superposition apart from a coin toss.

Postulate 1: the state is a unit vector

📘 DEFINITION

State-space postulate. The state of an isolated quantum system is a unit vector |ψ⟩ in a complex vector space with an inner product (a Hilbert space). For one qubit the space is ℂ2, with computational basis |0⟩ = (1, 0)T and |1⟩ = (0, 1)T.

A general qubit state is |ψ⟩ = α|0⟩ + β|1⟩ with α, β ∈ ℂ and |α|² + |β|² = 1. The numbers α and β are the amplitudes; the condition is called normalisation.

For n qubits the space is ℂ2n: a state is a list of 2n amplitudes, one per bitstring, whose squared magnitudes add to 1. The chapter on multi-qubit systems develops this; here we stay with one qubit and occasionally two.

If someone hands you an unnormalised vector v, you turn it into a state by dividing by its length: |ψ⟩ = v / ‖v‖, where ‖v‖ = √(|v0|² + |v1|²). Remember that |a + ib|² = a² + b², so the modulus of a complex amplitude counts its imaginary part too.

The Born rule: from amplitudes to probabilities

🧮 KEY EQUATION

P(x) = |⟨x|ψ⟩|²

P(x) is the probability of getting outcome x when you measure in a basis that contains the unit vector |x⟩; ⟨x|ψ⟩ is the inner product (the amplitude of |x⟩ in |ψ⟩); |·|² is the squared modulus. For the computational basis this gives P(0) = |α|² and P(1) = |β|².

Two facts make the Born rule consistent. First, normalisation guarantees the probabilities in any orthonormal basis add to 1, because ∑x|⟨x|ψ⟩|² = ⟨ψ|ψ⟩ = 1. Second, the rule only depends on the modulus of each amplitude in the chosen basis, which is exactly why some phases are invisible and some are not.

Global phase versus relative phase

Global phase. Multiply the whole state by eiγ (γ a real angle). For every basis vector |x⟩, |⟨x|eiγψ⟩|² = |eiγ|²·|⟨x|ψ⟩|² = |⟨x|ψ⟩|², because |eiγ| = 1. No measurement in any basis, after any unitary, can detect γ. So |ψ⟩ and eiγ|ψ⟩ are the same physical state; strictly, a state is a ray (a vector up to a phase), and we pick one representative.

Relative phase. Now change the phase of only one component: α|0⟩ + eiφβ|1⟩. The computational-basis probabilities |α|² and |β|² do not change, but the state has changed physically: apply the Hadamard gate

H = (1/√2) ×

11
1−1

(H maps |0⟩ to |+⟩ = (|0⟩ + |1⟩)/√2 and |1⟩ to |−⟩ = (|0⟩ − |1⟩)/√2) and the two amplitudes are made to interfere. For the equal superposition with relative phase φ:

H (|0⟩ + eiφ|1⟩)/√2 = ((1 + eiφ)/2)|0⟩ + ((1 − eiφ)/2)|1⟩

P(0) = |1 + eiφ|²/4 = cos²(φ/2)

Here φ is the relative phase and the factor 1/2 is (1/√2)·(1/√2), one from the state and one from H. Values checked with numpy:

relative phase φP(0) after HP(1) after H

So the relative phase is invisible in the computational basis and fully visible after one Hadamard. Every quantum algorithm works by steering relative phases so that wrong answers cancel and right answers reinforce.

Worked example: normalise, predict, then interfere

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Convention: |0⟩ = (1,0)T, |1⟩ = (0,1)T, H = (1/√2)[[1,1],[1,−1]]. All numbers below were computed with numpy and checked with Qiskit.

📊 FIGURE — Three states with identical Z statistics that H tells apart
All three states give 0.36 / 0.64 when measured directly. After one Hadamard the relative phase (+, i, −) shows up: P(0) becomes 0.98, 0.5 or 0.02.
  1. Normalise. Start from v = 3|0⟩ + 4i|1⟩. Its length is ‖v‖ = √(|3|² + |4i|²) = √(9 + 16) = 5, so |ψ⟩ = 0.6|0⟩ + 0.8i|1⟩.
  2. Born rule in the computational basis. P(0) = |0.6|² = 0.36 and P(1) = |0.8i|² = 0.64. Sanity check: 0.36 + 0.64 = 1.
  3. Global phase. eiπ/3|ψ⟩ has amplitudes of modulus 0.6 and 0.8, so it gives the same 0.36 and 0.64, and the same numbers in every other basis too.
  4. Relative phase. Compare three states with identical computational-basis statistics: |a⟩ = 0.6|0⟩ + 0.8|1⟩, |b⟩ = 0.6|0⟩ + 0.8i|1⟩, |c⟩ = 0.6|0⟩ − 0.8|1⟩. Apply H, which sends (α, β) to ((α + β)/√2, (α − β)/√2).
  5. For |a⟩: amplitudes (1.4/√2, −0.2/√2) = (0.9899, −0.1414), so P(0) = 0.98, P(1) = 0.02.
  6. For |b⟩: amplitudes ((0.6 + 0.8i)/√2, (0.6 − 0.8i)/√2) = (0.4243 + 0.5657i, 0.4243 − 0.5657i); each has squared modulus (0.36 + 0.64)/2 = 0.5.
  7. For |c⟩: amplitudes (−0.2/√2, 1.4/√2), so P(0) = 0.02, P(1) = 0.98.

Answer: three states that look identical when measured directly give P(0) = 0.98, 0.5 and 0.02 after a Hadamard. Sanity check: each pair sums to 1.

The numpy check (run it yourself; each line is one step above):

import numpy as np

v = np.array([3, 4j]); psi = v / np.linalg.norm(v) # [0.6, 0.8j]

H = np.array([[1, 1], [1, -1]]) / np.sqrt(2)

print(np.abs(psi)**2, np.abs(H @ psi)**2) # [0.36 0.64] [0.5 0.5]

The same state in Qiskit 2.x: from qiskit.quantum_info import Statevector then Statevector([0.6, 0.8j]).probabilities_dict() returns {'0': 0.36, '1': 0.64} (the second value prints as 0.6400000000000001, ordinary floating-point rounding).

Superposition is not ignorance

Compare |+⟩ = (|0⟩ + |1⟩)/√2 with a fair classical coin that is 0 or 1 with probability 1/2 each. Measured directly, both give 50/50. Apply H first: |+⟩ becomes |0⟩ and gives 0 every time, while the coin gives H|0⟩ = |+⟩ or H|1⟩ = |−⟩ with probability 1/2 each, and either way the result is 50/50. One Hadamard separates them perfectly. The coin is a mixed state (you meet its density matrix at the end of this chapter); |+⟩ is a pure superposition.

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE
  • Adding probabilities instead of amplitudes. For |a⟩ above, averaging the probabilities of the two paths, 0.36/2 + 0.64/2, gives 0.5; the true answer is |0.6/√2 + 0.8/√2|² = 0.98. Paths combine at the amplitude level, then you square.
  • Forgetting the modulus. |0.8i|² = 0.64, not (0.8i)² = −0.64. A probability is never negative.
  • Treating −|ψ⟩ as a different state. A minus sign on the whole vector is a global phase and changes nothing. A minus sign on one component (|+⟩ versus |−⟩) is a relative phase and changes everything.
  • Skipping normalisation. With v = 3|0⟩ + 4i|1⟩ unnormalised, |3|² = 9 is not a probability.

What the exam asks

★ ON THE EXAM
  • Normalise a vector with complex entries and give the Born-rule probabilities to 4 decimal places.
  • Decide whether two given vectors describe the same physical state (they do only if one is eiγ times the other).
  • Show that a relative phase is invisible in the computational basis but changes the result after H; quote P(0) = cos²(φ/2).
  • Explain, with an experiment, why a superposition is not a classical mixture.

Method marks are given for writing the state as a column vector, naming the convention, and checking that probabilities sum to 1.

"}, "QUANTUM/postulates/s2": {"body": "

This lesson lets you predict what a measurement will return, with what probability, and what state is left behind afterwards, in the computational basis, the Hadamard basis, or any basis you choose. It is the measurement postulate, the only place in quantum mechanics where randomness and irreversibility enter; the protocols, algorithms and error-correction chapters all end with a measurement you will analyse with exactly these formulas.

The idea in plain words

A measurement asks the qubit a multiple-choice question: which of these orthogonal states are you in? The answer is random, with probabilities given by the Born rule, and the question changes the state: after you see outcome m, the state jumps to the part of the old state consistent with m, rescaled to length 1. This jump is called collapse (or state update). Asking the same question again immediately gives the same answer with certainty. Asking a different question (a different basis) can give a fresh random answer.

Postulate 3: measurement operators

📘 DEFINITION

General measurement. A measurement is a set of operators {Mm}, one per outcome m, satisfying the completeness relation ∑m Mm†Mm = I.

Projective measurement is the special case Mm = Pm, where the Pm are orthogonal projectors (PmPm′ = δmm′Pm) summing to I. Measuring in an orthonormal basis {|m⟩} means Pm = |m⟩⟨m|.

🧮 KEY EQUATION

p(m) = ⟨ψ|Mm†Mm|ψ⟩ and |ψm⟩ = Mm|ψ⟩ / √p(m)

p(m) is the probability of outcome m; |ψ⟩ is the state before measurement; Mm† is the conjugate transpose of Mm; |ψm⟩ is the post-measurement state. For a projector Pm = |m⟩⟨m| this reduces to p(m) = |⟨m|ψ⟩|² (the Born rule) and |ψm⟩ = |m⟩ up to a phase. Completeness is what makes ∑m p(m) = 1.

Two bases you will use constantly

basisvectorshow to measure it on hardware
computational (Z)|0⟩, |1⟩measure directly
Hadamard (X)|+⟩ = (|0⟩ + |1⟩)/√2, |−⟩ = (|0⟩ − |1⟩)/√2apply H, then measure; outcome 0 means +, 1 means −
circular (Y)|+i⟩ = (|0⟩ + i|1⟩)/√2, |−i⟩ = (|0⟩ − i|1⟩)/√2apply S†, then H, then measure

Hardware almost always measures only in the computational basis, so to measure in another basis you first apply the unitary that rotates that basis onto |0⟩, |1⟩. H does this for the X basis because H|+⟩ = |0⟩ and H|−⟩ = |1⟩.

Observables and expectation values

A projective measurement is often packaged as an observable: a Hermitian operator A = ∑m amPm (its spectral decomposition). The possible outcomes are the eigenvalues am, and the average over many runs is

⟨A⟩ = ∑m am p(m) = ⟨ψ|A|ψ⟩, Var(A) = ⟨A²⟩ − ⟨A⟩²

For the Pauli observable Z = |0⟩⟨0| − |1⟩⟨1| the eigenvalues are +1 (outcome 0) and −1 (outcome 1), so ⟨Z⟩ = P(0) − P(1). For X = |+⟩⟨+| − |−⟩⟨−|, ⟨X⟩ = P(+) − P(−). Since Z² = X² = I, the variance is 1 − ⟨Z⟩² (or 1 − ⟨X⟩²).

Worked example: one state, two bases, and a partial measurement

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

State |ψ⟩ = (1/√3)|0⟩ + √(2/3)|1⟩ = (0.5774, 0.8165)T. Big-endian two-qubit convention |q0 q1⟩ in part C. Computed with numpy and checked with Qiskit.

📊 FIGURE — One state measured in the Z basis and in the rotated X basis
|ψ⟩ = (0.5774, 0.8165) drawn against both pairs of axes. Its shadow on each axis is an amplitude; squared, it gives the probability of that outcome and the state left behind.
  1. A. Z basis. P(0) = |⟨0|ψ⟩|² = 1/3 = 0.3333, P(1) = 2/3 = 0.6667. Post-measurement states: |0⟩ or |1⟩. ⟨Z⟩ = 1/3 − 2/3 = −1/3 = −0.3333.
  2. B. X basis. ⟨+|ψ⟩ = (1/√3 + √(2/3))/√2 = 0.9856, so P(+) = (3 + 2√2)/6 = 0.9714. ⟨−|ψ⟩ = (1/√3 − √(2/3))/√2, so P(−) = 0.0286. Post-measurement states: |+⟩ or |−⟩. ⟨X⟩ = 0.9714 − 0.0286 = 2√2/3 = 0.9428.
  3. Check with a circuit: prepare |ψ⟩, apply H, measure in Z. Qiskit gives {'0': 0.9714, '1': 0.0286}, matching P(+) and P(−).
  4. C. Measuring one qubit of two. Take |Φ⟩ = (|00⟩ + |01⟩ + |11⟩)/√3 and measure only q0. The projector for q0 = 0 is P0 ⊗ I = |0⟩⟨0| ⊗ I, which keeps |00⟩ and |01⟩: p(0) = 2/3 = 0.6667.
  5. Post-measurement state for q0 = 0: (|00⟩ + |01⟩)/√3 divided by √(2/3) gives (|00⟩ + |01⟩)/√2 = |0⟩ ⊗ |+⟩. Note the rescaling: 1/√3 ÷ √(2/3) = 1/√2 = 0.7071.
  6. For q0 = 1: p(1) = 1/3 and the state becomes |11⟩.

Answer: P(0) = 0.3333, P(+) = 0.9714, ⟨Z⟩ = −0.3333, ⟨X⟩ = 0.9428; measuring q0 of |Φ⟩ gives 0 with probability 2/3, leaving |0⟩|+⟩. Sanity checks: each set of probabilities sums to 1, and ⟨X⟩² + ⟨Z⟩² = 8/9 + 1/9 = 1, as it must for a pure real state (see the Bloch-sphere lesson).

The numpy lines behind part C:

s = np.array([1, 1, 0, 1]) / np.sqrt(3) # order |00⟩, |01⟩, |10⟩, |11⟩

P0 = np.kron(np.diag([1, 0]), np.eye(2)) # |0⟩⟨0| on q0, identity on q1

p = np.vdot(s, P0 @ s).real; print(p, P0 @ s / np.sqrt(p)) # 0.6667 [0.7071 0.7071 0 0]

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE
  • Qiskit bit order. Qiskit is little-endian: qubit 0 is the rightmost bit and index 1 of a statevector means q0 = 1. Feed the textbook array [1, 1, 0, 1]/√3 into Statevector(...) and .probabilities([0]) returns [0.3333, 0.6667] for q0, the reverse of the textbook 2/3 : 1/3, because Qiskit reads that array as a different state. Always say which convention you use.
  • \"Measure in the X basis\" is not \"apply X, then measure\". The X gate swaps |0⟩ and |1⟩ and leaves the basis unchanged; you need H.
  • Forgetting to renormalise after collapse. (|00⟩ + |01⟩)/√3 has length √(2/3), so it is not a state until you divide.
  • Reading ⟨Z⟩ as an outcome. ⟨Z⟩ = −1/3 is an average; every individual shot returns +1 or −1.

POVMs in brief

If you only care about outcome probabilities (not the post-measurement state), all you need are the operators Em = Mm†Mm. A POVM (positive operator-valued measure) is any set of positive semidefinite Em with ∑m Em = I, and p(m) = ⟨ψ|Em|ψ⟩. The Em need not be projectors and there can be more outcomes than dimensions. A realistic example is a noisy readout that reports 0 for a true |0⟩ 95% of the time and reports 0 for a true |1⟩ 8% of the time:

E0 = 0.95|0⟩⟨0| + 0.08|1⟩⟨1|, E1 = I − E0 = 0.05|0⟩⟨0| + 0.92|1⟩⟨1|

For our |ψ⟩, p(read 0) = 0.95 × 1/3 + 0.08 × 2/3 = 0.37 instead of the ideal 0.3333. (These 95%/8% figures are illustrative numbers for the calculation, not measurements of any particular device.) Naimark's theorem says every POVM can be realised as a projective measurement on a larger system, so nothing new is being assumed.

📊 YOUR DATA EDGE

A quantum computer never hands you probabilities; it hands you shots, a sample of outcomes. Estimating ⟨Z⟩ from N shots is estimating the mean of a ±1 random variable, with standard error √(Var/N). For our state Var(Z) = 1 − 1/9 = 0.8889, so N = 1000 shots give a standard error of √(0.8889/1000) = 0.0298. One simulated run of 1000 shots returned −0.308, well within about one standard error of −0.3333.

The readout POVM above is exactly a confusion matrix, [[0.95, 0.08], [0.05, 0.92]] (columns = true state, rows = reported bit). Inverting it to correct measured frequencies is the same algebra you would use to correct a misclassification rate, and it has the same weakness: it amplifies sampling noise.

What the exam asks

★ ON THE EXAM
  • Given a state and a basis, give each outcome probability and the post-measurement state (renormalised).
  • Compute ⟨Z⟩ or ⟨X⟩ as ⟨ψ|A|ψ⟩ and as ∑ amp(m), and show they agree.
  • Measure one qubit of a two-qubit state using P ⊗ I, stating the bit order.
  • Verify completeness for a proposed set of measurement operators, or decide whether a set of operators is a valid POVM.

Examiners reward the explicit division by √p(m); a post-measurement state that is not normalised usually loses the mark.
