and CNOT with q0 as control flips q1 when q0 = 1: it maps |00⟩→|00⟩, |01⟩→|01⟩, |10⟩→|11⟩, |11⟩→|10⟩.

🧮 KEY EQUATION

Encoding a message b1b2: Alice applies Xb2 first, then Zb1, to her qubit:

(Zb1Xb2 ⊗ I) |Φ+⟩ = |βb1b2⟩

Decoding: (H ⊗ I) · CNOT · |βb1b2⟩ = |b1b2⟩

Symbols: b1, b2 ∈ {0,1} are the message bits; X0 = Z0 = I; ⊗ I means \"do nothing to Bob's qubit\"; |β00⟩ = |Φ+⟩, |β01⟩ = |Ψ+⟩, |β10⟩ = |Φ−⟩, |β11⟩ = |Ψ−⟩ (up to a global sign). The decoder is the Bell-state preparation circuit (H then CNOT) run backwards.

The whole protocol as a gate list, time running left to right:

stepq0 (Alice)q1 (Bob)who
1H—source
2control of CNOTtarget of CNOTsource
3X if b2 = 1—Alice
4Z if b1 = 1—Alice
5qubit is sent to Bob—channel
6control of CNOTtarget of CNOTBob
7H—Bob
8measure → b1measure → b2Bob

Worked example: sending the message 11

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Computed with numpy (state vectors in the order |00⟩, |01⟩, |10⟩, |11⟩; 1/√2 ≈ 0.7071). Message b1b2 = 11.

  1. Start: |00⟩ = (1, 0, 0, 0).
  2. H on q0: (|00⟩ + |10⟩)/√2 = (0.7071, 0, 0.7071, 0).
  3. CNOT q0→q1: |10⟩ becomes |11⟩, so (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2 = (0.7071, 0, 0, 0.7071) = |Φ+⟩. Qubits are now separated.
  4. Alice applies X (because b2 = 1): X flips the left bit, |00⟩→|10⟩ and |11⟩→|01⟩, giving (|01⟩ + |10⟩)/√2 = (0, 0.7071, 0.7071, 0).
  5. Alice applies Z (because b1 = 1): Z puts a minus sign on every term whose left bit is 1, giving (|01⟩ − |10⟩)/√2 = (0, 0.7071, −0.7071, 0) = |Ψ−⟩. She sends q0.
  6. Bob applies CNOT: |01⟩ stays, |10⟩→|11⟩, giving (|01⟩ − |11⟩)/√2 = (0, 0.7071, 0, −0.7071). This is (|0⟩ − |1⟩)/√2 ⊗ |1⟩, a product state.
  7. Bob applies H to q0: H(|0⟩ − |1⟩)/√2 = |1⟩, so the state is |1⟩|1⟩ = (0, 0, 0, 1).
  8. Measuring gives 11 with probability 1.

The other three messages, also computed:

messagestate after Aliceafter CNOT and HBob reads
00(0.7071, 0, 0, 0.7071) = Φ+(1, 0, 0, 0)00
01(0, 0.7071, 0.7071, 0) = Ψ+(0, 1, 0, 0)01
10(0.7071, 0, 0, −0.7071) = Φ−(0, 0, 1, 0)10
11(0, 0.7071, −0.7071, 0) = Ψ−(0, 0, 0, 1)11

Sanity check: each final vector has a single entry of modulus 1, so the probabilities sum to 1 and decoding is deterministic.

The same thing in Qiskit 2.x (message 01, so only X is applied). This runs as written:

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from qiskit.quantum_info import Statevector
qc = QuantumCircuit(2)
qc.h(0); qc.cx(0, 1)
qc.x(0)
qc.cx(0, 1); qc.h(0)
print(Statevector(qc).probabilities_dict(decimals=4))

It prints {'10': 1.0}. That is not a decoding error: Qiskit writes bitstrings little-endian, qubit 0 as the rightmost character. Read right to left, q0 = 0 and q1 = 1, which is the message 01 in our big-endian convention.

Why it does not beat the Holevo bound

Holevo's theorem says that if Alice encodes classical data into states of a system of dimension d and sends only that system, Bob can extract at most log2 d bits of information about her data. For one qubit, d = 2, so one qubit on its own carries at most one classical bit, however cleverly it is prepared and measured.

🧮 KEY EQUATION

I(X : Y) ≤ χ = S(∑x px ρx) − ∑x px S(ρx) ≤ log2 d

Symbols: I(X : Y) is the mutual information between Alice's message X and Bob's measurement result Y; ρx is the state Bob receives for message x, sent with probability px; S is the von Neumann entropy (defined properly in the information-theory chapter); χ is the Holevo quantity; d is the dimension of whatever Bob actually receives and measures.

In superdense coding the system Bob finally measures is two qubits, d = 4, and log2 4 = 2 bits, exactly what the protocol delivers. The bound is met, not beaten. The \"one qubit\" slogan hides the ebit that was distributed beforehand. The careful statement is the entanglement-assisted bound: with unlimited prior shared entanglement, each transmitted qubit can carry at most two classical bits, and superdense coding reaches that ceiling. As a resource inequality: 1 ebit + 1 qubit ≥ 2 cbits.

A second check, also computed: Bob's qubit on its own has reduced density matrix I/2 = diag(0.5, 0.5) in all four encoded states. Nothing Alice does to her qubit changes Bob's local statistics, so no information reaches Bob until her qubit physically arrives. The protocol is limited by the speed of the qubit's journey, not faster.

✅ VERIFIED

The protocol was introduced in C. H. Bennett and S. J. Wiesner, \"Communication via one- and two-particle operators on Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen states\", Physical Review Letters 69(20), 2881-2884 (1992), doi 10.1103/PhysRevLett.69.2881. Source: bibliographic record. Checked 28 Sep 2026.

The traps

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE
  • Forgetting the H in the decoder. For message 01, CNOT alone leaves (|01⟩ + |11⟩)/√2, so Bob gets 01 or 11 with probability 0.5 each (computed). CNOT alone does not complete a Bell measurement.
  • Reading Qiskit output big-endian. Message 01 prints as '10'. Always say which convention your bitstrings use.
  • \"Alice's gate changes Bob's qubit instantly.\" It changes the joint state, but Bob's reduced state stays I/2. Only the pair, once reunited, reveals the message.
  • \"Two bits per qubit, so quantum channels double capacity for free.\" Every message spends one ebit, and that ebit had to be distributed through a quantum channel too.
  • Swapping the roles of X and Z. X fixes the parity bit (whether the two qubits agree), Z fixes the sign bit. With our decoder, Z goes with b1, X with b2. Applying XZ instead of ZX only changes a global sign, which is harmless.

What the exam asks

★ ON THE EXAM
  • Write the circuit and give the state after each gate for a named message (as in the worked example).
  • Show that the four encoded states are orthonormal, which is why decoding is error-free.
  • Explain why it does not contradict Holevo: count the qubits Bob measures (two), and name the ebit as a pre-shared resource.
  • Show that Bob's reduced state is I/2 before Alice's qubit arrives, so there is no signalling.
  • Compare with teleportation: dense coding turns 1 ebit + 1 qubit into 2 bits; teleportation turns 1 ebit + 2 bits into 1 qubit.

Teleportation moves an unknown qubit state from Alice to Bob without sending the qubit itself: they spend one shared Bell pair and two classical bits. After this lesson you can derive the protocol algebraically, run it on a concrete state with every amplitude shown, choose Bob's correction from Alice's two bits, explain why it sends nothing faster than light, and extend it to entanglement swapping, the building block of quantum repeaters. It is the reverse of superdense coding and reappears in error correction (gate teleportation) and in the networks chapter.

The idea in plain words

Alice holds a qubit in some state |ψ⟩ = α|0⟩ + β|1⟩ that nobody knows. She cannot measure it to learn α and β (one measurement gives one bit and destroys the rest), and she cannot copy it (no-cloning). What she can do is entangle it with her half of a Bell pair shared with Bob, then measure her two qubits in the Bell basis. That measurement gives two random bits and, at the same instant, leaves Bob's qubit in one of four states, each equal to |ψ⟩ up to a known Pauli gate. Alice phones Bob with the two bits; Bob undoes the Pauli; he now holds |ψ⟩. Alice's copy has been destroyed by her measurement, so no cloning occurred.

📘 DEFINITION

Quantum teleportation (Bennett, Brassard, Crépeau, Jozsa, Peres and Wootters) is the protocol that transfers an arbitrary, unknown one-qubit state from sender to receiver by consuming one ebit and two classical bits, using only local operations on each side plus classical communication (LOCC).

Resource statement: 1 ebit + 2 cbits ≥ 1 qubit. Compare superdense coding: 1 ebit + 1 qubit ≥ 2 cbits.

The circuit and the key equation

Three qubits, big-endian order |q0 q1 q2⟩: q0 holds |ψ⟩ (Alice), q1 is Alice's half of the pair, q2 is Bob's half. Gates in time order:

📊 FIGURE — Teleportation circuit: Bell pair, Bell measurement, two bits, fix-up
Double lines are classical wires: Alice's results m₁, m₂ travel to Bob and switch his X and Z on or off. Each outcome has probability 1/4, and after the correction Bob holds |ψ⟩ in every branch.
stepq0 (|ψ⟩, Alice)q1 (Alice)q2 (Bob)
1—H—
2—control of CNOTtarget (now q1,q2 are |Φ+⟩)
3control of CNOTtarget—
4H——
5measure → m1measure → m2— (waits for the bits)
6——X if m2 = 1, then Z if m1 = 1

Steps 3 to 5 are exactly the Bell measurement from the previous lesson. The algebra hinges on one regrouping identity, which you should be able to derive by expanding both sides:

🧮 KEY EQUATION

After steps 1-4 the three-qubit state is

(1/2) ∑m1,m2 |m1 m2⟩ ⊗ Xm2Zm1|ψ⟩

Written out: (1/2)[ |00⟩(α|0⟩ + β|1⟩) + |01⟩(α|1⟩ + β|0⟩) + |10⟩(α|0⟩ − β|1⟩) + |11⟩(α|1⟩ − β|0⟩) ]

Bob's correction: Zm1Xm2 · Xm2Zm1|ψ⟩ = |ψ⟩

Symbols: m1 is Alice's result on q0 and controls Z; m2 is her result on q1 and controls X; α, β ∈ ℂ with |α|2 + |β|2 = 1; the 1/2 in front means each of the four outcomes has probability (1/2)2 = 1/4, independent of α and β.

Worked example: teleporting |ψ⟩ = 0.6|0⟩ + 0.8i|1⟩

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Computed with numpy; amplitudes listed for |000⟩, |001⟩, |010⟩, |011⟩, |100⟩, |101⟩, |110⟩, |111⟩ (q0 q1 q2). Check first: |0.6|2 + |0.8i|2 = 0.36 + 0.64 = 1. Its Bloch vector is (0, 0.96, −0.28).

  1. Start: |ψ⟩ ⊗ |Φ+⟩ = 0.6 × 0.7071 (|000⟩ + |011⟩) + 0.8i × 0.7071 (|100⟩ + |111⟩), i.e. amplitudes 0.4243 on |000⟩ and |011⟩, 0.5657i on |100⟩ and |111⟩, zero elsewhere.
  2. CNOT q0→q1 flips q1 wherever q0 = 1: |100⟩→|110⟩ and |111⟩→|101⟩. Now 0.4243 on |000⟩, |011⟩ and 0.5657i on |101⟩, |110⟩.
  3. H on q0 sends |0⟩ → (|0⟩ + |1⟩)/√2 and |1⟩ → (|0⟩ − |1⟩)/√2, multiplying every amplitude by 0.7071 and splitting it: the vector becomes (0.3, 0.4i, 0.4i, 0.3, 0.3, −0.4i, −0.4i, 0.3).
  4. Group by Alice's bits (first two positions) and read Bob's amplitudes, then renormalise by dividing by 1/2:

m1m2probabilityBob holdsBob appliesBob ends with
000.250.6|0⟩ + 0.8i|1⟩I0.6|0⟩ + 0.8i|1⟩
010.250.8i|0⟩ + 0.6|1⟩X0.6|0⟩ + 0.8i|1⟩
100.250.6|0⟩ − 0.8i|1⟩Z0.6|0⟩ + 0.8i|1⟩
110.25−0.8i|0⟩ + 0.6|1⟩X then Z0.6|0⟩ + 0.8i|1⟩

Final answer: in every branch Bob ends with 0.6|0⟩ + 0.8i|1⟩; fidelity |⟨ψ|ψBob⟩|2 = 1.0000. Sanity check: four branches of probability 0.25 sum to 1, and each renormalised Bob state has 0.36 + 0.64 = 1.

The same run in Qiskit, with the measurements replaced by controlled gates (the deferred measurement principle: a classically controlled X or Z after measuring equals a quantum-controlled one before measuring). This runs as written and prints 1.0:

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from qiskit.quantum_info import Statevector, partial_trace, state_fidelity
qc = QuantumCircuit(3)
qc.initialize([0.6, 0.8j], 0)
qc.h(1); qc.cx(1, 2)
qc.cx(0, 1); qc.h(0)
qc.cx(1, 2); qc.cz(0, 2)
bob = partial_trace(Statevector(qc), [0, 1])
print(round(state_fidelity(bob, Statevector([0.6, 0.8j])), 6))

Qiskit indexes qubits the same way here (qubit 0 holds |ψ⟩), but any bitstring it prints is little-endian: outcome m1m2 = 01 appears with q2 on the left and q0 on the right.

Why nothing travels faster than light

Right after Alice measures, but before her bits arrive, Bob does not know which of the four branches he is in. Averaging over them, his qubit's density matrix is

ρBob = (1/4) ∑ P|ψ⟩⟨ψ|P† = I/2

(computed: diag(0.5, 0.5) for our example). I/2 is the same state he had before Alice did anything, so no measurement Bob makes can detect whether, when, or what Alice teleported. For our |ψ⟩, if Bob skips the correction his fidelity per branch is 1, 0, 0.0784 and 0.9216, averaging exactly 0.5, no better than guessing a random state. The two classical bits, limited by the speed of light, are what turn noise into |ψ⟩. Two bits are also necessary: if one bit sufficed, Alice could teleport a qubit prepared by superdense coding and so push two classical bits through a one-bit channel, which is impossible.

Entanglement swapping

Teleportation works on any qubit, including one that is itself entangled. Let Alice share |Φ+⟩ with a middle station (qubits A, B1) and the station share |Φ+⟩ with Charlie (qubits B2, C). The station makes a Bell measurement on B1 and B2. A and C, which never interacted, end up in a Bell state (computed in numpy, each outcome with probability 0.25):

station outcomestate of A and C
00|Φ+⟩
01|Ψ+⟩
10|Φ−⟩
11|Ψ−⟩

After the station announces its two bits, Charlie can apply a Pauli to turn the pair into |Φ+⟩. Chaining this across many stations extends entanglement over distances too lossy for a single photon: that is the core of a quantum repeater. It is also how the Delft 2015 Bell test (next lesson) heralded entanglement between distant electron spins.

✅ VERIFIED

The protocol is from C. H. Bennett, G. Brassard, C. Crépeau, R. Jozsa, A. Peres and W. K. Wootters, \"Teleporting an unknown quantum state via dual classical and Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen channels\", Physical Review Letters 70, 1895 (1993). Source: APS record.

The 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics went to Alain Aspect, John F. Clauser and Anton Zeilinger \"for experiments with entangled photons, establishing the violation of Bell inequalities and pioneering quantum information science\"; the Nobel summary credits Zeilinger's group with demonstrating quantum teleportation. Source: NobelPrize.org. Both checked 28 Sep 2026.

The traps

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE
  • Mixing up which bit controls which gate. With this circuit, m1 (from the qubit that got the H) controls Z, and m2 controls X. Swapping them fails on outcomes 01 and 10.
  • Worrying about X-then-Z versus Z-then-X. For outcome 11, XZ instead of ZX gives −|ψ⟩ (computed: −0.6|0⟩ − 0.8i|1⟩). That is a global phase, physically identical. A relative phase error would matter; this is not one.
  • \"Teleportation is faster than light.\" Bob's state is I/2 until the classical bits arrive.
  • \"Teleportation copies the state.\" Alice's qubit is left in |m1⟩, a computational-basis state with no trace of α, β. Exactly one copy exists at the end.
  • \"Alice learns α and β.\" Her outcomes are uniformly random, probability 1/4 each, whatever |ψ⟩ is.
  • Forgetting the 1/2 in the regrouped state. Without it the four branch probabilities would sum to 4.

What the exam asks

★ ON THE EXAM
  • Derive the regrouped state for general α, β by expanding |ψ⟩|Φ+⟩, applying CNOT and H, and collecting terms by Alice's bits.
  • Given m1m2, write Bob's uncorrected state and the correction.
  • Prove no signalling by computing Bob's averaged density matrix, I/2.
  • Explain consistency with no-cloning: the original is destroyed by the measurement.
  • Entanglement swapping: show which Bell state the outer qubits share for a given middle outcome.
  • Count resources and contrast with superdense coding.

Bell's theorem is the reason entanglement is a resource and not just correlated coin flips. This lesson turns it into a game you can score: two separated players, a classical ceiling of 75% wins, a quantum strategy that reaches about 85.4%, and a proof that nothing quantum can do better. After it you can prove the CHSH inequality, compute S for any measurement angles, find the optimal angles, and judge what the 2015 loophole-free experiments did and did not establish. The CHSH game returns later in device-independent cryptography (security chapter) and in the complexity chapter.

The idea in plain words

A referee sends Alice a random bit x and Bob a random bit y. They are far apart and cannot talk once play starts. Alice answers a bit a, Bob answers b. They win if a ⊕ b = x · y: their answers must agree unless both got 1, in which case they must differ. They may agree a strategy in advance and share anything they like, including random numbers. Einstein-style \"hidden variables\" are exactly such a shared, pre-arranged instruction set. Bell's insight was that any such set obeys a numerical limit, and entangled qubits exceed it.

📘 DEFINITION

A local hidden variable (LHV) model assigns each run a shared variable λ, drawn from a distribution p(λ) that does not depend on the settings (measurement independence), and outcome functions A(x, λ), B(y, λ) ∈ {+1, −1}, where Alice's outcome does not depend on Bob's setting y and vice versa (locality).

The correlator E(x, y) is the average of the product of the ±1 outcomes for settings x, y: E = P(same) − P(different). A Bell inequality is a bound on combinations of correlators that every LHV model obeys.

The CHSH inequality and its proof

🧮 KEY EQUATION

S = E(0,0) + E(0,1) + E(1,0) − E(1,1)

LHV: |S| ≤ 2 quantum: |S| ≤ 2√2 ≈ 2.8284 (Tsirelson) Pwin = 1/2 + S/8

Symbols: E(x, y) is the correlator for Alice's setting x and Bob's setting y; the one minus sign sits on the (1,1) pair, the only pair that must disagree. With outcome a = 0 written as +1 and a = 1 as −1, \"win\" means product +1 on three pairs and −1 on the fourth, hence Pwin = (1/4) ∑ (1 ± E)/2 = 1/2 + S/8.

Proof of the classical bound. Fix λ. Write A0, A1, B0, B1 for the four ±1 answers. Then

A0B0 + A0B1 + A1B0 − A1B1 = A0(B0 + B1) + A1(B0 − B1)

Since B0, B1 = ±1, one bracket is 0 and the other is ±2, so the expression is ±2 for every λ. Averaging over λ cannot leave [−2, 2], so |S| ≤ 2. A brute-force enumeration in Python of all 24 = 16 deterministic strategies confirms the maximum is 2, reached by 8 of them (for example, \"always answer +1\"). Shared randomness is just a mixture of these 16 and cannot help. Hence Pwin ≤ 1/2 + 2/8 = 0.75.

The quantum strategy and the optimal angles

Share |Φ+⟩. Each player measures a spin along a direction in the x-z plane of the Bloch sphere at angle θ from the z axis, the observable

📊 FIGURE — Optimal CHSH angles in the x-z plane of the Bloch sphere
The four directions sit 45° apart, so three setting pairs have E = cos 45° and the (1, 1) pair, 135° apart, has E = −0.7071. That gives S = 2√2 and a win rate of 0.8536.

A(θ) = cos θ · Z + sin θ · X

with eigenvalues ±1. For |Φ+⟩ the correlator is E(a, b) = ⟨Φ+| A(a) ⊗ A(b) |Φ+⟩ = cos(a − b), where a and b are Alice's and Bob's Bloch angles. To make three terms large and the fourth very negative, spread the four directions 45° apart: Alice uses a0 = 0° (Z) and a1 = 90° (X); Bob uses b0 = 45° and b1 = −45°, that is B0 = (Z + X)/√2 and B1 = (Z − X)/√2.

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Computed with numpy by building A(θ) ⊗ A(φ) and taking ⟨Φ+| · |Φ+⟩:

pair (x, y)Alice angleBob anglea − bE = cos(a − b)sign in S
(0, 0)0°45°−45°0.7071+
(0, 1)0°−45°45°0.7071+
(1, 0)90°45°45°0.7071+
(1, 1)90°−45°135°−0.7071−

  1. S = 0.7071 + 0.7071 + 0.7071 − (−0.7071) = 4 × 0.7071 = 2.8284 = 2√2, above the classical 2.
  2. Pwin = 1/2 + 2.8284/8 = 0.8536, which equals cos2(π/8) (both computed as 0.853553).
  3. Why no quantum strategy beats this: the CHSH operator A0⊗(B0+B1) + A1⊗(B0−B1) for these angles has eigenvalues −2.8284, 0, 0, +2.8284 (numpy eigvalsh). In general, squaring the operator gives 4I − [A0, A1] ⊗ [B0, B1], whose norm is at most 8, so |S| ≤ √8 = 2√2: Tsirelson's bound.
  4. Contrast with poor choices: all four angles 0° gives S = 1 + 1 + 1 − 1 = 2 (merely classical); Alice {0°, 90°} with Bob {0°, 90°} gives S = 1 + 0 + 0 − 1 = 0.

Sanity check: each |E| ≤ 1, and Alice's own outcome is ±1 with probability 0.5 each for every setting, so no message is encoded in her marginals.

Noise: mix the Bell state with white noise, ρ = v|Φ+⟩⟨Φ+| + (1 − v)I/4. Every correlator is scaled by v, so S = 2√2 v. Computed: v = 0.9 gives 2.5456, v = 0.8 gives 2.2627, v = 0.7 gives 1.9799. A violation needs v > 1/√2 ≈ 0.7071, a useful benchmark for real hardware.

Loopholes and the 2015 experiments

A real test must make the LHV assumptions physically unavoidable. The main loopholes:

  • Locality: each side's setting choice and measurement must finish before light from the other side's choice could arrive (space-like separation).
  • Detection (fair sampling): if many particles are lost, an LHV model can fake S > 2 by choosing which runs get detected. Closing it needs high-efficiency detection or heralded (event-ready) trials.
  • Freedom of choice (measurement independence): settings must be independent of λ; fast random number generators are used. This one can be pushed back but never fully proven; theories that reject it are called superdeterministic.
  • Memory: devices may remember earlier runs; handled by the statistical analysis rather than assumed away.
✅ VERIFIED

Delft (Hensen et al., Nature 526, 682-686, 2015): electron spins in diamond separated by 1.3 km, entanglement heralded by an event-ready scheme; 245 trials gave S = 2.42 ± 0.20, with probability at most P = 0.039 that a local-realist model could produce a violation at least that large, allowing for memory. Source: Nature and arXiv:1508.05949. The heralding worked by entanglement swapping of photons at a station between the sites: arXiv:2101.05370.

Vienna (Giustina et al., Physical Review Letters 115, 250401, 2015): entangled photons with superconducting detectors; the probability of the result under local realism was reported as at most 3.74 × 10−31 (an 11.5 standard deviation effect). Source: APS.

NIST Boulder (Shalm et al., \"Strong Loophole-Free Test of Local Realism\", Physical Review Letters 115, 250402, 2015): entangled photons with space-like separated, fast random setting choices. Source: APS.

CHSH inequality: Clauser, Horne, Shimony and Holt, Physical Review Letters 23, 880 (1969), Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. All checked 28 Sep 2026.

❓ NOT VERIFIED

An event-ready Bell test with entangled atoms (Rosenfeld et al., Physical Review Letters 119, 010402, 2017) is reported to have closed the detection and locality loopholes together; search snippets quoted S = 2.221 ± 0.033, but I could not tie that number to the paper reliably. Confirm before you rely on this.

📊 YOUR DATA EDGE

An S value is a sample statistic, so read it like one. Each trial's product of outcomes is ±1 with mean E, so its variance is 1 − E2. With N trials per setting pair, SD(S) ≈ √(4(1 − E2)/N). At the ideal E = 0.7071 and N ≈ 61 per pair (245 trials in total) this gives 0.18, close to Delft's quoted ± 0.20; with N = 1,000 per pair it drops to 0.045. A seeded simulation of 1,000 trials per pair gave S = 2.846.

So Delft's P = 0.039 is modest evidence from a tiny sample (the price of the hardest loopholes closed), while the photon experiments had huge samples. Always ask: how many trials, what p-value, and which assumptions (fair sampling, memory) the test depends on.

The traps

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE
  • Bloch angle versus polariser angle. For photon polarisation a polariser at angle φ corresponds to Bloch angle 2φ, so the optimal settings are 0°, 45° (Alice) and 22.5°, −22.5° (Bob) on the bench.
  • Singlet sign. For |Ψ−⟩, E(a, b) = −cos(a − b) (computed: −1 at equal angles). Flip Bob's outcomes or signs accordingly.
  • \"S > 2 means faster-than-light signalling.\" Each player's marginal statistics are 50/50 whatever the other does; the correlation is only visible when results are compared over a classical channel.
  • Using the maximum algebraic value 4. Four ±1 terms could naively sum to 4, but no LHV model exceeds 2 and no quantum state exceeds 2√2.
  • Dropping the minus sign. Without it, S = E00 + E01 + E10 + E11 tests nothing.

What the exam asks

★ ON THE EXAM
  • Prove |S| ≤ 2 for LHV models by the bracket argument.
  • Compute E(a, b) and S for given angles and state; convert S to a win probability.
  • State Tsirelson's bound 2√2 and give the optimal angles.
  • Find the visibility threshold 1/√2 for a noisy Bell state.
  • Name the locality, detection and freedom-of-choice loopholes and how 2015 experiments closed them.
  • Explain why a Bell violation does not allow signalling.

This lesson lets you build the \"black box\" that almost every textbook quantum algorithm is phrased around, turn it into a phase oracle with the |−⟩ trick, and run the first quantum algorithm ever written down: Deutsch's algorithm, which answers a question about a function with one query where a classical computer needs two. It sits right after multi-qubit gates and entanglement in the degree; everything later (Deutsch-Jozsa, Bernstein-Vazirani, Simon, Grover, and the order-finding core of Shor) reuses the oracle and phase-kickback ideas you meet here.

The idea in plain words: counting questions, not seconds

Imagine a colleague holds a function f that you may not read, only call. Each call costs you one query. Query complexity asks: how many calls do you need, at minimum, to answer some question about f? We ignore all the other work you do between calls. This sounds artificial, but it is the one setting where computer scientists can prove lower bounds, so it is where the first rigorous quantum-versus-classical separations live.

The quantum twist: a quantum computer is allowed to call the same box on a superposition of inputs. That does not mean it \"learns every value at once\" (a measurement still returns only a few bits). It means the answers can interfere, and a clever circuit arranges the interference so the one global property you want survives while everything else cancels.

Bit oracles: the reversible way to call a function

📘 DEFINITION

For a Boolean function f: {0,1}n → {0,1}, the bit oracle (also called the standard or XOR oracle) is the unitary Uf acting on an n-qubit input register and a 1-qubit target:

Uf|x⟩|y⟩ = |x⟩|y ⊕ f(x)⟩

Here x is an n-bit string, y ∈ {0,1} is the target bit, and ⊕ is addition mod 2 (XOR). One application of Uf counts as one query, whether the input is a basis state or a superposition.

Why XOR instead of simply writing f(x) into the target? A quantum gate must be unitary, hence reversible. The map |x⟩ → |f(x)⟩ is not reversible when f is constant (two inputs land on the same output). XOR-ing into a separate target keeps x and lets you undo the call: applying Uf twice gives y ⊕ f(x) ⊕ f(x) = y, so Uf is its own inverse. In matrix form Uf is a permutation matrix: it only shuffles basis states.

For one input bit there are exactly four functions, and each oracle is a gate you already know (basis order |x y⟩ = |00⟩, |01⟩, |10⟩, |11⟩, input qubit first):

Namef(0), f(1)TypeUf as a circuit
f00, 0constantidentity (do nothing)
f11, 1constantX on the target
f20, 1 (f(x) = x)balancedCNOT, input controls target
f31, 0 (f(x) = NOT x)balancedCNOT, then X on the target

The matrix of Uf2 (printed by numpy from the definition) is the CNOT matrix, rows and columns in the order |00⟩, |01⟩, |10⟩, |11⟩:

1000
0100
0001
0010

It swaps |10⟩ and |11⟩ because f(1) = 1 flips the target only when x = 1.

Phase oracles and the |−⟩ trick (phase kickback)

Many algorithms want the answer as a sign, not as a bit. Put the target in |−⟩ = (|0⟩ − |1⟩)/√2 and watch what the bit oracle does:

  1. If f(x) = 0 the target is untouched: |x⟩|−⟩.
  2. If f(x) = 1 the target gets an X, and X|−⟩ = (|1⟩ − |0⟩)/√2 = −|−⟩, so the state becomes −|x⟩|−⟩.
  3. Both cases in one line: the target is unchanged and a sign (−1)f(x) appears. Because a scalar can be moved onto either factor of a tensor product, we may say the sign now belongs to the input register: it has been kicked back.
🧮 KEY EQUATION

Uf|x⟩|−⟩ = (−1)f(x)|x⟩|−⟩

Dropping the idle |−⟩ gives the phase oracle Of|x⟩ = (−1)f(x)|x⟩, a diagonal matrix with ±1 on the diagonal. On a superposition ∑x αx|x⟩ it multiplies each amplitude αx by (−1)f(x). Symbols: x the input string, f(x) ∈ {0,1} the function value, |−⟩ the target state, which ends exactly where it began, unentangled.

Numpy check (bit oracle built from the definition, applied to |x⟩|−⟩, vector in the order |00⟩, |01⟩, |10⟩, |11⟩): for f2(x) = x, input |0⟩|−⟩ returns (0.7071, −0.7071, 0, 0) = +|0⟩|−⟩, and input |1⟩|−⟩ returns (0, 0, −0.7071, 0.7071) = −|1⟩|−⟩. The sign appears exactly where f(x) = 1.

A single phase (−1)f(x) on a basis state is a global phase and is invisible. It only becomes useful when the input is a superposition, because then different branches get different signs: a relative phase, which a later Hadamard can turn into a measurable difference.

Deutsch's problem and the algorithm

📘 DEFINITION

Deutsch's problem: given oracle access to f: {0,1} → {0,1}, decide whether f is constant (f(0) = f(1)) or balanced (f(0) ≠ f(1)). Equivalently, compute the single bit f(0) ⊕ f(1).

📊 FIGURE — Deutsch's algorithm: one query decides constant or balanced
With the target in |−⟩ the oracle stamps (−1)^f(x) on the query qubit, making it ±|+⟩ or ±|−⟩. The last H turns that into 0 (constant) or 1 (balanced) with certainty; the global sign is invisible.

The circuit uses two qubits, qubit 0 (the query qubit) and qubit 1 (the target), one query, and three kinds of gate:

Time stepQubit 0 (query)Qubit 1 (target)
0 (prepare)|0⟩|1⟩ (X applied to |0⟩)
1HH
2Uf (qubit 0 is the input x, qubit 1 the target y)
3H(idle)
4measure(ignore)

Algebra, one line per step (convention: |0⟩ = (1,0)T, H = (1/√2)[[1,1],[1,−1]], input qubit written first):

  1. |ψ0⟩ = |0⟩|1⟩
  2. |ψ1⟩ = (H⊗H)|0⟩|1⟩ = |+⟩|−⟩ = (|00⟩ − |01⟩ + |10⟩ − |11⟩)/2
  3. Kickback on each branch: |ψ2⟩ = [(−1)f(0)|0⟩ + (−1)f(1)|1⟩]/√2 ⊗ |−⟩
  4. Factor out (−1)f(0): the query qubit is (−1)f(0)·(|0⟩ + (−1)f(0)⊕f(1)|1⟩)/√2, which is ±|+⟩ if f is constant and ±|−⟩ if f is balanced.
  5. H maps |+⟩ → |0⟩ and |−⟩ → |1⟩, so |ψ3⟩ = (−1)f(0)|f(0) ⊕ f(1)⟩ ⊗ |−⟩
  6. Measure qubit 0: outcome 0 means constant, 1 means balanced, with probability 1.
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

All four oracles simulated in numpy (state vectors in the order |00⟩, |01⟩, |10⟩, |11⟩; Uf built entry by entry from Uf|x y⟩ = |x, y ⊕ f(x)⟩). Every row starts from |ψ1⟩ = (0.5, −0.5, 0.5, −0.5).

f|ψ2⟩ after Uf|ψ3⟩ after H on qubit 0P(qubit 0 = 0)
f0 (0,0)(0.5, −0.5, 0.5, −0.5)(0.7071, −0.7071, 0, 0) = |0⟩|−⟩1
f1 (1,1)(−0.5, 0.5, −0.5, 0.5)(−0.7071, 0.7071, 0, 0) = −|0⟩|−⟩1
f2 (0,1)(0.5, −0.5, −0.5, 0.5)(0, 0, 0.7071, −0.7071) = |1⟩|−⟩0
f3 (1,0)(−0.5, 0.5, 0.5, −0.5)(0, 0, −0.7071, 0.7071) = −|1⟩|−⟩0

The overall sign in the third column is (−1)f(0), exactly as the algebra predicts, and it is a global phase that no measurement can see. Sanity check: each final vector has two entries of size 0.7071, and 0.7071² + 0.7071² = 1.

The same run in Qiskit 2.x for f2 (the oracle is one CNOT):

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from qiskit.quantum_info import Statevector
qc = QuantumCircuit(2)
qc.x(1); qc.h(0); qc.h(1)
qc.cx(0, 1) # U_f for f(x) = x
qc.h(0)
print(Statevector.from_instruction(qc).probabilities_dict())

Output (rounded; the zero entries print as round-off of about 5 × 10−34): {'00': 0.0, '01': 0.5, '10': 0.0, '11': 0.5}. Qiskit writes bitstrings little-endian: qubit 0 is the rightmost bit. Both surviving strings end in 1, so qubit 0 reads 1 with certainty: balanced. The left bit is the target qubit in |−⟩, which is 50/50 and carries no information. Asking for probabilities_dict(qargs=[0]) prints qubit 0 alone: {'0': 0.0, '1': 1.0} (rounded).

What the speed-up is, and against which classical model

A classical algorithm can only feed basis states into the same box. With one classical query it learns one of f(0), f(1), and the other value is still free, so both \"constant\" and \"balanced\" remain possible. A deterministic classical algorithm therefore needs 2 queries. A randomized classical algorithm limited to one query can do no better than guessing the missing value: worst-case success probability 1/2. The quantum algorithm uses 1 query and succeeds with probability 1.

So the separation is 2 versus 1: a constant factor, of no practical use. Its importance is conceptual: it is the smallest demonstration that interference between branches of a superposition can extract a global property (the parity f(0) ⊕ f(1)) using fewer queries than any classical procedure. Note what it does not do: it does not reveal f(0) and f(1) individually. You get exactly one bit, and it is the parity.

✅ VERIFIED

David Deutsch posed this problem in \"Quantum theory, the Church-Turing principle and the universal quantum computer\", Proc. R. Soc. A 400, 97-117 (1985), Royal Society. His original method gave only a partial (sometimes-inconclusive) answer; the one-query, probability-1 circuit taught here is the version in Cleve, Ekert, Macchiavello and Mosca, \"Quantum algorithms revisited\", Proc. R. Soc. A 454, 339-354 (1998), arXiv:quant-ph/9708016; history summarised in arXiv:quant-ph/0610220. Checked 28 Sep 2026.

The traps

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE
  • Target left in |0⟩. Without X then H on the target there is no kickback: Uf writes f into the target and entangles the two qubits. Numpy with target |0⟩ gives P(qubit 0 = 0) = 0.5 for both balanced functions, so the algorithm fails half the time.
  • H then X instead of X then H. H|0⟩ = |+⟩ and X|+⟩ = |+⟩, so the target is |+⟩, an eigenstate of X with eigenvalue +1. No sign is kicked back and qubit 0 always reads 0, for every f (checked in numpy).
  • \"It computes f(0) and f(1) at the same time.\" One measurement gives one bit. You learn f(0) ⊕ f(1), never both values.
  • Reading the wrong Qiskit bit. In '01' the rightmost character is qubit 0. Reading the left bit gives the target, which is random.
  • Treating (−1)f(0) as information. It is a global phase on the final state; only the relative phase between |0⟩ and |1⟩ in step 4 matters.
★ ON THE EXAM

Expect to: (1) write Uf as a 4×4 permutation matrix for a given f; (2) derive Uf|x⟩|−⟩ = (−1)f(x)|x⟩|−⟩ in two lines using X|−⟩ = −|−⟩; (3) write |ψ1⟩, |ψ2⟩, |ψ3⟩ for the Deutsch circuit and read off the answer; (4) state the classical cost precisely: 2 queries deterministic, success 1/2 with one randomized query, versus 1 exact quantum query. Markers reward saying \"global phase, unobservable\" when a minus sign appears on the whole state.

This lesson scales Deutsch's one-bit trick up to n-bit functions. You will learn the single identity behind every algorithm in this chapter (what n Hadamards do to a basis state), use it to solve the Deutsch-Jozsa problem and the Bernstein-Vazirani problem with one query each, run both on 3- and 4-qubit instances, and, most importantly for an exam or a job interview, say exactly which classical model each speed-up beats and which it does not. It builds on the phase oracle from the previous lesson and sets up Simon's algorithm next.

The idea in plain words

Put all 2n inputs in equal superposition, let the phase oracle stamp a sign (−1)f(x) on each one, then apply Hadamards again. The final Hadamards act like a \"pattern detector\": the amplitude of each output string y measures how well the sign pattern of f matches the pattern (−1)x·y. If f matches one pattern perfectly, you see that y with certainty. If f matches the all-plus pattern (f constant), you see 00…0.

The Hadamard identity

🧮 KEY EQUATION

H⊗n|x⟩ = (1/√2n) ∑y ∈ {0,1}n (−1)x·y |y⟩

Symbols: x and y are n-bit strings; H⊗n is a Hadamard on each of the n qubits; x·y = x0y0 ⊕ x1y1 ⊕ … ⊕ xn−1yn−1 is the bitwise inner product mod 2 (AND the bits, then take the parity). Special case x = 0…0: every sign is +, giving the uniform superposition.

Why it holds: one Hadamard gives H|xi⟩ = (|0⟩ + (−1)xi|1⟩)/√2 = (1/√2)∑yi(−1)xiyi|yi⟩. Take the tensor product over i; the signs multiply, and multiplying signs adds exponents mod 2. Numpy check for x = 101: √8·H⊗3|101⟩ = (1, −1, 1, −1, −1, 1, −1, 1) over y = 000, 001, …, 111. For example y = 101 gives x·y = 1 ⊕ 0 ⊕ 1 = 0, a plus sign.

Because H⊗n is its own inverse, the identity also runs backwards: the state (1/√2n)∑x(−1)s·x|x⟩ is mapped by H⊗n to exactly |s⟩. That single fact is the Bernstein-Vazirani algorithm.

The Deutsch-Jozsa problem and circuit

📘 DEFINITION

f: {0,1}n → {0,1} is constant if it gives the same value on all 2n inputs and balanced if it outputs 0 on exactly half the inputs (2n−1 of them) and 1 on the other half. The Deutsch-Jozsa problem is a promise problem: you are guaranteed f is one of the two, and must say which.

📊 FIGURE — The Hadamard sandwich and its outputs on four 3-bit functions
H⊗n, one phase query, H⊗n again. Bars show P(y) over y = 000 to 111: a constant f always gives 000, a balanced f never does, and a linear f = s·x returns s itself (Bernstein-Vazirani).

The Bernstein-Vazirani problem: you are promised f(x) = s·x (mod 2) for a hidden string s ∈ {0,1}n; find s.

The circuit (\"Hadamard sandwich\") is the same for both problems:

StepInput register (n qubits)Target qubit
0|0…0⟩|1⟩
1H⊗nH (target becomes |−⟩)
2Uf, one query; acts as the phase oracle (−1)f(x)
3H⊗n(idle)
4measure all n qubits(ignore)

Following the state:

  1. After step 1: (1/√2n)∑x|x⟩ ⊗ |−⟩.
  2. After step 2 (kickback): (1/√2n)∑x(−1)f(x)|x⟩ ⊗ |−⟩.
  3. After step 3, using the Hadamard identity on each |x⟩ and collecting terms:
🧮 KEY EQUATION

amplitude of |y⟩ = (1/2n) ∑x (−1)f(x) ⊕ x·y

For y = 0…0 this is (1/2n)∑x(−1)f(x): it equals +1 or −1 if f is constant (every term has the same sign) and exactly 0 if f is balanced (2n−1 pluses cancel 2n−1 minuses). Rule: all zeros measured means constant; any other string means balanced. For BV with f(x) = s·x the amplitude is 1 at y = s and 0 elsewhere.

Worked example: four 3-bit functions

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

n = 3, simulated in numpy with the phase-oracle form (a diagonal of (−1)f(x) between two H⊗3). Bit strings are written x0x1x2, left to right (textbook order). Truth tables list f(000), f(001), …, f(111).

fTruth tableTypeNonzero output amplitudesResult
f = 00000 0000constant000: 1000 with P = 1
f = x20101 0101balanced, linear (s = 001)001: 1001 with P = 1
f = x0 ⊕ x10011 1100balanced, linear (s = 110)110: 1110 with P = 1
majority(x)0001 0111balanced, not linear001: 0.5, 010: 0.5, 100: 0.5, 111: −0.5each with P = 0.25

Step by step for majority:

  1. Truth table has four 1s out of eight, so it is balanced.
  2. Phase vector (−1)f(x) = (1, 1, 1, −1, 1, −1, −1, −1).
  3. Amplitude of 000 = (1/8)(1 + 1 + 1 − 1 + 1 − 1 − 1 − 1) = 0/8 = 0, so 000 never appears and the verdict \"balanced\" is certain.
  4. The remaining probability sits on 001, 010, 100, 111 at 0.5² = 0.25 each; sanity check 4 × 0.25 = 1.

The two linear functions are Bernstein-Vazirani instances: the output is the hidden string itself. Majority is balanced but matches no single pattern, so its weight spreads over several y, none of them 000.

Bernstein-Vazirani: reading a hidden string in one query

With f(x) = s·x, step 2 produces (1/√2n)∑x(−1)s·x|x⟩, which is precisely H⊗n|s⟩. The final H⊗n undoes it and leaves |s⟩. Numpy for s = 101 (n = 3): the output amplitude is 1 on 101 and 0 elsewhere.

Building the oracle is easy: for every i with si = 1, put a CNOT from input qubit i to the target, because the target then accumulates the XOR of exactly those bits. Qiskit 2.x (same two imports as in the Deutsch example), s = 1011 with si assigned to qubit i:

s = '1011'; n = 4
qc = QuantumCircuit(n + 1)
qc.x(n); qc.h(range(n + 1))
for i, c in enumerate(s):
    if c == '1': qc.cx(i, n)
qc.h(range(n))
print(Statevector.from_instruction(qc).probabilities_dict(qargs=list(range(n))))

Every key is printed, but all except one are floating-point round-off (below 10−33); the only real entry is '1101': 1.0 (printed as 0.9999999999999986). That is not a wrong answer: Qiskit puts qubit 0 on the right, so '1101' read right to left is s0s1s2s3 = 1011. Recovered s = 1011 with one query.

What the speed-up really is, and against which classical model

ProblemQuantumDeterministic classical (exact)Randomized classical (bounded error)
Deutsch-Jozsa1 query, error 02n−1 + 1 queries in the worst case (n = 10: 513)O(1): k random queries, error at most 21−k, independent of n
Bernstein-Vazirani1 query, error 0n queries (query ei to read si)Ω(n): each answer is one bit and s carries n bits

Deutsch-Jozsa is exponentially better only than an exact deterministic classical algorithm. The deterministic bound comes from an adversary: after 2n−1 answers that are all 0, f could still be constant or balanced. A randomized algorithm that samples k uniform inputs (with replacement) and says \"constant\" when all answers agree is never wrong on a constant f, and on a balanced f all k answers agree with probability 2·(1/2)k = 21−k. Three queries give error ≤ 0.25; eleven give ≤ 0.000977, for any n. So against bounded-error randomized algorithms the separation is 1 versus a constant: essentially nothing.

Bernstein-Vazirani beats every classical model, including randomized, but only by 1 versus n, a polynomial (linear) gap. Bernstein and Vazirani also built a recursive version of the problem that gives a superpolynomial oracle separation; the full exponential oracle separation from randomized algorithms arrives with Simon's algorithm in the next lesson.

Both results are query-complexity separations relative to an oracle. They say nothing about a problem whose f is handed to you as a circuit you can read: given a circuit for s·x, a classical programmer just reads s off the gates.

📊 YOUR DATA EDGE

The randomized Deutsch-Jozsa test is a sampling problem you already know: null hypothesis \"f is constant\", test statistic \"did any two samples disagree?\". The false-\"constant\" rate on a balanced f is 21−k, exactly like the chance that k fair coin flips all agree. Seeing that a constant number of samples controls the error regardless of population size 2n is the same insight as \"a poll of 1,000 people works for a country of any size\", and it is why Deutsch-Jozsa is not evidence of practical quantum advantage.

✅ VERIFIED

D. Deutsch and R. Jozsa, \"Rapid solution of problems by quantum computation\", Proc. R. Soc. A 439, 553-558 (1992), doi:10.1098/rspa.1992.0167; the abstract claims the speed-up against classical deterministic computation. E. Bernstein and U. Vazirani, \"Quantum complexity theory\", STOC 1993 pp. 11-20, journal version SIAM J. Comput. 26(5), 1411-1473 (1997), summary at Wikipedia: Bernstein-Vazirani algorithm. Checked 28 Sep 2026.

The traps

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE
  • \"Deutsch-Jozsa is exponentially faster than classical.\" Only than exact deterministic classical; a randomized classical test needs a constant number of queries.
  • Ignoring the promise. For f with 1s on only two of eight inputs (neither constant nor balanced), numpy gives amplitude 0.5 on 000, so P(000) = 0.25: the circuit outputs \"constant\" a quarter of the time and \"balanced\" otherwise. The answer is meaningless when the promise fails.
  • Treating x·y as an integer product. It is AND-then-parity: 101·111 = 1 ⊕ 0 ⊕ 1 = 0.
  • Expecting DJ to identify which balanced function. Only for linear f does the output equal a hidden string; majority gives a random nonzero string.
  • Bit order. Qiskit printed '1101' for s = 1011. Reverse the string, or build the oracle with si on qubit n−1−i if you want the printout to read directly.
★ ON THE EXAM

Typical tasks: expand H⊗2|11⟩ or H⊗3|x⟩ with signs; show that the amplitude of 0…0 is ±1 for constant f and 0 for balanced f; run BV by hand for a given s and draw its CNOT oracle; and a short essay \"is Deutsch-Jozsa an exponential speed-up?\", where full marks need the words deterministic, randomized, bounded error, promise and oracle (query) model, plus the counts 2n−1 + 1, O(1), n and 1.

This lesson teaches Simon's algorithm, the first proof that a quantum computer can beat every classical randomized algorithm by an exponential factor, in the query model. You will run the circuit on a 3-bit instance, see why every measurement returns a string orthogonal to the hidden string s, recover s with Gaussian elimination over GF(2), and count queries on both sides honestly. The structure (superpose, query, Fourier transform, measure, classical post-processing) is the template for Shor's algorithm in the next chapters, with the Hadamard transform replaced by the quantum Fourier transform.

The idea in plain words

A function f scrambles n-bit strings, but secretly pairs them up: x and x ⊕ s always give the same output, for one hidden nonzero string s, and no other inputs collide. Classically, the only way to learn anything about s is to stumble on a collision f(x) = f(x′), and with 2n inputs that takes about 2n/2 tries (the birthday paradox). A quantum computer instead prepares a superposition of a colliding pair, (|x⟩ + |x ⊕ s⟩)/√2, and a Hadamard transform turns it into a uniformly random string y with y·s = 0. Each run hands you one linear equation about s; about n runs pin s down.

Definition and circuit

📘 DEFINITION

Simon's problem. You get oracle access to f: {0,1}n → {0,1}n with the promise that there is a string s ∈ {0,1}n such that, for all x and x′,

f(x) = f(x′) ⇔ x′ = x or x′ = x ⊕ s

Find s. If s = 0…0, f is one-to-one; otherwise f is exactly two-to-one and \"periodic\" under XOR: f(x ⊕ s) = f(x). This is the hidden subgroup problem for the group ({0,1}n, ⊕), with hidden subgroup {0…0, s}.

GF(2) is arithmetic on {0, 1} mod 2: addition is XOR (1 + 1 = 0) and multiplication is AND. The inner product y·s = y0s0 ⊕ … ⊕ yn−1sn−1 lives in GF(2).

The circuit uses 2n qubits: an input register and an output register of n qubits, both starting in |0…0⟩ (no |−⟩ here; this oracle writes n-bit values).

StepInput register (n qubits)Output register (n qubits)
0|0…0⟩|0…0⟩
1H⊗n(idle)
2Uf|x⟩|z⟩ = |x⟩|z ⊕ f(x)⟩, one query
3(idle)measure (optional; result discarded)
4H⊗n(idle)
5measure, giving y(ignore)
  1. After steps 1-2: (1/√2n)∑x|x⟩|f(x)⟩. The registers are entangled.
  2. Measuring the output gives some value f(x0), and the input collapses onto the two inputs with that value: (|x0⟩ + |x0 ⊕ s⟩)/√2. (By the principle of deferred measurement, skipping this measurement gives the same statistics for y.)
  3. Apply H⊗n using the Hadamard identity to each term and factor out (−1)x0·y:
🧮 KEY EQUATION

amplitude of |y⟩ = (−1)x0·y [1 + (−1)s·y] / √2n+1

If s·y = 1 the bracket is 0; if s·y = 0 it is 2, giving amplitude magnitude 2/√2n+1 and probability 4/2n+1 = 1/2n−1. So for s ≠ 0 each run returns a uniformly random y from the 2n−1 strings with y·s = 0. The unknown x0 only contributes a sign, which the measurement cannot see. (If s = 0, y is uniform over all 2n strings.)

Worked example: n = 3, hidden s = 110

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

The oracle (chosen by hand, then checked in Python that f(x ⊕ 110) = f(x) for every x) pairs the inputs as:

📊 FIGURE — Simon's circuit and the strings it returns for s = 110
Each run returns a uniformly random y orthogonal to s (the four blue strings, P = 0.25 each). Two independent nonzero samples give linear equations over GF(2) whose only nonzero solution is s = 110.
Pair {x, x ⊕ s}f value
000, 110101
001, 111010
010, 100000
011, 101110

Numpy simulation of the full 6-qubit state (64 amplitudes, textbook bit order x0x1x2):

  1. After H⊗3 and Uf: eight terms |x⟩|f(x)⟩, each with amplitude 1/√8 ≈ 0.3536.
  2. Suppose the output register reads 101. The input becomes (|000⟩ + |110⟩)/√2.
  3. After H⊗3: amplitudes 0.5 on 000, 001, 110, 111 and 0 on the other four. Had it read 010 instead (pair 001, 111), the amplitudes are +0.5, −0.5, +0.5, −0.5 on the same four strings: same probabilities, different signs.
  4. Overall distribution of y: P = 0.25 each for 000, 001, 110, 111, and 0 for 010, 011, 100, 101. Check: 001·110 = 0, 110·110 = 1 ⊕ 1 ⊕ 0 = 0, 111·110 = 1 ⊕ 1 ⊕ 0 = 0. Sanity: 4 × 0.25 = 1.

Classical post-processing. Say two runs give y = 001 and y = 111 (000 carries no information and is discarded). Each is an equation over GF(2):

SampleEquationConsequence
001s2 = 0s2 = 0
111s0 ⊕ s1 ⊕ s2 = 0s0 = s1

The solutions are 000 and 110 (Python brute force over all nonzero s confirms 110 is the only nonzero one). Two rank-(n−1) equations leave exactly one nonzero candidate, s = 110. Finally spend two classical queries to rule out s = 0: f(000) = 101 = f(110), so s = 110 is confirmed.

The same instance in Qiskit 2.x uses a standard oracle construction: copy x into the output with three CNOTs, then, controlled on qubit 0 (a position where s has a 1), XOR s into the output. This implements a different (but valid) f with the same s = 110:

qc = QuantumCircuit(6)
qc.h([0, 1, 2])
for i in range(3): qc.cx(i, 3 + i) # copy x
qc.cx(0, 3); qc.cx(0, 4) # XOR s = 110 when x0 = 1
qc.h([0, 1, 2])
sv = Statevector.from_instruction(qc); sv.seed(7)
print(sv.sample_counts(1000, qargs=[0, 1, 2]))

Output: {'000': 257, '011': 245, '100': 245, '111': 253}. Remember Qiskit's little-endian printing: reversed, these are 000, 110, 001, 111, exactly the four strings orthogonal to s = 110, each near the predicted 250 of 1000 shots.

How many queries, and against which classical model

Quantum. You need n − 1 linearly independent nonzero samples. Samples are uniform over an (n−1)-dimensional space, so the k-th new sample is independent of the earlier ones with probability 1 − 2k−1/2n−1. Exact values computed with Python fractions:

nP(first n − 1 samples already span)Expected number of runs to reach rank n − 1
33/8 = 0.37510/3 ≈ 3.3333 (Monte Carlo, 200,000 trials: 3.3353)
421/64 ≈ 0.32814.4762
100.289410.6047
500.288850.6067

So O(n) queries (in these examples, fewer than n + 1 runs on average), each followed by O(n3) classical Gaussian elimination at the end: polynomial overall.

Classical. Until a collision f(x) = f(x′) turns up, the answers are just distinct values that reveal almost nothing about s. Any pair of queried points collides only if their XOR equals s, so with q queries there are q(q − 1)/2 chances, each about 1 in 2n − 1. For n = 50 and q = 225 = 33,554,432 queries, this union bound on the success probability is still only about 0.5. Simon proved that every bounded-error randomized classical algorithm needs Ω(2n/2) queries, and a birthday-style search achieves O(2n/2). Deterministic algorithms are no better.

The honest summary: about 50 quantum queries versus tens of millions of classical queries for n = 50, an exponential separation in query complexity, relative to an oracle, against bounded-error randomized algorithms. This is the key upgrade over Deutsch-Jozsa, whose gap disappears once randomness is allowed. It is not a proof that BQP ≠ BPP for ordinary, non-oracle problems; that remains open.

✅ VERIFIED

D. R. Simon, \"On the power of quantum computation\", Proceedings of the 35th Annual Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science (FOCS), Santa Fe, November 1994, pp. 116-123; journal version SIAM J. Comput. 26(5), 1474-1483 (1997), PDF of the SIAM paper. Its abstract states the problem is solved exponentially faster in the quantum model than in the classical probabilistic one, and that Shor built on this work for factoring and discrete logarithms. Checked 28 Sep 2026.

The traps

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE
  • Putting the output register in |−⟩. Simon's oracle writes an n-bit value into an n-qubit register starting at |0…0⟩. The entanglement between registers is what collapses the input onto a pair; there is no phase kickback here.
  • Thinking y is s. Each y satisfies y·s = 0. When s·s = 0 (as for s = 110) the string s itself can appear among the samples, but so can others; you still need n − 1 independent equations.
  • Real-number arithmetic. Solve over GF(2): 1 + 1 = 0, and \"s0 + s1 = 0\" means s0 = s1.
  • Counting samples, not independent samples. 000 and repeated or dependent strings add no information; for n = 3 the first two samples span only 3/8 of the time.
  • Forgetting s = 0. The equations always allow s = 0; finish with a classical check f(0…0) = f(s) on your candidate.
  • Overclaiming. \"Exponential speed-up\" is true for queries relative to this oracle, not for a known practical task, and not an unconditional complexity-class separation.
★ ON THE EXAM

Expect: (1) derive the amplitude (−1)x0·y[1 + (−1)s·y]/√2n+1 and conclude P(y) = 1/2n−1 for y·s = 0; (2) list the possible outcomes for a given s; (3) solve a 2- or 3-equation GF(2) system for s; (4) state the query counts: O(n) quantum, Ω(2n/2) classical randomized; (5) explain why Simon beats randomized algorithms while Deutsch-Jozsa does not; (6) name the link to Shor: both find a hidden subgroup, with H⊗n replaced by the quantum Fourier transform over the integers mod N.

This lesson gives you the quantum Fourier transform (QFT): what it does to a state, why it is the same maths as the discrete Fourier transform you know from numpy, how to build it from Hadamards and controlled phase gates, and how many gates it costs. It is the engine inside phase estimation (next lesson), order finding (the lesson after) and Shor's algorithm (next chapter), so every later \"exponential speed-up\" story in this degree passes through the circuit you learn here.

The idea in plain words

A classical discrete Fourier transform takes a list of N numbers and re-expresses it as a list of N frequency components. The QFT does exactly the same linear map, but the list is the amplitude vector of an n-qubit state, with N = 2n. A state with a regular pattern in its amplitudes (a period, or a steadily turning phase) is turned into a state whose amplitude is concentrated on a few basis states that name that pattern. Measuring then reveals the pattern.

Two honest caveats up front. First, the QFT acts on amplitudes you cannot read: measuring the output gives you one index k, sampled with probability |yk|², not the list of Fourier coefficients. Second, the QFT is only useful as a subroutine inside an algorithm that has already written the pattern into the phases. On its own it is not a faster FFT.

The definition and the matrix

Throughout this chapter we use the textbook (big-endian) convention: an n-qubit basis state |j1j2…jn⟩ stands for the integer j = j12n−1 + j22n−2 + … + jn20, so qubit 1 is the most significant bit.

📘 DEFINITION

The quantum Fourier transform on n qubits (N = 2n) is the unitary that maps each computational basis state |j⟩, j = 0, 1, …, N−1, to

QFT|j⟩ = (1/√N) ∑k=0N−1 e2πi jk/N |k⟩

Here i is the imaginary unit, e2πi jk/N is a phase of modulus 1, and 1/√N makes the output a unit vector. By linearity a general state ∑j xj|j⟩ goes to ∑k yk|k⟩ with yk = (1/√N) ∑j e2πi jk/N xj.

Write ω = e2πi/N (a primitive N-th root of unity). The matrix has entry Fkj = ωjk/√N in row k, column j. For one qubit (N = 2, ω = −1) the QFT is exactly the Hadamard gate. For two qubits (N = 4, ω = i):

F4 = (1/2) ×

j = 0j = 1j = 2j = 3
k = 01111
k = 11i−1−i
k = 21−11−1
k = 31−i−1i

Column j is the output state for input |j⟩. Every entry has modulus 1/2, so every output of a basis input is a uniform-magnitude superposition: all the information is in the phases. The columns are orthonormal, which is why F is unitary (checked numerically below: F†F = I).

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Sign and scale conventions. numpy's np.fft.fft uses e−2πi jk/N and no normalisation; the QFT uses e+2πi jk/N and 1/√N. Checked in numpy on a random 8-vector: QFT x = √N · np.fft.ifft(x) is True, while QFT x = np.fft.fft(x)/√N is False. If a textbook result looks complex-conjugated, you have mixed the two conventions.

Also: forgetting the 1/√N gives a vector of length √N, not a quantum state. Always check the probabilities sum to 1.

The product form: why the QFT has a small circuit

Use binary fractions: 0.jljl+1…jm means jl/2 + jl+1/4 + … + jm/2m−l+1. For example 0.01 = 1/4 and 0.11 = 3/4. Writing the output index k in binary, the phase e2πi jk/N splits into one factor per output bit, and the integer part of each exponent drops out because e2πi·integer = 1. What is left is a tensor product:

🧮 KEY EQUATION

QFT|j1…jn⟩ = (1/2n/2) (|0⟩ + e2πi 0.jn|1⟩) ⊗ (|0⟩ + e2πi 0.jn−1jn|1⟩) ⊗ … ⊗ (|0⟩ + e2πi 0.j1j2…jn|1⟩)

j1…jn are the input bits (j1 most significant); the l-th output qubit carries the relative phase 2π × 0.jn−l+1…jn; 1/2n/2 = 1/√N is the normalisation. Two consequences: the QFT of a basis state is a product state (no entanglement), and the first output qubit depends only on the last input bit.

The phase rotation that adds one more binary digit is

Rk = diag(1, e2πi/2k)

so R1 = Z, R2 = S, R3 = T. A controlled-Rk multiplies |11⟩ by e2πi/2k and leaves the other three basis states alone, so control and target are interchangeable (Qiskit calls it cp(2π/2k, c, t)).

The circuit: Hadamards, controlled phases and swaps

Why a Hadamard starts each qubit: H|j1⟩ = (|0⟩ + (−1)j1|1⟩)/√2 = (|0⟩ + e2πi 0.j1|1⟩)/√2, because eiπ j1 = (−1)j1. Then a controlled-R2 from qubit 2 adds j2/4 to the phase, making it 0.j1j2; a controlled-R3 from qubit 3 adds j3/8; and so on. The recipe:

📊 FIGURE — Three-qubit QFT circuit: Hadamards, controlled phases, one swap
Blue labels show the binary-fraction phase each qubit has collected: H starts it, each controlled-R_k adds one more digit. The final SWAP puts the product-form factors back in order.
  1. Qubit 1: H, then controlled-R2 (control qubit 2), controlled-R3 (control qubit 3), …, controlled-Rn (control qubit n). Qubit 1 now holds (|0⟩ + e2πi 0.j1…jn|1⟩)/√2.
  2. Qubit 2: H, then controlled-R2, …, controlled-Rn−1 from qubits 3 … n. It now holds phase 0.j2…jn.
  3. Continue down to qubit n, which gets only an H (phase 0.jn).
  4. The factors are now in reverse order compared with the product formula, so finish with ⌊n/2⌋ SWAPs (qubit 1 ↔ n, 2 ↔ n−1, …).

For n = 3 the full gate list, in time order, is:

StepGateActs on
1Hq1
2controlled-R2 (angle π/2)control q2, target q1
3controlled-R3 (angle π/4)control q3, target q1
4Hq2
5controlled-R2 (angle π/2)control q3, target q2
6Hq3
7SWAPq1, q3

I multiplied these gates as 8×8 numpy matrices (big-endian) and compared with the definition: the product equals F8 to machine precision. The same check passed for n = 2, 4 and 5.

🧮 KEY EQUATION

gates(n) = n Hadamards + n(n−1)/2 controlled phases + ⌊n/2⌋ SWAPs = Θ(n²)

Counted from my circuit builder: n = 2 gives 2, 1, 1; n = 3 gives 3, 3, 1; n = 4 gives 4, 6, 2; n = 5 gives 5, 10, 2. Each SWAP is 3 CNOTs. The classical FFT needs Θ(N log N) = Θ(n 2n) arithmetic operations on the full vector; the QFT circuit uses Θ(n²) gates, but see the caveat about read-out above.

The inverse QFT, needed in the next lesson, is the same circuit run backwards with every angle negated (Rk† = diag(1, e−2πi/2k)); H and SWAP are their own inverses.

Worked example: QFT of |01⟩ three ways

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Compute QFT|01⟩ on two qubits (big-endian, so |01⟩ is j = 1), by the matrix, the product form and the circuit. All numbers checked in numpy.

  1. Matrix. Take column j = 1 of F4: (1, i, −1, −i)/2. So QFT|01⟩ = (|00⟩ + i|01⟩ − |10⟩ − i|11⟩)/2. numpy prints [0.5, 0.5j, −0.5, −0.5j].
  2. Product form. j1 = 0, j2 = 1. First factor: e2πi 0.j2 = e2πi·(1/2) = eiπ = −1, giving (|0⟩ − |1⟩)/√2. Second factor: e2πi 0.j1j2 = e2πi·(1/4) = i, giving (|0⟩ + i|1⟩)/√2. Tensor product: (|00⟩ + i|01⟩ − |10⟩ − i|11⟩)/2, the same vector.
  3. Circuit. Start |0⟩|1⟩. H on q1: (|0⟩ + |1⟩)|1⟩/√2. Controlled-R2 (control q2 = 1, so it fires) puts i on the |1⟩ of q1: (|0⟩ + i|1⟩)|1⟩/√2. H on q2 turns |1⟩ into (|0⟩ − |1⟩)/√2: state (|0⟩ + i|1⟩)(|0⟩ − |1⟩)/2. SWAP: (|0⟩ − |1⟩)(|0⟩ + i|1⟩)/2 = (|00⟩ + i|01⟩ − |10⟩ − i|11⟩)/2.

Answer: QFT|01⟩ = (|00⟩ + i|01⟩ − |10⟩ − i|11⟩)/2. Sanity check: each outcome has probability |±1/2|² = |±i/2|² = 0.25 and 4 × 0.25 = 1. The pattern of phases 1, i, −1, −i is a phase turning a quarter-turn per step: that is the \"frequency 1\" signature.

The numpy check you can run on the iPad:

import numpy as np
N = 4; w = np.exp(2j*np.pi/N)
F = np.array([[w**(j*k) for j in range(N)] for k in range(N)]) / np.sqrt(N)
print(np.round(F @ np.array([0, 1, 0, 0]), 4)) # 0.5, 0.5i, -0.5, -0.5i
print(np.allclose(F.conj().T @ F, np.eye(N))) # True

In Qiskit 2.x, Operator(QFTGate(n)).data (from qiskit.circuit.library) equals the same FN matrix for n = 2 and 3 when rows and columns are read as integers. The difference is only in labelling wires: Qiskit prints bitstrings little-endian, so qubit 0 is the rightmost bit. The integer j = 1 is the Qiskit string \"01\" with qubit 0 = 1; in our big-endian notation the same integer is |01⟩ with the second qubit = 1. Convert through the integer, never by copying bitstrings between conventions.

The approximate QFT

For large n, the controlled-Rk gates with big k rotate by a tiny angle 2π/2k. The approximate QFT simply drops every controlled-Rk with k > m. Each dropped gate differs from the identity by at most |e2πi/2k − 1| ≤ 2π/2k in operator norm, and errors of a gate sequence add at worst, so

‖QFT − AQFTm‖ ≤ ∑dropped gates 2π/2k ≤ 2πn/2m

Choosing m ≈ log2 n + c keeps the error around 2π/2c while cutting the gate count to O(n log n). My numpy check (operator norm = worst case over input states):

nmcontrolled phases kepterror ‖F − AQFT‖
8522 of 280.4142
8625 of 280.1226
8727 of 280.0245
10635 of 450.2995
10739 of 450.1043

The measured error sits almost exactly on the gate-by-gate sum, and well under the loose 2πn/2m bound. On real hardware a rotation of 2π/220 is far below gate-calibration error anyway, so keeping it adds noise and buys nothing.

Traps

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE
  • \"The QFT is an exponentially faster FFT.\" It is not, for data you want to read. Loading N classical numbers into amplitudes can itself cost about N operations, and a measurement returns one sampled index k, not the N coefficients. The speed-up only appears when the input state is produced by a quantum process and you need one sample from its spectrum.
  • Forgetting the SWAPs (or forgetting to reinterpret the bit order instead). Without them you have the QFT followed by a bit reversal, which is a different unitary.
  • Wrong phase on the controlled gate. Rk rotates by 2π/2k, so R2 is π/2 (the S gate), not π/4.
  • Thinking the QFT entangles basis states. The product form shows QFT|j⟩ is a product state; entanglement only appears when the input is itself a superposition.
📊 YOUR DATA EDGE

You already know the periodogram: the squared magnitudes of an FFT show which frequencies dominate a time series. Measuring after a QFT samples an index k with probability |yk|², so each shot is one draw from a normalised power spectrum. Estimating that spectrum from S shots has the usual binomial error √(p(1−p)/S) per bin. That is why algorithms use the QFT only where the spectrum is sharply peaked (a few bins hold almost all the probability): then a handful of shots is enough.

★ ON THE EXAM
  • Write the definition of QFT|j⟩ with normalisation and the + sign.
  • Write F4 and apply it to a basis state or a simple superposition.
  • Derive or use the product form; say which output qubit depends on which input bits.
  • Draw (as a gate list) the n = 3 circuit and count gates: n H, n(n−1)/2 controlled phases, ⌊n/2⌋ SWAPs.
  • Explain why this is not a way to compute a classical FFT faster, and what the approximate QFT drops and why the error is small.

This lesson lets you read the eigenvalue of a unitary into a register of qubits: quantum phase estimation (QPE). You will follow the circuit state by state, predict the outcome distribution when the phase is exact and when it is not, and choose how many counting qubits you need. QPE is the bridge between the QFT of the previous lesson and every algorithm that uses it: order finding (next lesson), Shor's algorithm, and later the quantum-chemistry and linear-systems algorithms in the simulation chapter.

The idea in plain words

Every eigenvalue of a unitary has modulus 1, so it is a pure phase e2πiφ. If you apply U to its eigenvector, nothing observable happens: the phase is global. The trick is to apply U conditionally. A controlled-U turns that global phase into a relative phase on the control qubit (\"phase kickback\"). Doing controlled-U, controlled-U2, controlled-U4, … on a register of control qubits writes φ, 2φ, 4φ, … into their phases. That is exactly the pattern the QFT recognises, so an inverse QFT turns the phases into the binary digits of φ.

📘 DEFINITION

Phase estimation problem. Given a unitary U (as a circuit you can control and raise to powers 2j) and a state |u⟩ with U|u⟩ = e2πiφ|u⟩, estimate the eigenphase φ ∈ [0, 1). φ is measured in turns: the rotation angle is 2πφ radians.

Phase kickback. For an eigenstate |u⟩, controlled-U maps (|0⟩ + |1⟩)|u⟩/√2 to (|0⟩ + e2πiφ|1⟩)|u⟩/√2: the target is unchanged and the phase lands on the control.

The circuit

Two registers: t counting qubits starting in |0⟩, and a target register holding |u⟩. Label the counting qubits by the power of 2 they stand for, so the counting register reads the integer k = ∑ kj2j.

📊 FIGURE — Phase estimation circuit and the outcomes when φ = 1/3
Counting qubit of weight 2ʲ controls U^(2ʲ), so |k⟩ collects the phase e^(2πiφk); the inverse QFT turns that into m. For φ = 1/3 the peak is the nearest grid point m = 3 (P = 0.6878), not a certainty.
  1. Apply H to every counting qubit: (1/√2t) ∑k |k⟩|u⟩.
  2. For each j = 0, …, t−1, apply controlled-U2j with the counting qubit of weight 2j as control. Kickback gives that qubit the phase e2πi 2jφ. Multiplying all the kicked-back phases, basis state |k⟩ collects e2πiφk.
  3. Apply the inverse QFT to the counting register.
  4. Measure the counting register, get an integer m, and report φ̃ = m/2t.
🧮 KEY EQUATION

After step 2 the counting register is

(1/√2t) ∑k=02t−1 e2πiφk |k⟩ ⊗ |u⟩

which is exactly QFT|2tφ⟩ when 2tφ is an integer. In general, after the inverse QFT the probability of reading m is

P(m) = | (1/2t) ∑k=02t−1 e2πik(φ − m/2t) |² = sin²(π2tδ) / (22t sin²(πδ)), δ = φ − m/2t

t = number of counting qubits; m = measured integer; δ = distance from φ to the grid point m/2t (the closed form is a geometric series; I checked it agrees with the sum to 4 decimals). If δ = 0 then P(m) = 1.

In the textbook (big-endian) drawing, the top counting qubit is the most significant bit, so it controls U2t−1 and the bottom one controls U1. In Qiskit it is natural to let qubit j control U2j; then Qiskit's little-endian bitstring reads directly as the binary of m. Both are the same algorithm with different wire labels.

Worked example 1: an exact phase (the T gate)

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

U = T = diag(1, eiπ/4), eigenstate |u⟩ = |1⟩ with T|1⟩ = eiπ/4|1⟩. Since π/4 = 2π × 1/8, the eigenphase is φ = 1/8 = 0.001 in binary. Use t = 3 counting qubits.

  1. Powers needed: U1 = T, U2 = S (phase π/2), U4 = Z (phase π).
  2. After the Hadamards every |k⟩ has amplitude 1/√8 = 0.3536.
  3. After the controlled powers, |k⟩ has amplitude e2πik/8/√8. Table below (numpy).
  4. That vector equals QFT|1⟩ for N = 8 (column 1 of F8), so the inverse QFT returns |001⟩ exactly.
  5. Measure: m = 1 with probability 1, so φ̃ = 1/8.
kphase 2πk/8amplitude before inverse QFT
000.3536
1π/40.25 + 0.25i
2π/20.3536i
33π/4−0.25 + 0.25i
4π−0.3536

Result: m = 1 (binary 001) with probability 1.0000, so φ̃ = 1/8 exactly. Sanity check: eight amplitudes each of modulus 0.3536 give 8 × 0.125 = 1 before the inverse QFT, and all of it lands on one outcome after.

The Qiskit 2.x version (runs as written; the target is qubit 3 and counting qubit j controls U2j, done here as a controlled phase of angle 2j·π/4):

import numpy as np
from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from qiskit.quantum_info import Statevector
from qiskit.circuit.library import QFTGate
qc = QuantumCircuit(4); qc.x(3)
for j in range(3): qc.h(j)
for j in range(3): qc.cp(np.pi/4 * 2**j, j, 3)
qc.append(QFTGate(3).inverse(), range(3))
print(Statevector(qc).probabilities_dict(qargs=[0, 1, 2])) # 001 with probability 1.0

With φ = 3/8 the same circuit gives Qiskit string \"011\" (m = 3). If you read that string big-endian with qubit 0 as the most significant bit you would say 110 = 6 and report φ̃ = 6/8: wrong. Qiskit's rightmost bit is qubit 0.

Worked example 2: a phase that is not on the grid

Take U = P(2π/3) = diag(1, e2πi/3) on |1⟩, so φ = 1/3 = 0.0101… in binary, which never terminates. With t = 3 the grid is 0, 1/8, …, 7/8, and 1/3 falls between 2/8 = 0.25 and 3/8 = 0.375. The formula above (and the Qiskit statevector, which agreed) gives:

mm/8P(m)
00.0000.0156
10.1250.0316
20.2500.1749
30.3750.6878
40.5000.0469
50.6250.0186
60.7500.0126
70.8750.0119

The most likely outcome is m = 3, the grid point nearest to 1/3 (distance 0.0417, less than half a bin, 1/16). P(m ∈ {2, 3, 4}) = 0.9097. Sanity check: the eight probabilities sum to 1.0000. More counting qubits sharpen the peak around 1/3 but do not make any single outcome certain: with t = 5 the best outcome is m = 11 (0.34375) with probability 0.6842; with t = 8 it is m = 85 (0.3320) with probability 0.6839.

Precision, success probability and cost

With t counting qubits the estimate lives on a grid of spacing 2−t. The worst case is φ exactly halfway between two grid points. I computed the probability of the single most likely outcome in that worst case: t = 2 gives 0.4268, t = 3 gives 0.4105, t = 4 gives 0.4066, t = 10 gives 0.4053, approaching 4/π² ≈ 0.4053 from above; the two nearest outcomes together approach 8/π² ≈ 0.8106.

🧮 KEY EQUATION

P(nearest t-bit estimate) ≥ 4/π² ≈ 0.405

To get φ accurate to n bits (error below 2−n) with probability at least 1 − ε, use

t = n + ⌈log2(2 + 1/(2ε))⌉

n = bits of precision wanted; ε = allowed failure probability; t = counting qubits (Nielsen & Chuang, section 5.2.1). Examples: n = 3, ε = 0.1 gives t = 6; n = 10, ε = 0.01 gives t = 16. Extra qubits are cheap insurance: failure falls roughly like 1/2t−n.

Cost. The circuit applies controlled-U2j for j up to t−1. If the only way to build U2j is to repeat U 2j times, QPE uses 2t − 1 controlled-U applications, exponential in the number of bits. QPE is efficient only when high powers of U have short circuits, as in modular exponentiation (next lesson) where a2j mod N is computed classically by repeated squaring. The precision-per-use is still remarkable: error about 1/(number of U applications), versus 1/√(shots) for estimating the same phase by repeating a one-qubit interference experiment.

Not an eigenstate? If the target is ∑u cu|u⟩, linearity gives ∑u cu|φ̃u⟩|u⟩: you obtain an estimate of φu with probability |cu|². This is a feature: order finding uses it deliberately.

Traps

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE
  • Global phase is not harmless once you control U. T and RZ(π/4) = diag(e−iπ/8, eiπ/8) differ only by a global phase, yet controlled versions differ: on |1⟩ the first has φ = 1/8 and the second φ = 1/16. QPE measures the eigenvalue of the exact matrix you control.
  • Degrees versus turns. φ is a fraction of a full turn. An eigenvalue eiπ/4 means φ = 1/8, not 1/4 and not π/4.
  • Bit order. Decide which counting qubit is 20 and read the outcome accordingly; the Qiskit example above turns 3/8 into 6/8 if you get this wrong.
  • Expecting certainty. Only phases on the 2−t grid give probability 1; φ = 1/3 never does.
📊 YOUR DATA EDGE

QPE output is a distribution, so treat it like data. The outcome histogram for φ = 1/3 is a peaked kernel centred on 2tφ with heavy tails (the sin² / sin² shape is the Fejér kernel from signal processing). Taking the mode of a few shots, or the median of several independent runs, is exactly the robust-estimation instinct you already use for skewed data: the median of k runs fails only if more than half the runs miss, which falls off exponentially in k.

★ ON THE EXAM
  • Write the counting-register state after the controlled-U2j gates and explain phase kickback.
  • Run a small example with an exact phase (T, S or Z on |1⟩) and give m.
  • Evaluate P(m) for a non-grid phase with t = 2 or 3, or state the 4/π² bound.
  • Choose t for n bits at failure ε; explain why QPE is efficient only when U2j is cheap.
  • Say what happens if the target is a superposition of eigenstates.
