This lesson connects the codes you have learned to real machines. You will lay out a distance-3 surface code and check its stabilizers, use the scaling law for logical errors to estimate how many physical qubits a useful logical qubit needs, state the threshold theorem, see why magic-state distillation is the expensive part of fault tolerance, and read the recent below-threshold experiments critically. It is the bridge from this chapter to the hardware and cryptography chapters.

1. The idea in plain words: a code that only needs neighbours

The Steane code needs weight-4 checks between qubits that are not neighbours on a chip. The surface code arranges data qubits on a square grid and uses checks that each touch at most four adjacent qubits, so it fits superconducting and many other chips directly. Its price is a low rate (one logical qubit per patch); its reward is the highest known tolerance to circuit-level noise among practical codes and a simple recipe: to make errors rarer, make the patch bigger.

2. The definitions

📘 DEFINITION

Rotated surface code of distance d: d × d data qubits on a grid. Between each 2 × 2 group of data qubits sits a weight-4 check, alternately X-type and Z-type like a chessboard; weight-2 checks close the boundaries. There are d2 − 1 checks, each measured by its own ancilla (measure qubit), so one logical qubit costs 2d2 − 1 physical qubits: 17 for d = 3, 49 for d = 5, 97 for d = 7. It is a [[d2, 1, d]] code.

📊 FIGURE — Surface-code patch of distance 3, and the threshold as a crossing
Left: circles are data qubits, squares the measure qubits of the X (blue) and Z (amber) checks. Right: below threshold logical error falls with d; above it, it grows.

Logical operators: XL is a straight line of X across the patch from one side to the opposite side; ZL is a line of Z in the perpendicular direction. Both have weight d, which is why d is the distance.

Code cycle: one round of measuring every check. Errors show up as detection events: a check whose value changes between rounds. A decoder (e.g. minimum-weight perfect matching) pairs detection events to guess the error chain.

Threshold pth: the physical error rate below which increasing d decreases the logical error rate.

The distance-3 patch, data qubits numbered 1–9 row by row (1 2 3 / 4 5 6 / 7 8 9):

CheckTypeQubitsWeight
AX1, 2, 4, 54
BZ2, 3, 5, 64
CZ4, 5, 7, 84
DX5, 6, 8, 94
EZ1, 22
FZ8, 92
GX4, 72
HX3, 62
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Checking the d = 3 surface code in numpy (strings of 9 Pauli letters, 512 × 512 matrices).

  1. Commutation. For all 28 pairs of checks the conflict count is 0 or 2, never odd. Example: A = X on {1,2,4,5} and B = Z on {2,3,5,6} overlap on qubits 2 and 5: 2 conflicts, commute. All commute.
  2. Size. 8 independent checks on 9 qubits: k = 9 − 8 = 1. The projector ∏(I + g)/2 has trace 2.0000.
  3. Logical operators. XL = X1X2X3 (top row) meets Z-checks B and E in 2 places and C, F in 0: commutes with all. ZL = Z1Z4Z7 (left column) meets X-checks A and G in 2 places each. XL and ZL share only qubit 1: 1 conflict, anticommute.
  4. Distance. Exhaustive search finds no logical operator of weight 1 or 2 and several of weight 3: d = 3.
  5. Syndromes. X on the centre qubit 5 flips the two Z-checks B and C; Z on qubit 5 flips the two X-checks A and D; X on corner qubit 1 flips only boundary check E.

Answer: a valid [[9,1,3]] code needing 9 + 8 = 17 physical qubits. Sanity check: a bulk error lights two checks (the ends of a length-1 chain), which is what a matching decoder pairs up.

3. Distance, logical error scaling and the threshold theorem

🧮 KEY EQUATION

εd ≈ A (p / pth)(d+1)/2     Λ = εd / εd+2 ≈ pth / p

εd is the logical error per code cycle at distance d, p the physical error rate per operation, pth the threshold (around 1% for the surface code under standard circuit noise models, per Fowler et al. 2012), A a fitted constant, and Λ (Lambda) the error suppression factor gained each time d grows by 2. The exponent (d+1)/2 counts how many faults a logical error needs. Below threshold (p < pth, Λ > 1) errors fall exponentially in d; above it, bigger codes are worse.

Threshold theorem: if every component fails with probability below a constant pth and faults are sufficiently independent and local, an ideal circuit of size N can be simulated with error at most ε using only O(N polylog(N/ε)) physical operations. For concatenated codes the level-k logical rate is p(k) = pth (p/pth)2k: doubly exponential in the number of levels.

The threshold idea in a spreadsheet. For the repetition code with independent flips the exact failure rate is a binomial tail. numpy gives:

pd = 1d = 3d = 5d = 7
0.010.01002.98×10−49.85×10−63.42×10−7
0.10.10000.02800.008560.00273
0.50.50000.50000.50000.5000
0.60.60000.64800.68260.7102

Below p = 0.5 every row falls as d grows; at 0.5 it is flat; above it, larger codes are worse. That crossing is a threshold (0.5 here only because this toy model ignores phase errors and faulty measurements; realistic circuit noise pushes the surface-code threshold to about 1%). A 200,000-shot Monte Carlo at p = 0.1 gave 0.02808, 0.00863, 0.00267 for d = 3, 5, 7, each within two standard errors of the exact values.

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

How big must a surface code be? Start from Google’s measured ε7 = 0.143% per cycle and Λ = 2.14 (see the verified box), assume Λ stays constant, and use εd = ε7 · Λ−(d−7)/2.

  1. d = 9: 0.00143 / 2.14 = 6.68×10−4; d = 11: 3.12×10−4; d = 15: 6.82×10−5.
  2. Target 10−6 per cycle: need Λm ≥ 1430, m = ⌈ln 1430 / ln 2.14⌉ = ⌈9.55⌉ = 10 steps, so d = 7 + 20 = 27 (ε27 = 7.10×10−7).
  3. Qubits: 2 × 272 − 1 = 1457 physical per logical qubit.
  4. If hardware improved to Λ = 4: d = 19, 721 qubits. At Λ = 10: d = 15, 449 qubits.

Answer: about 1,457 physical qubits per logical qubit at Λ = 2.14 for 10−6 per cycle; improving Λ is worth far more than adding qubits. Sanity check: each +2 in distance divides the error by 2.14, and 2.1410 ≈ 2,000 ≥ 1,430. This is an extrapolation: it assumes no new error mechanisms (correlated bursts, leakage) appear at larger sizes.

4. Magic states: the expensive part

In the surface code the Pauli, H, CNOT and (with more work) S gates are cheap, but by Eastin–Knill the T gate cannot be transversal. Instead one prepares many noisy copies of the magic state |T⟩ = (|0⟩ + eiπ/4|1⟩)/√2, purifies them, and consumes one per T gate by gate teleportation (a CNOT, a measurement and a Clifford correction). In the standard 15-to-1 distillation protocol, 15 input states with error p give one output with error about pout ≈ 35 p3 (leading order, perfect Cliffords assumed). With p = 10−3: 35 × 10−9 = 3.5×10−8. From p = 10−2, one round gives 3.5×10−5 and a second round 35 × (3.5×10−5)3 = 1.5×10−12, at a cost of 152 = 225 raw states per output. These “magic-state factories” historically dominated resource estimates; newer ideas such as magic-state cultivation shrink them.

✅ VERIFIED
  • Google Quantum AI, “Suppressing quantum errors by scaling a surface code logical qubit”, Nature 614, 676 (2023): a distance-5 code slightly beat the average distance-3 code, 2.914% versus 3.028% logical error per cycle. nature.com/articles/s41586-022-05434-1
  • Google Quantum AI, “Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold”, Nature (published 9 Dec 2024), Willow processor: Λ = 2.14 ± 0.02; a 101-qubit distance-7 memory at 0.143% ± 0.003% error per cycle; logical lifetime 2.4 ± 0.3 times the best physical qubit. nature.com/articles/s41586-024-08449-y (the bare layout above needs 97; see the paper for the full qubit count).
  • Harvard, MIT and QuEra, “A fault-tolerant neutral-atom architecture for universal quantum computation”, Nature (2025): 448 atomic qubits with below-threshold error correction reported. nature.com/articles/s41586-025-09848-5
  • QuEra, Harvard and MIT, “Experimental demonstration of logical magic state distillation”, Nature (2025): a 5-to-1 distillation run on distance-3 and distance-5 colour-code logical qubits. nature.com/articles/s41586-025-09367-3
  • C. Gidney, “How to factor 2048 bit RSA integers with less than a million noisy qubits” (arXiv, May 2025): under a million noisy qubits and under a week, versus his 2019 estimate of about 20 million qubits. arxiv.org/abs/2505.15917
  • Threshold near 1%: A. G. Fowler et al., Physical Review A 86, 032324 (2012). link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevA.86.032324

All checked 28 Sep 2026.

❓ NOT VERIFIED

Secondary sources report a June 2026 Microsoft–Quantinuum Nature paper with repeated mid-circuit error correction on up to 12 logical qubits (11-fold to 800-fold error reductions), and logical-qubit counts of 48 on Quantinuum Helios and 96 on QuEra hardware. I could not check these against the primary papers; confirm before you rely on this.

5. The traps

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE
  • “The threshold is 1%” as a universal constant. It depends on the noise model, the circuit and the decoder; the repetition-code toy gives 50%.
  • Counting d2 qubits. The measure qubits roughly double it: 2d2 − 1.
  • Applying Λ per unit of d. Λ is the gain per step of two (d → d + 2), because odd distances are the useful ones.
  • Equating below-threshold with useful. 0.143% per cycle is far from the 10−6 to 10−12 needed for long algorithms, and a quantum memory is not a logical gate set.
  • Per-cycle versus per-algorithm error. An algorithm with 109 cycles needs roughly 10−9 or better per cycle per logical qubit.
  • Forgetting the T-gate cost when estimating resources: factories can use a large share of the machine.

6. What the exam asks

★ ON THE EXAM
  • Draw a d = 3 patch, list its checks and show two of them commute.
  • Given Λ and εd, find the distance and qubit count for a target logical error rate.
  • State the threshold theorem and its assumptions (independent, local, below-threshold faults).
  • Compute one or two rounds of 15-to-1 distillation from pout ≈ 35p3.
  • Explain what “below threshold” did and did not demonstrate in the 2024 experiment.

This lesson gives you the checklist and the measuring sticks for every physical qubit in the rest of the chapter. By the end you can list what any quantum computer must be able to do, turn a spec sheet (T1, T2, gate time, gate fidelity) into a quick estimate of how big a circuit it can run, and read a benchmark claim with the scepticism of a data analyst. It sits right after quantum error correction in the degree: error correction tells you what error rates you need; this chapter tells you which machines get there, and at what cost.

1. The idea in plain words: isolated but controllable

A qubit is not an abstract vector; it is a physical two-level system: two energy levels of an ion, two charge-and-current states of a superconducting circuit, the spin of one electron, or which of two optical fibres a photon is travelling in. Building one means solving a contradiction. The qubit must be isolated from its environment, because every stray interaction leaks information out and destroys superposition (decoherence). But it must also be strongly coupled to your control system, because you need to rotate it, entangle it with neighbours and measure it quickly. Every platform in this chapter is a different compromise between those two demands, and every number on a spec sheet measures one side of that compromise.

2. The definition: DiVincenzo's criteria

📘 DEFINITION

In 2000 David DiVincenzo listed the requirements a physical system must meet to be a quantum computer. The five for computation are:

📊 FIGURE — DiVincenzo's five-plus-two criteria and the number behind each
Criteria 1–5 are needed to compute, 6–7 to communicate. Each yes/no box turns into a quantity on a spec sheet; the bottom line gives the rules for combining them.
  1. Scalable system of well-characterised qubits: you know the two levels and their couplings, and you can add more.
  2. Initialisation to a simple reference state such as |00…0⟩.
  3. Long relevant coherence times, much longer than the time one gate takes.
  4. A universal set of gates (for example arbitrary single-qubit rotations plus one entangling gate such as CNOT or CZ).
  5. Qubit-specific measurement: you can read out each qubit you choose.

Two more are needed for quantum communication: (6) the ability to convert between stationary qubits and flying qubits (usually photons), and (7) faithful transmission of flying qubits between locations. Hence \"five plus two\".

Criteria 1-5 are yes/no questions; the interesting part is how well. The next table turns each criterion into the quantity you would actually look up for a real device.

CriterionWhat you measureTypical unit
1 Scalable, well-characterisedNumber of qubits; yield; crosstalk; leakage out of the two-level subspacecount, %
2 InitialisationState-preparation error (often lumped with readout as SPAM)%
3 CoherenceT1 (energy relaxation), T2 (dephasing); ratio T2 / gate timeµs, ms, s
4 Universal gatesSingle- and two-qubit gate fidelity; gate duration; connectivity (which pairs can interact directly)%, ns or µs, graph
5 MeasurementReadout fidelity and readout time; can you measure mid-circuit without disturbing neighbours?%, µs
6-7 CommunicationPhoton collection efficiency; remote entanglement rate and fidelityHz, %

3. The key numbers: T1, T2, gate time and fidelity

T1 (energy relaxation time) is how long it takes a qubit prepared in |1⟩ to fall to |0⟩: the probability it is still in |1⟩ decays exponentially. T2 (coherence or dephasing time) is how long a superposition keeps a well-defined relative phase. Energy loss also kills phase, so T2 can never exceed 2T1. A pure-dephasing time Tφ collects everything else (fluctuating fields that jiggle the qubit frequency). T2* is the dephasing time measured without refocusing echoes; echo sequences remove slow noise and give the longer T2.

🧮 KEY EQUATION

P1(t) = e−t/T1   (probability still excited after time t)

1/T2 = 1/(2·T1) + 1/Tφ   so   T2 ≤ 2·T1

Ncoh ≈ T2 / tgate   (rough number of gates that fit in one coherence time)

ε = 1 − F   and   Fcircuit ≈ F1·F2·…·FN ≈ e−(ε1+…+εN)

Symbols: t is elapsed time; T1, T2, Tφ are the relaxation, total dephasing and pure-dephasing times; tgate is the duration of one (usually two-qubit) gate; F is a gate fidelity (1 is perfect) and ε its error; N is the number of gates. The product rule assumes independent errors, which is a model, not a law: correlated errors and crosstalk make real circuits worse, clever compilation can make them a little better.

Gate fidelity is usually quoted as an average from randomized benchmarking (RB): you run long random sequences of gates that should multiply to the identity, watch the survival probability fall as the sequence lengthens, and fit an error per gate. An RB number is an average over input states and gates; it is not a worst case, and it depends on whether gates were run one pair at a time (\"isolated\") or all at once (\"simultaneous\"), which is usually worse because of crosstalk. Connectivity matters because a two-qubit gate between qubits that are not directly coupled has to be built from SWAPs, and each SWAP costs three CNOTs. Gate speed matters twice: it sets how many gates fit in T2, and it sets the wall-clock time for algorithms that need millions of runs.

4. Worked example: from spec sheet to circuit budget

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Setting: two made-up but realistic devices, computed in Python (numpy/math). Device A (superconducting-like): T2 = 100 µs, two-qubit gate 50 ns. Device B (trapped-ion-like): T2 = 1 s, two-qubit gate 200 µs.

  1. Gates per coherence time. A: 100×10−6 / 50×10−9 = 2,000. B: 1 / 200×10−6 = 5,000. B is 4,000 times slower per gate, yet fits more gates in its coherence window. Speed alone and coherence alone both mislead; the ratio is what counts for depth.
  2. Fidelity compounding. A circuit with N = 1,000 two-qubit gates at F = 0.999: 0.9991000 = 0.3677. At F = 0.995: 0.9951000 = 0.0067. At F = 0.9999: 0.99991000 = 0.9048. One extra \"9\" moves you from hopeless to usable.
  3. How many gates before success falls to 50%? Solve FN = 0.5, so N = ln 0.5 / ln F. For F = 0.999: N = 692.8; for F = 0.99: 69.0; for F = 0.9999: 6,931.1. Rule of thumb: N50% ≈ 0.69/ε.
  4. A whole circuit. 20 qubits, 200 two-qubit gates at 0.997, 400 single-qubit gates at 0.9997, 20 readouts at 0.99: 0.997200 = 0.5483; 0.9997400 = 0.8869; 0.9920 = 0.8179. Product = 0.3978. The two-qubit gates dominate, but readout alone costs 18%.
  5. Idle decoherence. If the same circuit has depth 40 and each layer takes 75 ns, it lasts 3 µs, and e−3/100 = 0.9704 for T2 = 100 µs. Here decoherence while waiting is a smaller effect than gate error.

Sanity check: every factor is between 0 and 1, so the product can only fall as the circuit grows; and 0.5483 × 0.8869 × 0.8179 = 0.3978, matching the direct Python product.

Notice what the example does not say: that Device B is \"better\". B wins on depth per coherence time, but a 1,000-gate circuit on B takes about 0.2 s of gate time if the gates run one after another, against 50 µs on A. For algorithms that need millions of repetitions (sampling, variational loops, error-correction cycles), that wall-clock gap matters.

5. Benchmarks and their limits

Quantum volume (QV), introduced by IBM researchers in 2019, runs random \"square\" circuits: m qubits and m layers of random two-qubit blocks. For each circuit it computes, classically, which output bitstrings are \"heavy\" (above the median ideal probability). A device passes size m if the measured probability of heavy outputs exceeds 2/3 with about two-sigma confidence. QV = 2m for the largest m passed, so a QV of 33,554,432 is just m = log2(33,554,432) = 25. QV rewards high fidelity and good connectivity together, which is why trapped-ion machines have led it. Its limits: it needs classical simulation of each circuit (so it cannot go much past about 50 qubits), it says nothing about devices with thousands of qubits, and compiler tricks can inflate it.

Other benchmarks answer other questions: IonQ's #AQ (algorithmic qubits) aggregates a suite of application circuits; random circuit sampling and related \"beyond classical\" tasks test whether a device does something a supercomputer cannot, not whether it does something useful; logical-qubit metrics (logical error per cycle, below-threshold scaling) are becoming the ones that matter for fault tolerance. The recurring pattern is that a \"beyond classical\" claim triggers classical rebuttals with better algorithms, and the gap narrows. That is science working, not failure, but it means a headline speed-up factor is a snapshot, not a constant.

✅ VERIFIED

DiVincenzo, \"The Physical Implementation of Quantum Computation\", Fortschritte der Physik 48 (9-11), 771-783 (2000): five requirements plus two for communication. Wiley.

Quantum volume definition (heavy-output probability above 2/3, square circuits): Cross et al., arXiv:1811.12926 (2019). arXiv.

Quantinuum reported QV = 225 = 33,554,432 on its 56-qubit H2 system in September 2025, four times its May 2025 figure. Quantum Computing Report. IonQ reported #AQ 64 on its 100-qubit Tempo system in September 2025 (a different benchmark; not comparable to QV). The Quantum Insider.

Google's \"Quantum Echoes\" (out-of-time-order correlator) result on Willow, Nature, 22 Oct 2025, claimed about 13,000 times faster than the best classical estimate, using 65 of 105 qubits. Google Research. IBM and the University of Chicago announced on 30 Jul 2026 a certified computation on 70 logical qubits taking about 15 minutes, described as beyond leading classical methods; later commentary argued large GPU clusters can keep pace. IBM Newsroom, Technology Org. All checked 28 Sep 2026.

❓ NOT VERIFIED

The exact classical runtime quoted in rebuttals to the July 2026 IBM claim (one headline mentions 37.3 minutes) could not be tied to a specific hardware configuration from search snippets. Treat any single \"classical would take X\" figure as provisional and confirm before you rely on this.

📊 YOUR DATA EDGE

Read a hardware spec sheet the way you would read a dashboard someone else built. Ask: is the fidelity a mean or a median, over all pairs or the best pair? Isolated or simultaneous? What are the error bars? How many shots? A measured probability from n shots has standard error √(p(1−p)/n): with p = 0.5 and n = 1,000 that is 0.0158, so \"0.51 versus 0.49\" is noise. Selection bias (reporting the best chip, the best day) is the hardware version of cherry-picking a date range.

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE
  • \"More qubits means a better computer.\" A thousand qubits at 99% two-qubit fidelity cannot run a circuit of more than about 70 gates at 50% success; a hundred at 99.9% can run about ten times more.
  • Using the linear approximation too far. 1 − Nε works only when Nε ≪ 1. For N = 400 and ε = 0.005 it gives −1, a negative probability; the product 0.995400 = 0.1347.
  • Mixing up T1 and T2. T2 is the phase clock and is at most 2T1; a long T1 does not guarantee a long T2.
  • Comparing numbers from different protocols (RB versus cross-entropy versus a vendor benchmark) as if they measured the same thing.
★ ON THE EXAM
  • List the five DiVincenzo criteria plus the two communication criteria, and give a measurable quantity for each.
  • Compute T2 / tgate, FN, or N = ln 0.5 / ln F, showing units.
  • Explain what quantum volume measures, why log2 QV is the circuit size, and one limitation.
  • Given a table for two platforms, argue which suits a deep circuit and which suits many repetitions.

This lesson takes you inside the platform used by Google, IBM and several other large programmes: qubits made from superconducting electrical circuits. You will see why an ordinary circuit cannot be a qubit, how one component (the Josephson junction) fixes that, how a transmon is controlled with microwaves and read out through a resonator, and why the whole thing lives in a refrigerator colder than outer space. You will compute a transmon's frequency yourself and learn to read the spec sheets of real chips. It builds on section 1's T1, T2 and fidelity arithmetic.

1. The idea in plain words: an artificial atom on a chip

An inductor and a capacitor in a loop (an LC circuit) oscillate like a mass on a spring. Cooled until it is superconducting and has no resistance, that oscillator becomes quantum: its energy comes in levels Ek = (k + ½)hf. The problem is that the levels are equally spaced. A microwave pulse tuned to drive |0⟩ → |1⟩ is also exactly tuned to drive |1⟩ → |2⟩, |2⟩ → |3⟩ and so on, so you can never confine the system to two levels. You need a non-linear element that makes the gap 1→2 different from the gap 0→1. That element is the Josephson junction: two superconducting films (usually aluminium) separated by an insulating barrier about a nanometre thick, through which Cooper pairs tunnel. It behaves like an inductor whose inductance depends on the current through it, and that non-linearity makes the energy ladder uneven. Once 0→1 and 1→2 differ by a few hundred MHz, a carefully shaped pulse at the 0→1 frequency addresses just those two levels: you have an artificial atom you designed with lithography.

2. The definition: the transmon

📘 DEFINITION

A transmon is a Josephson junction (or two, forming a flux-tunable SQUID loop) shunted by a large capacitor. It is described by two energies: the Josephson energy EJ (how easily Cooper pairs tunnel) and the charging energy EC = e²/2C (the cost of adding one electron charge to the capacitance C). The large capacitor makes EJ/EC of order tens to about a hundred, which makes the qubit frequency almost independent of stray charges on the chip (charge noise), at the price of a smaller anharmonicity.

📊 FIGURE — Why a transmon is a qubit: equal versus unequal energy gaps
An LC circuit has equal gaps, so one tone climbs every rung. The junction bends the well, f₁₂ falls 277 MHz below f₀₁, and a pulse at f₀₁ addresses only |0⟩ and |1⟩ (gaps exaggerated).

The qubit is the lowest two levels |0⟩ and |1⟩; level |2⟩ is the nearest trap door, and population that falls into it is called leakage.

🧮 KEY EQUATION

H = 4EC(n̂ − ng)² − EJ cos φ̂

f01 ≈ √(8·EJ·EC) − EC    α = f12 − f01 ≈ −EC

Symbols: H is the Hamiltonian (energy operator); n̂ is the number of Cooper pairs that have tunnelled across the junction; ng is an offset charge set by stray fields (the charge noise); φ̂ is the superconducting phase difference across the junction; EJ and EC as defined above. Energies are written divided by Planck's constant h, so they are in GHz. f01 is the qubit frequency and α the anharmonicity (negative for a transmon). The approximations hold for EJ/EC ≫ 1.

3. Control, readout and the refrigerator

Single-qubit gates are microwave pulses at f01 (a few GHz) sent down coaxial lines. The pulse area sets the rotation angle and its phase sets the axis, so an X or Y rotation takes tens of nanoseconds. Pulses are shaped (a common scheme is called DRAG) so that they do not accidentally drive the 1→2 transition only a few hundred MHz away. Z rotations are usually \"virtual\": software simply shifts the phase of every later pulse, which costs no time and no error.

Two-qubit gates need neighbouring qubits to interact. Modern chips place a tunable coupler (itself a small flux-tunable circuit) between neighbours and switch the interaction on for tens of nanoseconds to produce a CZ gate; IBM's older fixed-frequency chips used a microwave-driven \"cross-resonance\" interaction. Couplers only link nearest neighbours on a planar grid, so connectivity is limited (a square lattice gives each qubit up to four neighbours), and distant qubits need SWAP chains.

Readout is dispersive: each qubit is coupled to its own microwave resonator, and the resonator's frequency shifts slightly depending on whether the qubit is in |0⟩ or |1⟩. You send a weak probe tone, a quantum-limited parametric amplifier boosts the reflected signal, and room-temperature electronics decide 0 or 1 from its phase and amplitude. Readout takes of order hundreds of nanoseconds to a microsecond and is often the least accurate operation on the chip.

The refrigerator. A 6 GHz photon carries very little energy. For the qubit to sit reliably in |0⟩ the thermal energy kBT must be far smaller than hf, and the aluminium must be superconducting. That requires a dilution refrigerator, which mixes helium-3 and helium-4 to reach about 10-20 millikelvin. Every control line brings heat and noise down from room temperature, so each line is filtered and attenuated at several temperature stages. Wiring and fridge volume are among the hardest scaling problems: IBM's 1,121-qubit Condor needed over a mile of cryogenic flex cabling in one fridge.

4. Worked example: compute a transmon and its operating temperature

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Design values (energies over h): EJ = 20 GHz, EC = 0.25 GHz, so EJ/EC = 80. All numbers below were computed in Python with numpy and scipy-style constants (h = 6.62607015×10−34 J s, kB = 1.380649×10−23 J/K).

  1. Approximate frequency. √(8 × 20 × 0.25) = √40 = 6.3246 GHz; subtract EC: f01 ≈ 6.0746 GHz. Anharmonicity α ≈ −EC = −250 MHz.
  2. Exact check by diagonalisation. Write H in the charge basis n = −30…30: 4EC(n − ng)² on the diagonal and −EJ/2 on the two off-diagonals (because cos φ̂ shifts n by ±1). The eigenvalues give f01 = 6.0635 GHz and α = −277.4 MHz. The simple formula is within 0.2% for f01 but underestimates |α| by about 10%.
  3. Charge insensitivity. Changing the offset charge from ng = 0 to 0.5 (the worst case) moves f01 by about 9×10−5 MHz, i.e. roughly 90 Hz out of 6 GHz. That exponential suppression is the whole point of the transmon.
  4. Thermal population. For f = 6 GHz, hf/kBT at 10 mK is 28.80, so the Boltzmann factor e−28.80 = 3.1×10−13: effectively zero. At 100 mK: hf/kBT = 2.880, excited fraction e−x/(1+e−x) = 0.0532, a 5% initialisation error. At 4 K (liquid helium): 0.482, nearly a coin flip.
  5. Energy decay during a computation. With T1 = 68 µs, the chance a qubit is still in |1⟩ after 20 µs is e−20/68 = 0.7452. With a 50 ns two-qubit gate, 68 µs holds about 1,360 gate durations.

Sanity check: f01 is a few GHz and α a few hundred MHz, the right ballpark for real transmons; the thermal fraction can never exceed 0.5 for a two-level system at positive temperature, and at 4 K it approaches 0.5 from below.

The diagonalisation in step 2, as it ran (energies in GHz):

import numpy as np

EJ, EC, ng = 20.0, 0.25, 0.0

n = np.arange(-30, 31)

H = np.diag(4*EC*(n-ng)**2) - EJ/2*(np.eye(61, k=1) + np.eye(61, k=-1))

E = np.linalg.eigvalsh(H)

print(E[1]-E[0], (E[2]-E[1])-(E[1]-E[0])) # 6.0635 -0.2774

5. Typical numbers and the leading systems

Treat the following as ranges and trends, not permanent records. On large processors, average T1 is in the tens to about a hundred microseconds; the best individual laboratory transmons now exceed a millisecond. Two-qubit gates take tens of nanoseconds, with errors typically a few tenths of a percent on leading chips; single-qubit errors are around a few hundredths of a percent; readout is often the weakest link at around half a percent to a percent or more. The trend is steady improvement of coherence through materials (tantalum and silicon substrates reduce lossy surface defects) and a shift from \"more qubits\" to \"better qubits plus error correction\".

System (organisation)QubitsChecked figuresDate
Willow (Google)105Mean T1 68 ± 13 µs; CZ error 0.33% ± 0.18%; single-qubit error 0.036%; readout error 0.77% (error-correction configuration); surface-code logical error fell as distance grew from 3 to 5 to 7Dec 2024
Condor (IBM)1,121Scale and yield demonstration, not IBM's performance flagshipDec 2023
Heron (IBM)156 (r2)Tunable couplers; IBM's flagship for utility-scale experiments in 2024-25Dec 2023 onward
Nighthawk (IBM)120218 tunable couplers (square lattice); IBM says up to 5,000 two-qubit gates per circuitNov 2025
Zuchongzhi 3.0 (USTC)105Parallel two-qubit fidelity 99.62%, readout 99.13%, coherence about 72 µs; random-circuit sampling on 83 qubits2025 (PRL)
Tantalum-on-silicon transmons (Princeton)single devicesT1 up to 1.68 msNov 2025 (Nature)

Strengths: fast gates, fabrication with chip-industry tools, flexible circuit design, the most mature control stacks, and the first clear below-threshold surface-code demonstration. Bottlenecks: millikelvin cryogenics and wiring per qubit, limited nearest-neighbour connectivity, device-to-device variation (every junction is slightly different, so every qubit needs calibration), two-level-system defects in materials that make T1 fluctuate over hours, and correlated errors from cosmic rays and radioactivity that can hit many qubits at once.

✅ VERIFIED

Willow: 105 qubits, announced 9 Dec 2024; mean T1 improved from about 20 µs to 68 ± 13 µs; below-threshold surface code up to distance 7 published in Nature. Google Research. Spec-sheet error rates (CZ 0.33%, single-qubit 0.036%, readout 0.77%): Willow spec sheet.

IBM Condor (1,121 qubits, over a mile of flex wiring) and Heron (156 qubits in r2) announced 4 Dec 2023: IBM Heron summary, PostQuantum. Nighthawk (120 qubits, 218 tunable couplers, 5,000 two-qubit gates) and the experimental Loon chip for qLDPC codes, 12 Nov 2025: IBM Newsroom.

Zuchongzhi 3.0: Phys. Rev. Lett. 134, 090601 (2025). APS. Princeton tantalum-on-silicon transmons with T1 up to 1.68 ms, Nature, Nov 2025: Nature. Transmons operate at about 10-20 mK in dilution refrigerators: QuEra glossary. All checked 28 Sep 2026.

❓ NOT VERIFIED

IBM's roadmap lists a multi-chip \"Kookaburra\" processor for 2026 and a fault-tolerant \"Starling\" system for 2029. Search results did not confirm that Kookaburra had been delivered by late September 2026. Roadmap items are plans, not results: confirm before you rely on this.

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE
  • Quoting a hero number as typical. A 1.68 ms T1 on a test device is not the average T1 of a 100-qubit processor, which is currently tens of microseconds to around 0.1 ms.
  • Thinking \"cold\" means liquid helium. At 4 K a 6 GHz transmon is 48% thermally excited; it needs about 10-20 mK.
  • Forgetting the third level. A transmon is a weakly anharmonic ladder; fast, badly shaped pulses leak population into |2⟩, which ordinary qubit error models do not describe.
  • Reading 1,121 qubits as progress over 105. Condor showed wiring and fabrication at scale; the performance frontier moved to smaller, better chips.
★ ON THE EXAM
  • Explain why an LC circuit alone cannot be a qubit and what the Josephson junction adds.
  • Use f01 ≈ √(8EJEC) − EC and α ≈ −EC; explain the EJ/EC trade-off.
  • Compute a Boltzmann excited-state fraction or an e−t/T1 survival probability.
  • Describe dispersive readout and list three scaling bottlenecks.

This lesson covers the two platforms that use nature's own qubits: single atoms. Trapped ions hold the fidelity records; neutral-atom arrays hold the qubit-count records and have moved fastest in error-correction experiments since 2023. You will learn how each traps, controls and entangles its atoms, compute the entangled state a trapped-ion gate makes, and compare an ion machine with a superconducting one on the same circuit. It uses the fidelity arithmetic from section 1 and contrasts with the engineered circuits of section 2.

1. The idea in plain words: identical qubits, held by fields and light

Every atom of a given isotope is identical to every other one. A superconducting qubit's frequency depends on how a particular junction was fabricated; a ytterbium-171 ion's qubit frequency is set by physics and is the same in every lab in the world. Atoms are also naturally well isolated: in ultra-high vacuum, with no solid material touching them, some atomic qubits keep their phase for seconds to far longer. The engineering challenge moves elsewhere: holding individual atoms still, pointing lasers at them precisely, and making two atoms interact on demand. Charged atoms (ions) are held by oscillating electric fields; neutral atoms, which feel no net electric force, are held by tightly focused laser beams.

2. Trapped ions: hyperfine qubits and gates through shared motion

📘 DEFINITION

A trapped-ion qubit is stored in two internal levels of a single ion held in a Paul trap (a radio-frequency electric quadrupole) in vacuum. Popular choices are hyperfine ground-state levels, split by the interaction between the electron and nuclear spins. In 171Yb+ the qubit is |F=0, mF=0⟩ ↔ |F=1, mF=0⟩ at about 12.6 GHz. These are clock states: their splitting does not change to first order with magnetic field, which is why they keep coherence so long.

Ions in one trap repel each other and form a line (a Coulomb crystal). Their shared vibrations, the motional modes, act like a quantum data bus: a laser (or, in newer designs, microwave or electronic control) pushes on two ions with a force that depends on their qubit states, which briefly entangles qubits with motion and then leaves the two qubits entangled with each other. That is the Mølmer-Sørensen (MS) gate.

Because every ion in the chain shares the same modes, any pair can be gated directly: all-to-all connectivity, no SWAP chains. Readout is by fluorescence: a laser makes the ion scatter many photons if it is in one state and almost none if it is in the other, and a camera or detector counts them. The price is speed. Two-qubit gates typically take tens to hundreds of microseconds, roughly a thousand times slower than superconducting gates, and long chains become crowded with modes that are hard to address. The main scaling answer is the QCCD (quantum charge-coupled device) architecture, used by Quantinuum: a chip with many trap zones, and ions physically shuttled between memory, gate and readout zones by changing electrode voltages.

🧮 KEY EQUATION

UMS(θ) = exp(−i·θ·X⊗X/2) = cos(θ/2)·I − i·sin(θ/2)·X⊗X

UMS(π/2)|00⟩ = (|00⟩ − i|11⟩)/√2

Symbols: X is the Pauli-X matrix [[0,1],[1,0]]; X⊗X flips both qubits (|00⟩ ↔ |11⟩, |01⟩ ↔ |10⟩); θ is the gate angle set by laser power and duration; I is the 4×4 identity. The second equality uses (X⊗X)² = I, which lets the exponential be written as a cosine plus a sine. Convention: |q0q1⟩ with qubit 0 on the left (textbook order).

The matrix of UMS(π/2) in the basis |00⟩, |01⟩, |10⟩, |11⟩, computed with scipy's matrix exponential and checked against the cosine-sine form:

1/√2 ×100−i
01−i0
0−i10
−i001

Together with single-qubit rotations it is equivalent to a CNOT, so {single-qubit rotations, MS} is a universal gate set (DiVincenzo criterion 4).

3. Neutral atoms: tweezer arrays and the Rydberg blockade

A neutral-atom machine starts with a cloud of laser-cooled atoms (rubidium, caesium, strontium or ytterbium are common). A spatial light modulator or acousto-optic deflectors split one laser into a grid of hundreds to thousands of optical tweezers, each a tight focus that can hold one atom. Loading is random: each tweezer ends up with one atom about half the time. A camera images which sites are full, then movable tweezers drag atoms into a defect-free pattern. The qubit is stored in two long-lived ground or metastable levels (hyperfine or nuclear-spin states).

📘 DEFINITION

A Rydberg state is an atomic state with the outer electron in a very high orbit, making the atom enormous and giving it very strong interactions with nearby Rydberg atoms. Rydberg blockade: if two atoms are closer than the blockade radius Rb, the interaction shifts the doubly-excited state so far that a laser can excite only one of them. A pulse sequence that tries to excite both therefore picks up a phase that depends on whether both qubits were in the \"excitable\" state, which implements a controlled-Z gate.

Key relation: Rb = (C6 / ħΩ)1/6, where C6 is the van der Waals coefficient of the Rydberg state (grows steeply with principal quantum number), ħ is the reduced Planck constant and Ω the Rabi frequency (drive strength) of the excitation laser.

Neutral atoms have two distinctive strengths. First, scale: arrays of thousands of atoms now exist, far beyond other platforms' physical-qubit counts. Second, reconfigurable connectivity: atoms can be moved mid-computation, so whole blocks of qubits can be shuttled next to each other and entangled in parallel. That makes \"transversal\" logical gates (the same gate on every physical qubit of two code blocks) natural, which is why this platform produced the first computations on dozens of logical qubits. The bottlenecks are atom loss (every atom eventually escapes, so continuous reloading is needed), slower measurement and reloading cycles than superconducting chips, two-qubit fidelities that only recently reached about 99.5%, and leakage out of the qubit levels during Rydberg excitation.

4. Worked example: ions versus a lattice, and filling an atom array

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

All values computed in Python (numpy, scipy.linalg.expm, math).

📊 FIGURE — Trapped ions, superconducting chips and neutral atoms side by side
Read across a row to compare one property. The bottom box is the worked example: fidelity and connectivity compound, so ions win on success while the chip wins on speed.
  1. The MS gate. expm(−i·(π/4)·X⊗X) applied to (1,0,0,0) gives (0.7071, 0, 0, −0.7071i): the state (|00⟩ − i|11⟩)/√2. Measuring gives 00 or 11 with probability 0.7071² = 0.5 each, never 01 or 10, a maximally entangled state.
  2. Same algorithm, two machines. A 1,000-two-qubit-gate circuit. Ion machine: F = 0.99921, all-to-all, so 1,000 gates: 0.999211000 = 0.4537. Superconducting lattice: F = 0.9967; with no routing 0.99671000 = 0.0367; if routing adds 300 SWAPs (×3 = 900 extra CZs), 0.99671900 = 0.0019. Connectivity and fidelity compound together.
  3. Wall-clock time for the same 1,000 gates run one after another: ions at 200 µs each take 0.2 s; superconducting at 50 ns each take 50 µs, 4,000 times faster. If an application needs 105 repetitions, that is 5.6 hours versus 5 seconds of gate time.
  4. Random loading. 12,000 tweezers, each filled with probability p = 0.5: the number of atoms is binomial with mean np = 6,000 and standard deviation √(np(1−p)) = 54.8. The probability that 100 specific sites are all filled is 0.5100 = 7.9×10−31, so rearrangement is not optional.
  5. Blockade scaling. Rb ∝ Ω−1/6. Doubling Ω shrinks Rb by 21/6 = 1.1225 (10.9% smaller); raising Ω 64-fold halves it, since 641/6 = 2. Faster gates (bigger Ω) cost interaction range.

Sanity checks: 0.5 + 0.5 = 1 for the MS outcomes; 0.999211000 lies between 0.9991000 = 0.3677 and 0.99991000 = 0.9048; 6,000 ± 55 atoms matches the roughly half-filled 12,000-site array reported by Caltech.

5. Where the two platforms stand (ranges and trends)

Platform and resultChecked figuresDate
171Yb+ single-ion memoryCoherence time estimated at about 5,500 s (over an hour) with dynamical decoupling and sympathetic cooling2021
Quantinuum Helios (trapped ions, barium)98 qubits, all-to-all; two-qubit fidelity 99.921%, single-qubit 99.9975%; 48 error-corrected logical qubits at 2:1 encoding, 94 in error-detected modeNov 2025; Nature 2026
IonQ / Oxford Ionics (trapped ions)Two-qubit fidelity above 99.99% on prototypes using electronic (not laser) control; previous record 99.97% (2024)Oct 2025
Harvard, QuEra, MIT, NIST/UMD (atoms)48 logical qubits from 280 atoms, with transversal logical gatesDec 2023
Harvard, MIT, QuEra (atoms)99.5% two-qubit gates in parallel on 60 atoms2023
Caltech (caesium tweezers)Over 6,100 atoms in about 12,000 sites; coherence 12.6 s; single-qubit fidelity 99.98%Sep 2025
Harvard, MIT, QuEra (atoms)Over 3,000 atoms kept for over two hours by reloading 300,000 atoms per second2025
Harvard, MIT, QuEra (atoms)448-atom fault-tolerant architecture, 2.14× below thresholdNature, 1 Jan 2026

The trends: ions push fidelity towards 99.99% and are moving from laser to chip-integrated electronic control to scale; atom arrays push qubit counts into the thousands and are solving loss by continuous reloading. Both communities now report logical qubits, and Google, previously a superconducting-only lab, added a neutral-atom hardware programme in March 2026, a sign that the field does not yet know which platform wins.

✅ VERIFIED

171Yb+ clock-state splitting 12.642812 GHz: arXiv:1803.02545. Single-ion coherence about 5,500 s: Nature Communications 12, 233 (2021), Nature Comms.

Helios figures: Quantinuum and Nature (2026); 94 error-detected versus 48 error-corrected: The Quantum Insider. IonQ 99.99% (21 Oct 2025): The Quantum Insider.

48 logical qubits (Dec 2023): Harvard Gazette. 99.5% parallel gates: QuEra. Caltech 6,100 atoms (Nature, 24 Sep 2025): Caltech. Continuous 3,000-qubit operation: Nature via PMC. 448-atom architecture: Nature. Google neutral-atom programme (24 Mar 2026): The Quantum Insider. Trapped-ion gate times of tens to hundreds of µs: review arXiv:1904.04178. All checked 28 Sep 2026.

❓ NOT VERIFIED
  • Secondary sites describe the 448-atom Nature paper as \"96 logical qubits\"; the primary sources found describe a 448-atom architecture without that count.
  • Reports that Atom Computing demonstrated repeated toric-code error correction in June 2026, and that neutral-atom two-qubit fidelity has reached 99.7%, came only from secondary summaries.

Confirm before you rely on this.

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE
  • \"All-to-all\" does not mean \"all at once\". Any pair can interact, but a single chain usually runs few gates in parallel, so depth in time can be long.
  • Counting logical qubits without the qualifier. Error-detected logical qubits (errors flagged, runs discarded) are not error-corrected ones; Helios's 94 versus 48 is exactly this distinction.
  • Equating atoms trapped with qubits computed on. An array of 6,100 atoms shows trapping and single-qubit control; it is not a 6,100-qubit entangling processor.
  • Forgetting the 1/√2. The MS output is (|00⟩ − i|11⟩)/√2; without the normalisation the probabilities would sum to 2.
★ ON THE EXAM
  • Explain why hyperfine clock states are long-lived and why ions have all-to-all connectivity.
  • Apply UMS(π/2) to a basis state and give outcome probabilities.
  • Describe Rydberg blockade and use Rb ∝ Ω−1/6.
  • Compare ions, atoms and superconducting qubits on fidelity, speed, connectivity and scale with numbers.

This lesson covers three very different routes to a qubit: photons (light that barely interacts with anything), spins of single electrons or defects in solids (qubits the size of a transistor), and topological qubits (information hidden in exotic quasiparticles, whose very existence in devices is still disputed). For each you will learn the physics, compute the key numbers, and, most importantly, separate what has been demonstrated from what has been claimed. That last skill matters more here than anywhere else in the degree, because this is where the headlines run furthest ahead of the data.

📊 FIGURE — Photonic, spin and topological qubits: physics and evidence
Each column is one route to a qubit. The status boxes separate what has been shown in the lab (green) from what has only been claimed (red).

1. Photonic qubits: perfect travellers, reluctant partners

A photon hardly interacts with its environment, so it keeps its quantum state at room temperature and can travel through kilometres of fibre: ideal for DiVincenzo's criteria 6 and 7. The same property is the problem for computing: two photons do not naturally interact, so an entangling gate is hard. Photonic computing therefore replaces interaction with measurement. Detecting photons after they have interfered on beam splitters is itself a strong non-linear operation, and the outcome tells you what happened.

📘 DEFINITION

Dual-rail encoding: one photon shared between two optical modes (waveguides) a and b; |0L⟩ = photon in a, |1L⟩ = photon in b. A beam splitter plus phase shifters implement any single-qubit gate deterministically.

Measurement-based (one-way) computing: prepare a large entangled cluster state first, then compute purely by measuring qubits one at a time in chosen bases, adapting later bases to earlier outcomes (feed-forward). Fusion-based computing builds that entanglement from many small \"resource states\" joined by fusion measurements (two-photon entangling measurements that succeed with some probability and herald whether they did).

🧮 KEY EQUATION

BS50:50 = (1/√2)[[1, 1], [1, −1]]   (acting on the amplitudes of modes a, b; the same matrix as H)

Psurvive = ηn    Pall k fusions succeed = pfk

Symbols: η is the transmission of one optical component (1 means lossless); n is the number of components a photon passes; pf is the success probability of one fusion or linear-optics Bell measurement (at most 1/2 for the basic scheme without extra photons); k is the number of fusions that must all succeed. Real beam splitters often use the convention (1/√2)[[1, i],[i, 1]]; it differs from H only by phases.

Loss is the dominant error: a photon absorbed or scattered simply vanishes. Sources must emit exactly one photon on demand, detectors (often superconducting nanowire detectors, which need a few kelvin) must catch nearly every photon, and every waveguide and switch must be nearly lossless. A second strategy, continuous-variable photonics, encodes qubits in the quadratures of light, for example Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) states, with error correction built into the encoding. Photonics produced early \"beyond classical\" boson sampling demonstrations (sampling from interfering photons, a task with no known practical use), and companies now build chips in commercial semiconductor foundries.

2. Spin qubits: silicon quantum dots and NV centres

An electron has a spin, a built-in magnetic moment that points \"up\" or \"down\" along an applied magnetic field B. In a silicon spin qubit, gate electrodes much like those of a transistor trap a single electron in a quantum dot about tens of nanometres across. The two spin states are split by the Zeeman energy, f = g·μB·B / h, where g ≈ 2 is the electron g-factor, μB the Bohr magneton, B the field and h Planck's constant. Single-qubit gates use microwaves at f (electron spin resonance, or electric driving with a micromagnet); two-qubit gates come from the exchange interaction J, switched on by lowering the barrier between neighbouring dots. Isotopically purified silicon-28 removes most nuclear spins, which are the main source of dephasing.

The appeal is industrial: spin qubits are tiny and can be made on 300 mm wafers in existing chip fabs, and some operate above 1 kelvin, where cooling power is far greater than at 10 mK. The difficulties: dots vary from device to device, each qubit needs several control wires, crosstalk grows with density, and arrays so far hold roughly a dozen qubits. Note the physics of \"hot\" operation: at 1 K a 20 GHz spin has hf/kBT = 0.96, so it is not thermally initialised; experiments use spin-selective tunnelling or algorithmic initialisation instead.

A nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centre is a defect in diamond: a nitrogen atom next to a missing carbon atom. Its ground state is a spin-1 triplet with a 2.87 GHz zero-field splitting; green light initialises it and its red fluorescence (zero-phonon line at 637 nm) depends on the spin state, giving optical readout even at room temperature, where its electron spin keeps coherence for milliseconds in purified diamond. Nearby 13C nuclear spins act as long-lived memory qubits. NV centres excel as sensors (of magnetic field, temperature) and as network nodes that link spins to photons, but they are hard to scale into processors: every defect sits in a slightly different environment and collecting its photons efficiently is difficult.

3. Topological qubits and the Majorana claims

📘 DEFINITION

A Majorana zero mode (MZM) is a predicted quasiparticle excitation at the ends of a one-dimensional topological superconductor (for example a semiconductor nanowire coated with a superconductor, in a magnetic field). Two MZMs together store one bit of fermion parity (whether an extra electron is present) non-locally: no local disturbance at one end can read or flip it. A topological qubit encodes quantum information in such parities (Microsoft's design, the tetron, uses four MZMs); its errors should be suppressed roughly as e−L/ξ, where L is the separation of the modes and ξ the superconducting coherence length. Exchanging (\"braiding\") MZMs would give Clifford gates protected by topology; non-Clifford gates would still need magic states.

That exponential suppression is the prize: if real, topological qubits would need far less error-correction overhead. The hard part is proving that a device really contains MZMs, because ordinary (topologically trivial) Andreev bound states caused by disorder can mimic many of their signatures. The record so far:

This lesson lets you set up and run a variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) by hand: write a Hamiltonian as a sum of Pauli strings, choose a parameterised circuit, estimate its energy from measurement counts, and let a classical optimiser push the energy down. It opens the NISQ chapter, which sits after error correction and hardware in the degree: we now ask what can be done on today's noisy machines without full fault tolerance, and how honest the evidence is.

The idea in plain words

John Preskill named the current period NISQ: Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum. Machines have tens to hundreds (now a few thousand) of physical qubits, but every gate has an error rate somewhere around 10-3 to 10-2, and there is no error correction running underneath. A circuit with thousands of two-qubit gates therefore returns mostly noise. Phase estimation (the qft chapter) is far too deep.

Variational algorithms split the work. The quantum computer does only what it is uniquely good at: prepare a state |ψ(θ)⟩ with a short circuit whose gate angles θ = (θ1, ..., θm) are knobs, and measure it. A classical computer reads the averaged results, computes a single number (usually an energy), and chooses new knobs. Round and round the loop goes, like training a model where each loss evaluation is a batch of shots on a quantum processor.

  1. Classical side picks θ.
  2. Quantum side runs the circuit U(θ)|0...0⟩ many times (shots) in a few measurement bases.
  3. Classical side averages the outcomes into an energy estimate E(θ).
  4. An optimiser (gradient descent, COBYLA, SPSA, ...) proposes a better θ; repeat until the energy stops falling.

The variational principle

📘 DEFINITION

An ansatz is a family of states |ψ(θ)⟩ = U(θ)|0...0⟩ produced by a fixed circuit layout with adjustable rotation angles θ. A hardware-efficient ansatz uses layers of native single-qubit rotations and entangling gates; a problem-inspired ansatz (for chemistry, unitary coupled cluster) is built from the physics. The variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) minimises E(θ) = ⟨ψ(θ)|H|ψ(θ)⟩ over θ to approximate the ground-state energy E0 of a Hamiltonian H.

Why minimising should work is the Rayleigh-Ritz variational principle. Write the state in the eigenbasis of H: |ψ⟩ = ∑k ck|Ek⟩ with H|Ek⟩ = Ek|Ek⟩ and E0 ≤ E1 ≤ .... Then

⟨ψ|H|ψ⟩ = ∑k |ck|2 Ek ≥ E0 ∑k |ck|2 = E0

because each Ek ≥ E0 and the weights |ck|2 are probabilities summing to 1. Equality holds only if all the weight sits on ground states. So every trial state gives an upper bound, and lowering the energy can only bring you closer to E0 from above.

🧮 KEY EQUATION

E(θ) = ⟨ψ(θ)|H|ψ(θ)⟩ ≥ E0 for every θ

H = ∑P cP P, cP = Tr(P H) / 2n

Here H is the n-qubit Hamiltonian (a 2n × 2n Hermitian matrix), E0 its lowest eigenvalue, θ the vector of circuit angles, P runs over Pauli strings such as Z⊗I or X⊗X (tensor products of I, X, Y, Z), and cP are real coefficients. Since Tr(PQ) = 2n δPQ, the trace formula picks out each coefficient. By linearity, E(θ) = ∑P cP ⟨P⟩θ: measure each Pauli expectation and add them with their weights.

Measuring a Hamiltonian as a sum of Paulis

Hardware measures in the computational (Z) basis only. To get ⟨Z⟩ you just count: ⟨Z⟩ = P(0) − P(1). To get ⟨X⟩ you first rotate the X eigenbasis onto the Z basis with a Hadamard (H maps |+⟩ to |0⟩ and |−⟩ to |1⟩), then count. For ⟨Y⟩ apply S† then H. For a multi-qubit string like Z⊗X, rotate each qubit into its own basis and use the product of the ±1 outcomes. Pauli strings that commute qubit-by-qubit (Z⊗I, I⊗Z and Z⊗Z) can share one set of shots; that grouping is a major saving because molecular Hamiltonians have hundreds to thousands of terms.

Worked example: a one-qubit VQE energy landscape

Convention: |0⟩ = (1,0)T, |1⟩ = (0,1)T, Ry(θ) = exp(−iθY/2). All numbers below were computed with numpy and checked with Qiskit.

📊 FIGURE — The VQE loop, run on H = Z + 0.5X with a one-angle ansatz
Top: the quantum side only prepares and measures; the classical side turns counts into E(θ) and a new angle. Bottom: gradient descent walks the landscape down to E₀ = −1.1180.
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Find the ground energy of the Hamiltonian below with the one-parameter ansatz |ψ(θ)⟩ = Ry(θ)|0⟩ = cos(θ/2)|0⟩ + sin(θ/2)|1⟩.

  1. Decompose into Paulis. cI = Tr(H)/2 = (1 − 1)/2 = 0; cZ = Tr(ZH)/2 = (1 + 1)/2 = 1; cX = Tr(XH)/2 = (0.5 + 0.5)/2 = 0.5; cY = 0 (H is real and symmetric). So H = Z + 0.5 X.
  2. Expectations for the ansatz. With a = cos(θ/2), b = sin(θ/2): ⟨Z⟩ = a2 − b2 = cos θ and ⟨X⟩ = 2ab = sin θ.
  3. Energy function. E(θ) = cos θ + 0.5 sin θ.
  4. Scan the landscape (the table below).
  5. Locate the minimum. Write E(θ) = R cos(θ − φ) with R = √(1 + 0.25) = √1.25 = 1.1180 and φ = arctan(0.5/1) = 0.4636 rad. The minimum is at θ* = φ + π = 3.6052 rad (206.57°), where E = −R = −1.1180.
  6. Check against exact diagonalisation. numpy.linalg.eigh(H) gives eigenvalues −1.1180 and +1.1180, ground eigenvector (0.2298, −0.9732). The optimal ansatz state is (cos 1.8026, sin 1.8026) = (−0.2298, 0.9732): the same vector times the global phase −1, which is physically identical.

Letting the optimiser do it. For gates of the form exp(−iθP/2) the parameter-shift rule gives an exact gradient from two extra energy evaluations: dE/dθ = [E(θ + π/2) − E(θ − π/2)] / 2. At θ = π/2 this is [E(π) − E(0)]/2 = (−1 − 1)/2 = −1, matching the analytic derivative −sin θ + 0.5 cos θ = −1. Gradient descent with step η = 0.5 from θ = π/2:

Six steps reach −1.1168, within 0.0012 of the exact −1.1180. In Qiskit (runs as written):

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from qiskit.quantum_info import Statevector, SparsePauliOp
H = SparsePauliOp([\"Z\", \"X\"], coeffs=[1.0, 0.5])
qc = QuantumCircuit(1); qc.ry(3.6052, 0)
print(Statevector(qc).expectation_value(H).real) # -1.11803...

Shot counts: the hidden cost

On hardware you never see ⟨Z⟩ exactly; you see a sample mean of ±1 outcomes. A single shot of a Pauli P has variance 1 − ⟨P⟩2, so the standard error after N shots is √((1 − ⟨P⟩2)/N). At the optimum above, ⟨Z⟩ = −0.8944 (variance 0.2) and ⟨X⟩ = −0.4472 (variance 0.8). Measuring each basis with N shots gives

Var(Ê) = 12 × 0.2/N + 0.52 × 0.8/N = 0.4/N

For a standard error of 0.01 you need N = 0.4/0.012 = 4,000 shots per basis. Chemists want \"chemical accuracy\", about 1.6 × 10-3 hartree; that needs N = 0.4/(0.0016)2 = 156,250 shots per basis for this toy problem, per energy evaluation, per optimiser step. Real molecules have far more terms with larger coefficients, and the shot bill is one of the main practical obstacles to VQE.

📊 YOUR DATA EDGE

This is ordinary sampling statistics. Each shot is a Bernoulli trial mapped to ±1; ⟨P⟩ is a mean; the standard error falls like 1/√N, so halving the error costs four times the shots. Treat an optimiser working on noisy energies like stochastic gradient descent on mini-batches: noisy steps are fine, but comparing two nearby energies that differ by less than their standard errors is reading tea leaves.

The traps

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Believing a VQE energy below the true E0. The bound holds for the exact expectation value of a physical state. Shot noise, readout error and error mitigation (next lessons) all produce estimates that can dip below E0; that is a statistical or systematic error, not a better answer.

Other slips: reading ⟨X⟩ from Z-basis counts without the Hadamard; forgetting that cP = Tr(PH)/2n includes the 1/2n; assuming a low energy means a good state (the bound says you are above E0, not how far); and assuming the ansatz can reach the ground state at all. Our one-parameter Ry ansatz only worked because H had no Y term.

✅ VERIFIED

Preskill, \"Quantum Computing in the NISQ era and beyond\", Quantum 2, 79 (2018): quantum-journal.org.

Peruzzo et al., \"A variational eigenvalue solver on a photonic quantum processor\", Nature Communications 5, 4213 (2014), the first VQE, finding the ground energy of HeH+: nature.com.

Kandala et al., \"Hardware-efficient variational quantum eigensolver for small molecules and quantum magnets\", Nature 549, 242-246 (2017): up to six superconducting qubits, more than one hundred Pauli terms, molecules up to BeH2: nature.com. All checked 28 Sep 2026.

Be honest about what these showed. A six-qubit Hamiltonian is a 64 × 64 matrix, which a laptop diagonalises instantly. These were demonstrations that the loop works, not computations beyond classical reach. There is no proof that VQE is faster than classical methods for any chemistry problem, and whether it can ever beat good classical methods (coupled cluster, DMRG) at scale is an open question.

What the exam asks

★ ON THE EXAM
  • State and prove the variational principle in two lines (expand in the eigenbasis).
  • Decompose a 2 × 2 or 4 × 4 Hermitian matrix into Paulis with cP = Tr(PH)/2n.
  • Compute E(θ) for an Ry ansatz and find its minimum, or apply the parameter-shift rule once.
  • Say which basis change measures X or Y, and estimate how many shots a target precision needs.
  • Explain what VQE has and has not demonstrated.

This lesson lets you turn a graph problem into a qubit Hamiltonian, build the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) circuit, and compute its p = 1 expectation value by hand for a triangle. It is the optimisation twin of VQE from the last lesson: same hybrid loop, but the Hamiltonian is diagonal and encodes a combinatorial cost. We finish with a sober account of what is and is not known about quantum advantage for optimisation.

The idea in plain words

Max-Cut: colour each vertex of a graph with one of two colours (0 or 1) so that as many edges as possible join vertices of different colours. Such an edge is \"cut\". Max-Cut is NP-hard in general, so nobody expects any algorithm, quantum or classical, to solve every instance efficiently; the interesting question is how good an approximate answer each method gets for a given amount of work.

QAOA writes the number of cut edges as an energy, starts in an equal superposition of all colourings, and alternates two kinds of layer: a cost layer that stamps each colouring with a phase proportional to its cut size, and a mixer layer that lets amplitude flow between colourings so the phases interfere. Two angles per layer, (γ, β), are tuned by a classical optimiser so that measuring gives large cuts often.

From Max-Cut to an Ising Hamiltonian

Give each vertex j a qubit. A bitstring z = z0z1...zn−1 is a colouring. For an edge (i, j), the operator ZiZj has eigenvalue +1 on |z⟩ if zi = zj and −1 if they differ. So (1 − ZiZj)/2 is 1 exactly when the edge is cut.

🧮 KEY EQUATION

C = ∑(i,j) ∈ E (1 − ZiZj)/2, C|z⟩ = cut(z)|z⟩

|γ, β⟩ = UB(βp)UC(γp) ... UB(β1)UC(γ1) |+⟩⊗n

UC(γ) = e−iγC, UB(β) = e−iβ B, B = ∑j Xj

E is the edge set, Zi the Pauli Z on qubit i, cut(z) the number of edges cut by colouring z, C the cost Hamiltonian (diagonal in the computational basis), B the transverse-field mixer, p the number of layers, and γ = (γ1, ..., γp), β = (β1, ..., βp) the 2p angles. The objective is Fp(γ, β) = ⟨γ, β|C|γ, β⟩ and the approximation ratio is r = Fp/Cmax.

📘 DEFINITION

QAOA (Farhi, Goldstone and Gutmann, 2014) is the variational algorithm that prepares |γ, β⟩ above, estimates Fp from samples, and optimises the 2p angles classically; the output is the best bitstring seen in the samples. It can be read as a Trotterised adiabatic evolution from the ground state of −B (which is |+⟩⊗n) toward the highest-cut states of C; as p → ∞ suitable angles reach the optimum, but that says nothing about how large p must be.

Gates. Because all the ZiZj commute, UC factorises into one two-qubit gate per edge: e−iγ(1 − ZZ)/2 = e−iγ/2 e+iγZZ/2. Qiskit defines RZZ(θ) = e−iθ Z⊗Z/2, so each edge is RZZ(−γ) up to a global phase. The mixer is e−iβX = RX(2β) on every qubit. One layer on a graph with |E| edges costs |E| two-qubit gates (more after routing on hardware with limited connectivity).

Worked example: QAOA p = 1 on a triangle

Graph: vertices 0, 1, 2 with edges (0,1), (1,2), (0,2). Bitstrings are written q0 q1 q2 (big-endian). Numbers were computed with numpy and checked with a Qiskit statevector.

📊 FIGURE — QAOA with one layer on a triangle: circuit and output distribution
After H on every qubit, the cost layer stamps a phase per cut edge and the mixer lets amplitudes interfere. At γ*, β* the uncut 000 and 111 cancel to zero.
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Find the p = 1 angles that maximise ⟨C⟩ for the triangle, and the resulting output distribution.

Strategy: tabulate the cut values, apply the two layers amplitude by amplitude, then confirm with the closed-form p = 1 formula.

  1. Cut values. Every colouring except all-equal cuts exactly 2 of the 3 edges (a triangle is an odd cycle, so no colouring cuts all 3).
z000001010011100101110111
cut(z)02222220
  1. Start. H on each qubit gives |+++⟩: every amplitude is 1/√8 = 0.3536. Here ⟨C⟩ = (0 + 6 × 2 + 0)/8 = 1.5, the same as colouring at random.
  2. Cost layer. UC(γ) multiplies amplitude z by e−iγ cut(z). With the optimal γ* = 0.6155 (found in step 5): 000 and 111 keep 0.3536; the six others become 0.3536 × e−1.2310i = 0.1179 − 0.3333i. Probabilities have not changed yet; only relative phases have.
  3. Mixer layer. Apply RX(2β*) with β* = 0.3077 to each qubit. Interference now cancels the two uncut strings exactly: amplitude of 000 and 111 = 0; each of the other six = −0.1237 − 0.3891i, probability 0.0153 + 0.1514 = 0.1667.
  4. Expectation. ⟨C⟩ = 6 × 0.1667 × 2 = 2.0000 = Cmax, so r = 1. Sanity check: 6 × 0.1667 = 1.000, probabilities sum to 1.

Where do γ*, β* come from? For p = 1 there is a published closed form for the expected cut of each edge (we checked it against the statevector at several angles). For the triangle, where every edge has one neighbour at each end and lies in one triangle, it reduces to

F1(γ, β) = 3/2 + (3/4) sin 4β sin 2γ − (3/2) sin22β sin2γ

Maximising numerically (a 1001 × 1001 grid, then a local optimiser) gives γ* = 0.6155 rad and β* = 0.3077 rad = γ*/2. In closed form cos γ* = √(2/3), so sin γ* = 1/√3, sin 2γ* = 2√2/3 = 0.9428, sin 4β* = sin 2γ* = 0.9428 and sin22β* = sin2γ* = 1/3. Then F = 1.5 + 0.75 × 0.8889 − 1.5 × (1/3)(1/3) = 1.5 + 0.6667 − 0.1667 = 2.0. A slice of the landscape:

from qiskit.quantum_info import Statevector
g, b = 0.6155, 0.3077

qc.rx(2 * b, [0, 1, 2])
print(Statevector(qc).probabilities_dict()) # 0.1667 on each of the six cut strings

Contrast: the 4-cycle. For the square 0-1-2-3-0 (no triangles) the p = 1 formula becomes F1 = 4[1/2 + (1/4) sin 4β sin 2γ], maximised at γ = π/4, β = π/8 with F1 = 3, while Cmax = 4 (colour 0101). So r = 0.75: p = 1 misses the optimum, even on a four-vertex graph that a child solves by eye. The perfect triangle result is a small-symmetry accident, not a trend.

What evidence for advantage exists

✅ VERIFIED

Farhi, Goldstone and Gutmann, \"A Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm\", arXiv:1411.4028 (2014): for p = 1 on 3-regular graphs, QAOA guarantees an approximation ratio of at least 0.6924 (arxiv.org).

Goemans and Williamson (J. ACM 1995) give a classical polynomial-time semidefinite-programming algorithm with ratio 0.878 on every graph (dl.acm.org).

Hastings (2019) showed a simple classical local algorithm beats p = 1 QAOA on triangle-free regular graphs for almost all degrees, and Marwaha extended this to p = 2 on high-girth regular graphs (Quantum 5, 437, 2021: quantum-journal.org).

Harrigan et al., Nature Physics 17, 332-336 (2021), ran QAOA on Google's Sycamore processor; performance held up on hardware-native planar problems but degraded with size on problems that needed routing (nature.com).

Shaydulin et al., Science Advances 10, eadm6761 (2024), reported numerical evidence that QAOA's time-to-solution on the LABS problem scales better than the classical solvers they compared, with small runs on Quantinuum hardware (science.org). All checked 28 Sep 2026.

The honest summary: there is no proof that QAOA beats the best classical algorithms on any natural optimisation problem, and at low depth on Max-Cut classical algorithms are provably at least as good in the cases analysed. The strongest positive evidence is empirical scaling from simulations at sizes classical computers can still handle, extrapolated to larger sizes; turning it into a practical speed-up would need deep circuits and fault-tolerant hardware. Treat any \"QAOA advantage\" headline as a claim about a specific problem, baseline and size range.

The traps

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Mixing up signs and factors of 2. Maximising C is the same as minimising −C; decide which one your optimiser does. In Qiskit, e−iγ(1 − ZZ)/2 is RZZ(−γ), not RZZ(γ) or RZZ(2γ), and e−iβX is RX(2β). Getting any one wrong still produces a circuit that runs, just on a rescaled or mirrored landscape.

Also: the approximation ratio uses the expected cut ⟨C⟩, not the best sampled bitstring; a random colouring already achieves half the edges on average (ratio 0.75 on the triangle); and the quality of the triangle answer says nothing about 1,000-vertex graphs.

What the exam asks

★ ON THE EXAM
  • Write the Max-Cut cost Hamiltonian for a given graph and evaluate cut(z) for a bitstring.
  • Write the QAOA state for p layers and translate each layer into gates (RZZ and RX with the right angles).
  • Track amplitudes through one cost layer, or evaluate a given p = 1 formula at stated angles.
  • Compute an approximation ratio and compare it with random guessing and with Goemans-Williamson.
  • Summarise the evidence for (and against) a QAOA advantage in three sentences.

This lesson lets you clean up noisy expectation values without error correction: undo readout errors with a confusion matrix, extrapolate to zero noise, cancel errors with quasi-probabilities, and discard shots that break a known symmetry. Each technique buys accuracy with extra samples, and you will learn to compute that bill. It follows the variational lessons because VQE and QAOA on real hardware are almost always run with mitigation, and it contrasts with the error-correction chapter, which fixes errors on the fly at the price of many extra qubits.

The idea in plain words

Error correction protects each run of the computation. Error mitigation does not: every individual shot is still noisy. Instead it runs many (often deliberately modified) circuits and combines their averages so the noise cancels in the final estimate of an expectation value ⟨O⟩. No extra qubits, but more shots, and the extra shots grow exponentially with the total amount of noise in the circuit. That growth is why mitigation is a bridge to fault tolerance, not a replacement for it.

📘 DEFINITION

Quantum error mitigation is any post-processing scheme that estimates the noiseless expectation value ⟨O⟩ideal from the outputs of noisy circuits. Its sampling overhead is the factor by which the number of shots must grow to reach the same statistical error as an unmitigated estimate. Mitigation returns better averages; it never returns a corrected output bitstring.

Readout-error mitigation

Prepare |0⟩ and |1⟩ many times and record what is read out. This fills the confusion matrix A, where Amt = P(read m | prepared t). Noisy readout maps the true distribution to the measured one linearly, so you invert it.

🧮 KEY EQUATION

pmeas = A ptrue ⇒ ptrue ≈ A−1 pmeas

E0 ≈ ∑i γi E(λi), γi = ∏j≠i λj/(λj − λi)

pmeas and ptrue are probability vectors over bitstrings; A is the column-stochastic confusion matrix. In the second line (Richardson extrapolation, used in zero-noise extrapolation below) E(λ) is the measured expectation value when the noise is amplified by a factor λ ≥ 1, the λi are the chosen scale factors, γi the Lagrange weights that evaluate the interpolating polynomial at λ = 0 (they sum to 1), and E0 the zero-noise estimate. The variance of the estimate grows by about ∑γi2.

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Readout calibration gives P(0|0) = 0.97, P(1|0) = 0.03, P(0|1) = 0.08, P(1|1) = 0.92. An experiment measures pmeas = (0.60, 0.40). Find the mitigated distribution and ⟨Z⟩.

  1. A has rows (0.97, 0.08) and (0.03, 0.92); det A = 0.97 × 0.92 − 0.08 × 0.03 = 0.89.
  2. A−1 = (1/0.89) × [[0.92, −0.08], [−0.03, 0.97]] = [[1.0337, −0.0899], [−0.0337, 1.0899]].
  3. ptrue = (1.0337 × 0.60 − 0.0899 × 0.40, −0.0337 × 0.60 + 1.0899 × 0.40) = (0.5843, 0.4157). Sum = 1.0000.
  4. ⟨Z⟩ goes from 0.60 − 0.40 = 0.2000 (raw) to 0.1685 (mitigated).

For n qubits the full matrix is 2n × 2n, so practical schemes assume readout errors are independent per qubit (A = A1 ⊗ ... ⊗ An) or only weakly correlated. Plain inversion can also give small negative \"probabilities\" from shot noise; a constrained least-squares fit fixes that.

Zero-noise extrapolation (ZNE)

You cannot turn the noise down, but you can turn it up in a controlled way and extrapolate back. The standard trick is gate folding: replace a gate G by G G† G. Ideally that is still G, but the hardware now executes three noisy gates, so the noise on that gate is roughly tripled (λ = 3). Folding twice (G G† G G† G) gives λ = 5. Measure E(λ) at several λ, fit a curve, and read off its value at λ = 0. Temme, Bravyi and Gambetta proposed Richardson extrapolation for this in 2017; stretching pulse durations is an alternative to folding.

📊 FIGURE — Zero-noise extrapolation: amplify the noise, then fit back to λ = 0
Dots are measured at noise ×1, ×3, ×5 by gate folding. A line through two points reaches 0.9973 at λ = 0; the Richardson curve through three reaches 0.9998, at a higher shot cost.
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Prepare a Bell state with H on q0 then CNOT (control q0), and measure ⟨Z⊗Z⟩ (ideal value 1). Model each CNOT as followed by two-qubit depolarising noise of probability p = 0.04 (computed with a numpy density matrix). Fold the CNOT to get λ = 1, 3, 5.

  1. Measured values: E(1) = 0.9573, E(3) = 0.8774, E(5) = 0.8041. (Each noisy CNOT multiplies ⟨ZZ⟩ by 1 − 16p/15 = 0.9573.)
  2. Linear through λ = 1, 3: E0 = (3E(1) − E(3))/2 = (2.8720 − 0.8774)/2 = 0.9973.
  3. Richardson through λ = 1, 3, 5: γ1 = (3/2)(5/4) = 1.875, γ3 = (1/(−2))(5/2) = −1.25, γ5 = (1/(−4))(3/(−2)) = 0.375 (sum 1). E0 = 1.875 × 0.9573 − 1.25 × 0.8774 + 0.375 × 0.8041 = 0.9998.
  4. Exponential fit E(λ) = A e−kλ through λ = 1, 3: k = ln(0.9573/0.8774)/2 = 0.0436, A = 0.9573 e0.0436 = 1.0000.
  5. Cost: Richardson weights give ∑γi2 = 3.516 + 1.5625 + 0.1406 = 5.22, so with the same shots at each λ you need about 5.2 times more shots for the same error bar; the linear fit costs 1.52 + 0.52 = 2.5.

Sanity check: all three estimates move from the raw 0.9573 toward the ideal 1 without overshooting it, and the exponential fit is exact only because our toy noise model is exactly exponential. Real noise is not, which is why ZNE results carry model error you cannot see from the fit alone.

Probabilistic error cancellation (PEC)

If you have learned the noise channel Λ that follows a gate, you can write its inverse as a quasi-probability mixture of operations you can actually run: Λ−1 = ∑i qi Bi, with real qi summing to 1 but some negative. Each shot you pick Bi with probability |qi|/γ, where γ = ∑|qi|, run it after the gate, and multiply the outcome by γ · sign(qi). The average is unbiased, but the variance grows by γ2 per gate, so by γ2N for N gates.

For single-qubit depolarising noise with error probability p, each Pauli is shrunk by f = 1 − 4p/3, the inverse has qI = (1 + 3/f)/4 and qX = qY = qZ = (1 − 1/f)/4 (negative), and γ = (3/f − 1)/2. Computed values:

p per gateγ per gateoverhead γ2N, N = 100N = 1000
0.0011.00201.4954.7
0.011.020355.32.7 × 1017

This is the exponential sampling cost in one line: the overhead is roughly e4pN for small p, exponential in the total expected number of errors pN. Mitigation is affordable while pN is of order 1 and hopeless when it is 50. Every unbiased mitigation method shares a bound of this kind.

Symmetry verification

Many problems conserve something you know in advance: particle number in chemistry, or parity. If the ideal state must have even parity (like the Bell state, whose outcomes are only 00 or 11), any shot with odd parity is certainly wrong, so you discard it. Example: 1,000 shots give 00: 470, 11: 450, 01: 45, 10: 35. Keep 920; P(00) goes from 0.470 raw to 470/920 = 0.5109 post-selected. The cost is the discarded fraction (8% here), which again grows exponentially with circuit size, and errors that preserve the symmetry (a Z error, or X on both qubits) slip through.

The traps

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Treating a mitigated number as if it had the error bar of the raw data. Every method amplifies variance (by ∑γi2, γ2N or 1/(kept fraction)), so the reported uncertainty must be propagated through the extrapolation or reweighting. A second trap is forgetting the model assumptions: ZNE assumes noise scales as you think it does; PEC assumes the learned noise model is accurate and stable in time; readout inversion assumes errors do not depend on what else is happening.

✅ VERIFIED

Temme, Bravyi and Gambetta, \"Error mitigation for short-depth quantum circuits\", Physical Review Letters 119, 180509 (2017), introduced Richardson zero-noise extrapolation and quasi-probability error cancellation: link.aps.org.

Kim et al., \"Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance\", Nature 618, 500-505 (2023), used zero-noise extrapolation on a 127-qubit IBM processor to estimate expectation values of a kicked Ising model beyond brute-force classical simulation: nature.com. Classical tensor-network simulations soon reproduced those values (Tindall et al., PRX Quantum 5, 010308, 2024: link.aps.org). All checked 28 Sep 2026.

What the exam asks

★ ON THE EXAM
  • Invert a 2 × 2 confusion matrix and correct a measured distribution.
  • Explain gate folding and compute linear or Richardson extrapolations from given E(λ) values.
  • Derive or apply the PEC overhead γ2N and say why it is exponential.
  • Post-select on a symmetry and state what errors it misses.
  • Contrast mitigation with correction: qubits, shots, what is returned.
