This lesson lets you judge when a variational algorithm is doomed before you spend the shots, and how to read a claim of quantum advantage like a referee. It closes the NISQ chapter by collecting the three forces working against near-term algorithms: flat training landscapes (barren plateaus), noise that flattens them further, and classical simulation methods that keep catching up with shallow circuits. The complexity chapter later makes the theory of advantage precise; here we stay practical.

The idea in plain words

A variational algorithm is only as good as its optimiser, and an optimiser needs a slope to follow. For many natural ansätze on many qubits, the cost function is almost perfectly flat almost everywhere: the gradients are not zero on average, they are exponentially small in the number of qubits. Estimating an exponentially small number from ±1 shots needs exponentially many shots, which silently removes any hoped-for speed-up. Noise makes it worse, because it contracts every expectation value toward the value for the maximally mixed state.

📘 DEFINITION

A cost function E(θ) has a barren plateau if, for parameters drawn at random, the partial derivatives have zero mean and a variance that vanishes exponentially with qubit number: Varθ[∂E/∂θk] ∈ O(b−n) for some b > 1. A noise-induced barren plateau is the same flattening caused by hardware noise rather than by the circuit's randomness.

Why random circuits are flat

McClean and co-authors showed in 2018 that once a parameterised circuit is random enough to mimic a Haar-random unitary (technically, a unitary 2-design), expectation values concentrate around their mean. You can see this with one observable. For a Haar-random n-qubit state with d = 2n amplitudes, the fourth moments are E|ψi|4 = 2/(d(d+1)) and E|ψi|2|ψj|2 = 1/(d(d+1)) for i ≠ j. Writing ⟨Z1⟩ = ∑i si|ψi|2 with signs si = ±1 (half of each):

📊 FIGURE — Barren plateaus: cost variance shrinks as 1/(2ⁿ + 1) with qubits
On a log scale the variance of ⟨Z₁⟩ falls in a straight line, so the shots needed double with every qubit. The table shows noise shrinking the signal again with depth.

Var⟨Z1⟩ = d × 2/(d(d+1)) + [(∑si)2 − d] × 1/(d(d+1)) = 2/(d+1) − 1/(d+1) = 1/(d+1)

🧮 KEY EQUATION

E[⟨Z1⟩] = 0, Var[⟨Z1⟩] = 1/(2n + 1), shots to resolve ≈ 2n + 1

⟨O⟩noisy ≈ (1 − p)L ⟨O⟩ideal (global depolarising, L layers)

n is the number of qubits, ⟨Z1⟩ the expectation of Z on qubit 1 in a random state, and the shot estimate comes from needing the standard error √(1/N) of a ±1 average to be as small as the typical signal √(1/(2n+1)). In the second line p is the depolarising probability per layer, L the number of layers and O any traceless observable; gradients shrink by the same factor.

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Check the 1/(2n+1) law numerically and translate it into shots. Method: draw 4,000 Haar-random states per n in numpy (normalised complex Gaussian vectors, seed 7), compute ⟨Z1⟩ for each, and take the sample variance.

nsampled variancetheory 1/(2n+1)typical |⟨Z1⟩|shots ≈ 2n+1
20.20800.20000.44725
40.06020.05880.242517
60.01580.01540.124065
80.00380.00390.0624257
100.000970.000980.03121,025
20(theory)9.5 × 10−70.000981,048,577
50(theory)8.9 × 10−163.0 × 10−81.1 × 1015

Sanity check: the sampled variances match theory to within a few per cent, the sampling error expected from 4,000 samples, and each step of 2 qubits divides the variance by about 4. At 50 qubits, merely detecting the sign of a typical cost value needs about 1015 shots; at a million shots per second that is over 30 years.

What causes plateaus, and what helps. Known culprits are deep, highly expressive ansätze; global cost functions (observables acting on all qubits); random initialisation; too much entanglement between the part you measure and the rest; and noise. Remedies studied include local cost functions, shallow or problem-structured ansätze, warm starts from classical solutions, and layer-by-layer training. Switching to a gradient-free optimiser does not help: it still has to compare cost values that differ by exponentially small amounts.

❓ NOT VERIFIED

A line of work since about 2023 argues that ansätze which provably avoid barren plateaus usually do so because their dynamics live in a small, structured subspace, and that this same structure often makes them efficiently simulable classically. We could not re-check the exact references and their precise scope while writing this lesson; confirm before you rely on this, for example by searching for \"absence of barren plateaus classical simulability\".

Noise-induced plateaus

Wang et al. (2021) proved that under local Pauli noise the gradient vanishes exponentially in n whenever the circuit depth grows linearly with n, regardless of how clever the ansatz is. The global-depolarising cartoon in the key equation shows the mechanism: with p = 0.02 per layer, the signal is multiplied by 0.9810 = 0.8171 after 10 layers, 0.98100 = 0.1326 after 100 layers and 0.98500 = 4.1 × 10−5 after 500. Since shots scale as 1/signal2, 100 layers already cost 1/0.13262 = 57 times more shots and 500 layers about 6 × 108 times more. Error mitigation can undo the shrinkage only by paying the same exponential factor, as the previous lesson showed.

Classical simulation of shallow circuits

The exponential cost of storing a state vector (2n complex numbers) is only the worst case. A matrix product state (MPS) stores an n-qubit state as n small tensors linked by bonds of dimension χ; memory is about n × 2 × χ2 complex numbers. The bond dimension needed across a cut equals the Schmidt rank there, which measures entanglement across the cut. A two-qubit gate straddling the cut can multiply the Schmidt rank by at most 4, and in a one-dimensional brickwork circuit of depth d about d/2 gates straddle each cut, so χ ≤ 4d/2 = 2d.

Example: 100 qubits in a line, depth 10. Exact MPS: χ ≤ 210 = 1,024, memory 100 × 2 × 1,0242 × 16 bytes = 3.4 GB, which fits on a laptop. The state vector would need 2100 × 16 bytes = 2.0 × 1031 bytes. Shallow one-dimensional circuits are therefore classically easy, and approximate tensor-network methods (truncating χ, or belief-propagation contraction on two-dimensional lattices) often handle more than their worst-case bounds suggest, especially when noise has already limited how much entanglement survives.

How to read an advantage claim

  1. What exactly was computed? A sample, an expectation value, an optimisation answer? Is its correctness checkable?
  2. Against which classical method? Brute-force state vectors are a straw man; the fair baseline is the best known method for that circuit family (tensor networks, Pauli-path methods, specialised heuristics).
  3. Scaling or one size? A single size can be overtaken by a better classical code; a measured scaling exponent over a range of sizes is stronger evidence.
  4. All costs counted? Shots, mitigation overhead, optimiser iterations, calibration and queue time, not only circuit run time.
  5. Error bars? Are mitigated values reported with their amplified uncertainty?
  6. Has the community replied? Look for classical rebuttals in the following year.
✅ VERIFIED

McClean et al., \"Barren plateaus in quantum neural network training landscapes\", Nature Communications 9 (2018): doi.org. Wang et al., \"Noise-induced barren plateaus in variational quantum algorithms\", Nature Communications 12, 6961 (2021): nature.com. \"Effect of barren plateaus on gradient-free optimization\", Quantum (Oct 2021): quantum-journal.org.

Case study: Kim et al. (Nature 618, 500-505, 2023) reported mitigated 127-qubit expectation values beyond brute-force simulation; soon afterwards tensor-network work reproduced them classically, with Tindall et al. (PRX Quantum 5, 010308, 2024) reporting results more accurate than the processor and extending to 433 and 1,121 qubits: link.aps.org; another classical study appeared in Science Advances as \"Fast and converged classical simulations of evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance\": science.org. All checked 28 Sep 2026.

The honest reading of that episode is not that the experiment failed: it was a careful demonstration that mitigated hardware can produce accurate numbers at 127 qubits. But the \"beyond classical\" part did not survive contact with the best classical methods. That pattern, a quantum claim followed by a faster classical method, has happened more than once, and it is exactly what checklist items 2 and 6 are for.

📊 YOUR DATA EDGE

Reading an advantage paper is reading a benchmark. Ask the questions you would ask of any vendor performance chart: is the baseline tuned, is the metric the one users care about, are the error bars honest, is the comparison at equal cost, and would a log-log plot of time against size show a genuinely different slope or just an offset.

The traps

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Thinking a barren plateau means the gradient is exactly zero, or that it only matters for gradient-based optimisers. The mean gradient is zero but individual gradients are merely tiny, and every optimiser that compares cost values faces the same exponentially small differences. A second trap is taking \"we could not simulate this with a state vector\" as evidence of advantage; tensor networks, not state vectors, are the baseline for shallow and noisy circuits.

What the exam asks

★ ON THE EXAM
  • Define a barren plateau and derive Var⟨Z1⟩ = 1/(2n+1) for Haar-random states, then convert it to a shot count.
  • Compute how depolarising noise per layer shrinks a signal and the shots needed to compensate.
  • Bound the MPS bond dimension of a shallow 1D circuit and estimate its memory.
  • Apply the six-question checklist to a described advantage claim.

This lesson shows you how a quantum computer runs the time evolution of a physical system, e−iHt, using only one- and two-qubit gates, and how to work out how many gates that costs for a given accuracy. Simulating nature was the first reason anyone proposed a quantum computer, and the Trotter formulas here reappear in phase estimation for chemistry (next lesson), in HHL (lesson 3) and in the complexity chapter. You need the unitary and Hamiltonian material from the postulates chapter, the gate identities from the single- and multi-qubit chapters, and the idea of an operator norm.

\n\n

The idea in plain words: why nature is hard to copy on a laptop

\n

A system of n qubits (or n spin-½ particles, or n electron orbitals) needs 2n complex amplitudes to describe a general state. Stored as double-precision complex numbers (16 bytes each), 30 qubits need 230 × 16 ≈ 17.2 GB, 40 qubits ≈ 17.6 TB and 50 qubits ≈ 18 PB. Every extra particle doubles the memory. Evolving that vector in time means multiplying it by a 2n × 2n matrix, so the cost explodes in the same way.

\n

Feynman's 1982 suggestion was to turn this round: use a controllable quantum system to imitate another one. Lloyd showed in 1996 that this works for any local Hamiltonian, meaning a sum of terms that each touch only a few particles. Most physical Hamiltonians are local (particles interact with neighbours, electrons interact in pairs), so the idea covers spin models, lattice models and molecules.

\n

Be honest about the limits. Not every quantum system is hard classically: weakly entangled states are handled well by tensor-network methods (such as DMRG), and many molecules are treated well by coupled-cluster methods. The quantum advantage for simulation is strongly believed, not proven: simulating general local Hamiltonians is BQP-complete, so if it were classically easy then every quantum algorithm would be classically easy.

\n\n
✅ VERIFIED

S. Lloyd, \"Universal Quantum Simulators\", Science 273, 1073-1078 (23 August 1996), shows that a quantum computer can efficiently simulate any local quantum system, confirming Feynman's 1982 conjecture: science.org/doi/10.1126/science.273.5278.1073.

A. M. Childs, Y. Su, M. C. Tran, N. Wiebe, S. Zhu, \"Theory of Trotter Error with Commutator Scaling\", Phys. Rev. X 11, 011020 (2021): tight Trotter bounds built from commutators: osti.gov/biblio/1769799. Checked 28 Sep 2026.

\n\n

The definition: the Hamiltonian simulation problem

\n
📘 DEFINITION

Hamiltonian simulation. Given a Hamiltonian H on n qubits written as a sum H = H1 + H2 + … + HL of terms we can exponentiate easily, a time t and an error ε, build a circuit V with ‖V − e−iHt‖ ≤ ε, using a number of gates polynomial in n, t and 1/ε.

Here ‖·‖ is the operator (spectral) norm, the largest singular value. If ‖V − U‖ ≤ ε then, for every input state, the two output states differ by at most ε in vector length, and every measurement probability differs by at most about 2ε. We use units with ħ = 1, so energy and 1/time are the same unit.

\n

The terms are chosen so each e−iHjδ is a short circuit. A single Pauli string such as Z⊗Z or X⊗I is ideal: e−iθX is the gate RX(2θ), e−iθZ is RZ(2θ), and e−iθ Z⊗Z is CNOT, then RZ(2θ) on the target, then CNOT. (Recall RZ(φ) = e−iφZ/2, which is where the factor 2 comes from.)

\n

The difficulty is that the terms usually do not commute, and for matrices eA+B ≠ eAeB unless AB = BA.

\n\n

The key equations: Lie-Trotter and second-order Suzuki

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

First-order (Lie-Trotter) formula, with n steps of size δ = t/n:

e−i(A+B)t ≈ S1(δ)n, S1(δ) = e−iAδ e−iBδ

‖e−i(A+B)t − S1(t/n)n‖ ≤ (t2 / 2n) · ‖[A, B]‖

Second-order (Strang / Suzuki) formula, symmetric:

S2(δ) = e−iAδ/2 e−iBδ e−iAδ/2, error = O(t3 / n2)

Symbols: A, B are Hermitian terms of H = A + B; t is the total simulated time; n the number of Trotter steps; δ = t/n the step size; [A, B] = AB − BA the commutator; ‖·‖ the operator norm. Suzuki's recursion builds order-2k formulas from 5k−1 copies of S2 with error O(t2k+1/n2k).

\n

Where the bound comes from: expand both sides to second order in δ. e−iAδe−iBδ = I − i(A+B)δ − (A2 + 2AB + B2)δ2/2 + …, while e−i(A+B)δ = I − i(A+B)δ − (A2 + AB + BA + B2)δ2/2 + …. The difference is (AB − BA)δ2/2 = [A,B]δ2/2 per step. Errors of unitaries add at most linearly, so n steps give about n · ‖[A,B]‖δ2/2 = ‖[A,B]‖t2/(2n). The symmetric S2 cancels that δ2 term, leaving δ3 per step and t3/n2 overall.

\n

Turning that into cost: to reach error ε, first order needs n ≈ ‖[A,B]‖t2/(2ε) steps (scales as 1/ε), second order needs n = O(t3/2/ε1/2). Two useful facts: if A and B commute, the Trotter error is exactly zero; and the error depends on the commutator, not on the sizes of A and B.

\n\n

Worked example: the two-qubit transverse-field Ising model

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Take H = A + B with A = Z⊗Z (the coupling) and B = X⊗I + I⊗X (a transverse field of strength 1), total time t = 1, start state |00⟩. Convention: |q0q1⟩ with qubit 0 on the left; both terms are symmetric under swapping the qubits, so Qiskit's little-endian ordering gives the same matrices here. All numbers below came from numpy/scipy (scipy.linalg.expm) and were checked against a Qiskit Operator of the circuit.

📊 FIGURE — One Trotter step for the two-qubit Ising model, and error vs steps
Top: one step applies the field (RX) then the coupling (CNOT–RZ–CNOT). Bottom: first-order error halves when n doubles, second-order quarters, so ε = 0.01 needs 71 versus 8 steps.
  1. Commutator. [Z⊗Z, X⊗I] = [Z,X]⊗Z = 2i Y⊗Z and [Z⊗Z, I⊗X] = 2i Z⊗Y, so [A,B] = 2i(Y⊗Z + Z⊗Y). Its eigenvalues are ±4, 0, 0, so ‖[A,B]‖ = 4 and the first-order bound is t2·4/(2n) = 2/n.
  2. Exact answer. H has eigenvalues ±√5 ≈ ±2.2361 and ±1. e−iH|00⟩ = (−0.0385 − 0.5967i)|00⟩ − 0.3518i|01⟩ − 0.3518i|10⟩ + (−0.5788 + 0.2448i)|11⟩, so P(00) = 0.3575, P(01) = P(10) = 0.1238, P(11) = 0.3949.
  3. One Trotter step (n = 1), B first on the state. e−iX = cos 1 · I − i sin 1 · X, with cos 1 = 0.5403, sin 1 = 0.8415. So e−iB|00⟩ = (0.5403|0⟩ − 0.8415i|1⟩)⊗(0.5403|0⟩ − 0.8415i|1⟩) = 0.2919|00⟩ − 0.4546i|01⟩ − 0.4546i|10⟩ − 0.7081|11⟩.
  4. Apply e−iA. Z⊗Z is +1 on |00⟩, |11⟩ and −1 on |01⟩, |10⟩, so it multiplies those amplitudes by e−i = 0.5403 − 0.8415i and e+i = 0.5403 + 0.8415i. Result: (0.1577 − 0.2456i)|00⟩ + (0.3826 − 0.2456i)(|01⟩ + |10⟩) + (−0.3826 + 0.5958i)|11⟩, so the one-step estimate of P(00) is 0.0852, far from the true 0.3575.
  5. Refine. The table below gives the operator-norm error for more steps. First order halves when n doubles (slope −1); second order quarters (slope −2).
\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
n‖U − S1n‖bound 2/n‖U − S2n‖P(00), first order

\n

Sanity checks: every error is below its bound; the ratio 0.0441/0.0220 = 2.00 and 0.0022/0.0005 ≈ 4; and P(00) converges to the exact 0.3575.

\n

Cost to reach ε = 0.01. Searching n directly: first order needs n = 71 (error 0.0099; n = 70 gives 0.0101); second order needs n = 8 (0.0088). The loose bound would have asked for n = 200. One first-order step is the circuit RX(2δ) on each qubit, then CNOT(0→1), RZ(2δ) on qubit 1, CNOT(0→1): two CNOTs. So first order costs 142 CNOTs. In second order, the half-steps e−iAδ/2 of neighbouring steps merge, giving n + 1 = 9 ZZ blocks and 18 CNOTs: about eight times cheaper for the same accuracy.

\n

The numpy check fits in a few lines (runs as written):

\n

import numpy as np; from scipy.linalg import expm
X = np.array([[0,1],[1,0]]); Z = np.diag([1,-1]); I = np.eye(2)
A = np.kron(Z,Z); B = np.kron(X,I) + np.kron(I,X); t = 1.0
U = expm(-1j*(A+B)*t)
for n in [1,2,4,8]:
S = expm(-1j*A*t/n) @ expm(-1j*B*t/n)
print(n, np.linalg.norm(U - np.linalg.matrix_power(S,n), 2))

\n\n
📊 YOUR DATA EDGE

Reading an error-versus-steps table is a regression problem you already know. Plot log(error) against log(n) and fit a line: slope −1 means first order, slope −2 means second order. Here log2(0.0887/0.0441) ≈ 1.01 and log2(0.0088/0.0022) ≈ 2.01. If a paper claims a \"fourth-order\" method and the fitted slope is −2, question the claim. Note too that the rigorous bound 2/n is an upper limit, not a prediction; it overestimates the true error by a factor of about 2.8 here, exactly as a worst-case confidence bound can be much wider than the typical error.

\n\n

Beyond product formulas

\n

Product formulas are simple and need no extra qubits, which is why they are the default on today's hardware. For a sum of L terms, first order is e−iH1δ ⋯ e−iHLδ, and the error is governed by the nested commutators of the terms. Terms that commute cost nothing extra, and physical Hamiltonians with local interactions have mostly commuting terms, which is why the careful commutator bounds (Childs et al., 2021) are much tighter than the older ones. Other methods trade circuit simplicity for better asymptotics: qDRIFT samples terms at random with probability proportional to their weights; linear combinations of unitaries (LCU) and qubitization with quantum signal processing reach a cost that grows roughly additively in t and log(1/ε), rather than polynomially in 1/ε, at the price of ancilla qubits and more complex control. For fault-tolerant chemistry estimates, qubitization is the usual choice.

\n\n
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE
  • Writing e−i(A+B)t = e−iAte−iBt for non-commuting A, B. This is exactly the error Trotterization controls; it is exact only when [A,B] = 0.
  • Thinking the error depends on how big A and B are. It depends on the commutator: huge commuting terms give zero error.
  • Forgetting the factor 2 in rotation gates: e−iθZ = RZ(2θ), not RZ(θ).
  • Assuming more steps are free. Each step adds gates, and on noisy hardware the gate error grows with n while the Trotter error shrinks, so there is an optimum n.
  • Confusing the step size δ = t/n with the total time t. Doubling t at fixed n quadruples the first-order bound (t2).
\n\n
★ ON THE EXAM
  • Derive the first-order error term [A,B]δ2/2 by expanding both exponentials to second order.
  • Given ‖[A,B]‖, t and ε, compute the number of steps from n ≥ ‖[A,B]‖t2/(2ε), and explain how n scales for second order.
  • Compile e−iθ Z⊗Z into CNOT-RZ-CNOT and count CNOTs for n steps.
  • State why simulation is believed hard classically (2n amplitudes, BQP-completeness) and one family of systems where classical methods do well.

This lesson takes you from a molecule to a list of Pauli strings with numbers in front of them: the object every quantum chemistry algorithm (phase estimation, VQE) actually works with. You will build the full 4-qubit Hamiltonian of the hydrogen molecule, check it against an exact classical calculation, and learn what \"chemical accuracy\" demands and what realistic resource estimates say. It builds on lesson 1 (Hamiltonian simulation) and feeds the NISQ chapter's VQE and the complexity chapter's discussion of advantage.

\n\n

The idea in plain words: electrons in orbitals

\n

Chemistry is mostly about the energy of electrons around fixed nuclei (the Born-Oppenheimer approximation: nuclei are thousands of times heavier, so we freeze them at a bond length R and solve for the electrons). To get a finite problem we choose a basis set: a finite list of spatial orbitals. Each spatial orbital holds a spin-up and a spin-down electron, giving 2 spin-orbitals per spatial orbital. With N spin-orbitals the electron state lives in a space of dimension 2N (each spin-orbital empty or occupied), which maps neatly onto N qubits.

\n

For H2 in the minimal STO-3G basis, each hydrogen contributes one 1s orbital (each approximated by 3 Gaussians). Combining them gives two molecular orbitals: the bonding σg (lower energy) and antibonding σu. Two spatial orbitals × 2 spins = 4 spin-orbitals = 4 qubits, holding 2 electrons.

\n\n

The definitions: second quantisation and Jordan-Wigner

\n
📘 DEFINITION

Second quantisation. For each spin-orbital p, ap† (creation) adds an electron to p and ap (annihilation) removes one. They obey the canonical anticommutation relations {ap, aq†} = δpq and {ap, aq} = 0, where {X, Y} = XY + YX. The minus signs encode the Pauli exclusion principle: ap†ap† = 0, and swapping two electrons flips the sign of the state.

📊 FIGURE — Jordan–Wigner: H₂ spin-orbitals become four qubits
Each spin-orbital becomes one qubit (1 = occupied), so the Hartree–Fock state is |1100⟩. An annihilation operator carries a string of Z on all earlier qubits for the fermion sign.

Jordan-Wigner (JW) transformation. Qubit j stores the occupation of spin-orbital j (|1⟩ = occupied, |0⟩ = empty) and aj = Z0 Z1 ⋯ Zj−1 · (Xj + iYj)/2. The factor (X + iY)/2 = |0⟩⟨1| empties qubit j; the string of Z's on all earlier qubits supplies the fermionic sign (−1)(number of occupied orbitals before j).

\n

The electronic Hamiltonian in second quantisation is

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

H = Enuc + ∑pq hpq ap†aq + ½ ∑pqrs (pq|rs) ap†ar†asaq

Enuc is the nuclear repulsion (a constant at fixed R); hpq are one-electron integrals (kinetic energy plus attraction to the nuclei); (pq|rs) are two-electron repulsion integrals in chemists' notation; all indices run over spin-orbitals and integrals vanish unless spins match. A classical program (here PySCF) computes the integrals; the quantum computer is needed only to find the ground state of the resulting operator.

After JW every term becomes a sum of Pauli strings: H = ∑k ck Pk, with real coefficients ck and Pk ∈ {I, X, Y, Z}⊗N. The number of terms grows roughly as N4.

\n

Two JW identities worth memorising (checked with numpy on 3 qubits): the number operator is aj†aj = (I − Zj)/2 = |1⟩⟨1|j, and hopping between neighbours is a0†a1 + a1†a0 = (X0X1 + Y0Y1)/2. Between orbitals 0 and 2 the string appears: a0†a2 + h.c. = (X0Z1X2 + Y0Z1Y2)/2. So JW strings grow up to length N; the Bravyi-Kitaev encoding reduces the worst case to about log2N qubits per operator, and the parity encoding lets you remove two qubits using symmetries (that is how Qiskit tutorials show H2 on 2 qubits).

\n

A sign check shows why the Z string is essential. On three qubits starting from |000⟩: a1†a0†|000⟩ = −|110⟩ but a0†a1†|000⟩ = +|110⟩: the order of creation matters by a sign, as it must for fermions. Without the Z string, the operators on different qubits would commute instead of anticommute (numpy confirms this), and every exchange sign in the chemistry would be wrong.

\n\n

Worked example: the H2 Hamiltonian, computed and checked

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Set-up: H2, bond length R = 0.735 Å, STO-3G basis, restricted Hartree-Fock orbitals, computed with PySCF 2.14, then mapped by a hand-written numpy Jordan-Wigner. Spin-orbital order (= qubit order, qubit 0 leftmost in the strings): 0 = σg↑, 1 = σg↓, 2 = σu↑, 3 = σu↓. Energies in Hartree (Ha).

  1. Integrals from PySCF. Enuc = 0.719969; hσgσg = −1.256339; hσuσu = −0.471896; (gg|gg) = 0.675710; (uu|uu) = 0.698574; (gg|uu) = 0.664582; exchange (gu|ug) = 0.180931.
  2. Build the 16 × 16 matrix from the key equation using aj = Z⋯Z(X+iY)/2, after checking {ai, aj†} = δij for all pairs.
  3. Decompose into Pauli strings with cP = Tr(P H)/16. Exactly 15 strings survive (table below).
  4. Hartree-Fock check. The HF state fills σg with both electrons: |1100⟩. Only I and Z strings contribute; Zj = −1 on occupied qubits 0, 1 and +1 on 2, 3. Summing cP × (product of those signs) gives −1.116998, matching PySCF's HF energy −1.116999 Ha.
  5. Exact ground state. Diagonalising the 16 × 16 matrix gives E0 = −1.137306 Ha, equal to PySCF's full configuration interaction (FCI) energy to 10 decimal places. The ground state is 0.9938|1100⟩ − 0.1115|0011⟩ (sanity check: 0.9876 + 0.0124 = 1.0000): mostly HF, with a small admixture of both electrons in σu.
  6. Correlation energy = EFCI − EHF = −0.020307 Ha = −12.7 kcal/mol: the part a quantum algorithm must capture beyond mean-field theory.
\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
Pauli string (q0 q1 q2 q3)coefficient (Ha)

\n

Read the table physically: single Z terms are orbital energies (σu costs more, so its Z coefficient has the opposite sign); ZZ terms are Coulomb and exchange repulsions between occupied orbitals; the four XXYY-type terms are the only ones that move electrons, taking the pair from σg into σu and back. They create the 0.1115 admixture that lowers the energy below HF. If you use different orbital ordering or Qiskit's little-endian labels, the same numbers appear on permuted strings, so always state the ordering.

\n\n

The bond-length scan below (same method) shows why correlation matters. Hartree-Fock gets worse and worse as the bond stretches, because a single configuration cannot describe two separated atoms.

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n

\n\n

Chemical accuracy and what it really asks for

\n
📘 DEFINITION

Chemical accuracy is the conventional target of 1 kcal/mol ≈ 1.6 × 10−3 Ha (1 Ha = 627.5 kcal/mol) in energy differences such as reaction energies and barrier heights, because at room temperature an error of that size changes a predicted reaction rate by a factor of about 5 (e1/0.593 ≈ 5.4, with RT = 0.593 kcal/mol at 298 K). It is a statement about the error of the method within the chosen model; it says nothing about whether STO-3G itself is a good model of the real molecule (it is not: minimal-basis energies are far from experiment).

\n

For H2, the HF error at equilibrium (20.3 mHa) is about 13 times the chemical-accuracy window, so a mean-field answer is not good enough, while any algorithm that finds the true ground state of the 15-term Hamiltonian is. Of course, H2 in STO-3G is trivial classically (a 16 × 16 matrix). The interesting targets are strongly correlated systems, such as transition-metal catalysts, where classical methods struggle.

\n

Algorithms: on fault-tolerant hardware, quantum phase estimation applied to e−iHt (built by Trotter formulas or qubitization) returns an energy eigenvalue, with the ground state found with probability equal to the squared overlap of the input state with it (0.9876 for HF here; for large molecules that overlap can be tiny). On today's noisy hardware, the variational quantum eigensolver (NISQ chapter) estimates ⟨ψ(θ)|H|ψ(θ)⟩ term by term; each Pauli string must be measured many times, and the shot count to reach 1.6 mHa is a serious cost.

\n\n
✅ VERIFIED
  • O'Malley et al., \"Scalable Quantum Simulation of Molecular Energies\", Phys. Rev. X 6, 031007 (2016): H2 energy surface on two superconducting (Xmon transmon) qubits with VQE and a phase-estimation variant: link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevX.6.031007.
  • Reiher, Wiebe, Svore, Wecker, Troyer, \"Elucidating reaction mechanisms on quantum computers\", PNAS 114, 7555-7560 (2017): nitrogenase's FeMo cofactor (FeMoco) as a target for quantum chemistry: pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1619152114.
  • Lee, Berry, Gidney, Huggins, McClean, Wiebe, Babbush, \"Even More Efficient Quantum Computations of Chemistry Through Tensor Hypercontraction\", PRX Quantum 2, 030305 (arXiv 2011.03494): FeMoco estimated at about four million physical qubits and under 4 days, assuming 1 μs cycle times and 0.1% physical error rates: arxiv.org/abs/2011.03494.
  • Zhai, Li, Zhang, Li, Lee, Chan, arXiv 2601.04621 (January 2026, preprint): classical coupled-cluster and DMRG calculations claim chemical accuracy for a widely used FeMoco model: arxiv.org/abs/2601.04621. Checked 28 Sep 2026.
\n

Put these together honestly: the flagship chemistry target needs millions of physical qubits in the best published estimates, and in 2026 a classical preprint claims to have reached chemical accuracy for a standard model of that same target. That does not settle the question (a preprint is not yet peer-reviewed, and larger or harder models remain), but it shows that \"quantum computers will solve chemistry\" is a conjecture that classical methods keep testing.

\n\n
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE
  • Mapping aj to (Xj + iYj)/2 alone and dropping the Z string: the operators then commute on different qubits and the fermionic signs are lost.
  • Forgetting Enuc. The identity coefficient −0.090579 includes +0.719969 Ha of nuclear repulsion; comparing an electronic-only energy with a total one gives a 0.72 Ha \"error\".
  • Quoting chemical accuracy as a total-energy tolerance of a basis set. It concerns energy differences, within a model.
  • Assuming ⟨H⟩ in the HF state is the ground energy: HF is an upper bound (−1.1170 above −1.1373).
  • Reading Pauli labels in the wrong qubit order, especially when moving between textbook (qubit 0 left) and Qiskit (qubit 0 right) conventions.
\n\n
★ ON THE EXAM
  • Count qubits: spin-orbitals = 2 × spatial orbitals under JW (e.g. H2/STO-3G gives 4).
  • Write aj under JW and derive aj†aj = (I − Zj)/2.
  • Evaluate ⟨HF|H|HF⟩ from a table of I/Z coefficients using Z = −1 on occupied qubits.
  • Convert between Hartree and kcal/mol and decide whether an error meets chemical accuracy.
  • Explain the trade-off between phase estimation (needs deep, fault-tolerant circuits and good initial overlap) and VQE (shallow circuits, many measurements, no guarantee).

This lesson explains the Harrow-Hassidim-Lloyd (HHL) algorithm for linear systems Ax = b, walks through it by hand on a 2 × 2 example, and then teaches you to read the fine print: the conditions under which its famous \"exponential speed-up\" is real, and the classical \"dequantization\" results that removed several claimed speed-ups. It uses phase estimation (QFT chapter), Hamiltonian simulation (lesson 1) and amplitude amplification (Grover chapter), and it is the background you need for the quantum machine learning chapter.

\n\n

The idea in plain words: invert the eigenvalues

\n

If A is Hermitian with eigenvectors |uj⟩ and eigenvalues λj, then solving Ax = b is easy in the eigenbasis: write b = ∑ βjuj, and the answer is x = ∑ (βj/λj) uj. HHL does exactly this on a quantum state. Phase estimation on eiAt writes each eigenvalue into a register; a controlled rotation puts an amplitude proportional to 1/λj on an ancilla; uncomputing the register and keeping the runs where the ancilla reads 1 leaves a state proportional to x.

\n

The catch, in one sentence: HHL does not give you the vector x. It gives you a quantum state whose amplitudes are the normalised entries of x, from which you can only sample or estimate expectation values.

\n\n
📘 DEFINITION

Quantum linear systems problem (QLSP). Given an N × N Hermitian matrix A (a non-Hermitian A is embedded in the Hermitian [[0, A],[A†, 0]]), rescaled so its eigenvalues satisfy 1/κ ≤ |λ| ≤ 1, and a routine that prepares |b⟩ = ∑ bi|i⟩/‖b‖, prepare a state within distance ε of |x⟩ = A−1|b⟩ / ‖A−1|b⟩‖.

Condition number κ = |λ|max/|λ|min measures how close A is to singular. Sparsity s is the maximum number of non-zero entries in any row; s-sparse A with efficiently computable entries can be simulated as eiAt efficiently. The number of qubits is log2N plus ancillas.

\n\n

The algorithm and its key equation

\n
  1. Load |b⟩ = ∑j βj|uj⟩ (expanded in A's eigenbasis, which the algorithm never needs to know).
  2. Phase estimation with the unitary eiAt gives ∑j βj|uj⟩|λ̃j⟩, where λ̃j is a register holding an estimate of λj.
  3. Controlled rotation of an ancilla, conditioned on λ̃j: |0⟩ → √(1 − C2/λj2)|0⟩ + (C/λj)|1⟩, with a constant C ≤ |λ|min (so C/λ ≤ 1).
  4. Uncompute phase estimation, returning the eigenvalue register to |0…0⟩.
  5. Measure the ancilla; on outcome 1 the system holds |x⟩. Repeat, or use amplitude amplification, until success.
\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

|x⟩ ∝ ∑j (βj / λj) |uj⟩, P(ancilla = 1) = ∑j |βj|2 C2 / λj2

📊 FIGURE — HHL in five moves, followed by hand on a 2 × 2 system
Phase estimation writes each eigenvalue into a register, a controlled rotation puts C/λ on the ancilla, and keeping ancilla = 1 leaves |x⟩. The box shows the 2 × 2 example.

βj = ⟨uj|b⟩ are the coefficients of |b⟩ in the eigenbasis; λj the eigenvalues; C the rotation constant. Because C/λj can be as small as 1/κ, the success probability can be as low as 1/κ2, and amplitude amplification needs about κ rounds.

Original HHL cost, as usually quoted: about log(N) · s2 · κ2 / ε (up to log factors). Classical conjugate gradient for a positive-definite s-sparse A costs about N · s · √κ · log(1/ε). Later algorithms (Childs, Kothari and Somma, 2017) improved the precision dependence from 1/ε to polylog(1/ε), and subsequent work brought the κ dependence down to linear.

\n

The exponential gap is the log N versus N. Everything else (κ, s, ε, the cost of preparing |b⟩, the cost of reading the answer) must stay small for that gap to survive.

\n\n

Worked example: HHL by hand on a 2 × 2 system

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Solve A x = b with A = [[1, −1/3], [−1/3, 1]] and b = (1, 0)ᵀ, i.e. |b⟩ = |0⟩ (one system qubit). Numbers checked with numpy (linalg.eigh and linalg.solve).

  1. Eigen-decomposition. λ1 = 2/3 with |u1⟩ = (|0⟩ + |1⟩)/√2; λ2 = 4/3 with |u2⟩ = (|0⟩ − |1⟩)/√2. Condition number κ = (4/3)/(2/3) = 2.
  2. Expand |b⟩. β1 = ⟨u1|0⟩ = 1/√2 = 0.7071, β2 = 1/√2 = 0.7071.
  3. Divide by eigenvalues. β1/λ1 = 0.7071 × 1.5 = 1.0607; β2/λ2 = 0.7071 × 0.75 = 0.5303.
  4. Back to the computational basis. x = 1.0607 |u1⟩ + 0.5303 |u2⟩ = (0.75 + 0.375)|0⟩ + (0.75 − 0.375)|1⟩ = (1.125, 0.375)ᵀ. Check: numpy.linalg.solve gives (1.125, 0.375).
  5. Normalise (‖x‖ = 1.1859): |x⟩ = 0.9487|0⟩ + 0.3162|1⟩. Measurement probabilities are 0.9 and 0.1 (sum 1), and ⟨Z⟩ = 0.9 − 0.1 = 0.8.
  6. Ancilla success. With C = λmin = 2/3, the ancilla-1 amplitudes are C/λ1 = 1 and C/λ2 = 0.5, so P(success) = 0.5 × 12 + 0.5 × 0.52 = 0.625.
\n

What you actually learn from the machine is the key point. The state |x⟩ is destroyed on measurement, so to estimate P(0) = 0.9 to ±0.01 (one standard error) you need M ≈ p(1 − p)/0.012 = 0.9 × 0.1/0.0001 = 900 successful runs, which is about 900/0.625 = 1,440 attempts. You also lose the norm ‖x‖ = 1.1859 and the overall sign; recovering all N entries of x this way would need at least on the order of N runs, wiping out the log N advantage.

\n\n
📊 YOUR DATA EDGE

You know that estimating a proportion p from M samples has standard error √(p(1 − p)/M). That formula alone kills many headline claims: reading out a 106-entry solution vector to useful precision needs far more than 106 shots, while conjugate gradient would already have returned every entry. When you see \"exponential speed-up for linear algebra\", ask the SQL question: what exactly is the output row, and how many samples does it take to fill it?

\n\n

The fine print: when is the speed-up real?

\n

Scott Aaronson's 2015 commentary \"Read the fine print\" lists the conditions; restated as a checklist:

\n
  • Input problem. Preparing |b⟩ for arbitrary data takes time proportional to N unless b has structure or is already stored in a quantum RAM (qRAM), a device that does not exist at scale.
  • Output problem. You get |x⟩, not x. Useful outputs are a few numbers such as ⟨x|M|x⟩ or overlaps.
  • Condition number. Cost grows with κ; if κ grows polynomially with N the exponential gap shrinks or vanishes. Real systems from discretised PDEs often have κ growing with N.
  • Sparsity and simulability. A must be simulable as eiAt efficiently (sparse with computable entries, or low rank with suitable access).
  • Precision. The original 1/ε scaling is poor; later algorithms fixed that.
\n

When all these hold, the speed-up is genuine in a complexity sense: HHL showed that matrix inversion in this setting is BQP-complete, so a fast classical algorithm for it would simulate every quantum computation classically. That is strong evidence, not a proof that no classical algorithm exists (BPP ≠ BQP is unproven). No end-to-end practical advantage on a real linear-algebra task has been demonstrated.

\n\n

Dequantization

\n

Several quantum machine-learning algorithms assumed a qRAM-style data structure that allows ℓ2-norm sampling of matrix entries, and their matrices were low rank. In 2018 Ewin Tang showed that a classical algorithm given the same sampling access can match the quantum recommendation-system algorithm of Kerenidis and Prakash up to a polynomial slowdown, running in time poly(k)·log(mn) for rank k. So that \"exponential\" speed-up was an artefact of comparing a quantum algorithm with a powerful input model against classical algorithms without it. Later work extended these quantum-inspired classical methods to low-rank linear systems and other QML subroutines; the remaining gaps are polynomial (sometimes large polynomials).

\n

What dequantization does not touch: sparse, full-rank, well-conditioned HHL, which remains BQP-complete. The lesson is to compare against the best classical algorithm given the same input access.

\n\n
✅ VERIFIED
  • A. W. Harrow, A. Hassidim, S. Lloyd, \"Quantum Algorithm for Linear Systems of Equations\", Phys. Rev. Lett. 103, 150502 (2009): Semantic Scholar record.
  • A. M. Childs, R. Kothari, R. D. Somma, \"Quantum algorithm for systems of linear equations with exponentially improved dependence on precision\", SIAM J. Comput. 46(6), 1920-1950 (2017), doi 10.1137/16M1087072: doi.org/10.1137/16M1087072.

Every quantum machine-learning (QML) method starts the same way: a row of your data table has to become a quantum state before any quantum circuit can touch it. This lesson teaches the three standard encodings (basis, angle and amplitude), what each costs in qubits and gates, and why that cost, the data-loading bottleneck, decides whether a claimed speed-up survives. It builds on single-qubit rotations (Chapter \"Single-Qubit Gates\") and tensor products (Chapter \"Multi-Qubit Systems\"), and it sets up the kernels and classifiers of the next lesson.

1. The idea in plain words

A quantum computer does not read a CSV file. Its only input is the circuit you run, so each feature value must be turned into something a gate can use: a bit that decides whether an X gate is applied, an angle for a rotation gate, or an amplitude of the state vector. The three choices trade qubits against gates:

  • Basis encoding stores bits as bits: the binary row 1,0,1 becomes the basis state |101⟩. One qubit per bit, at most one X gate per qubit.
  • Angle encoding stores each real feature as a rotation angle on its own qubit. One qubit and one rotation per feature.
  • Amplitude encoding stores a whole vector of N numbers in the N amplitudes of a log2N-qubit state. Exponentially few qubits, but in general about N gates to prepare.

That last line is the heart of the lesson: compressing N numbers into log2N qubits does not make loading them free, because a circuit that can produce an arbitrary state has to contain roughly one parameter per amplitude.

2. The definitions

📘 DEFINITION

Encoding (feature map). A rule x ↦ |φ(x)⟩ that turns a classical data vector x = (x1, …, xd) into a quantum state, implemented by a circuit U(x) acting on |0…0⟩: |φ(x)⟩ = U(x)|0…0⟩.

Basis encoding: a bitstring b1b2…bn ↦ |b1b2…bn⟩ (apply X to every qubit whose bit is 1).

Angle encoding: x ↦ RY(x1)|0⟩ ⊗ RY(x2)|0⟩ ⊗ … ⊗ RY(xd)|0⟩ (RX is also used; the idea is the same).

Amplitude encoding: x ∈ ℝN, N = 2n ↦ |x⟩ = (1/‖x‖) ∑i xi|i⟩, where ‖x‖ = √(∑ xi2) is the Euclidean norm and |i⟩ is the basis state whose binary label is i.

Convention for this chapter: |0⟩ = (1,0)T, |1⟩ = (0,1)T, and multi-qubit states are written textbook (big-endian) style, |q0 q1⟩ with qubit 0 on the left. Qiskit prints bitstrings the other way round (qubit 0 is the rightmost bit); the worked example shows both.

3. The key equations

The rotation used for angle encoding is

RY(θ) = exp(−iθY/2)

cos(θ/2)−sin(θ/2)
sin(θ/2)cos(θ/2)

so acting on |0⟩ it gives a real state whose amplitudes are set by the half-angle:

🧮 KEY EQUATION

RY(θ)|0⟩ = cos(θ/2)|0⟩ + sin(θ/2)|1⟩

P(1) = sin2(θ/2), P(0) = cos2(θ/2)

θ is the rotation angle in radians (your scaled feature value), Y is the Pauli-Y matrix, and P(1) is the probability of reading 1 when you measure in the computational basis. Because of the half-angle, a feature scaled to [0, π] sweeps the qubit from |0⟩ (θ = 0) to |1⟩ (θ = π); scaling to [0, 2π] would wrap round and map the smallest and largest values to the same state up to a sign.

For d features the angle-encoded state is a product state (a tensor product of one-qubit states), so it has no entanglement. Its 2d amplitudes are all products of cosines and sines:

|φ(x)⟩ = ⊗j=1..d [cos(xj/2)|0⟩ + sin(xj/2)|1⟩]

Costs in one table (d features, or N = 2n numbers for amplitude encoding):

EncodingQubitsGates to prepareWhat you can read back
Basisone per bit≤ one X per qubitthe bits, exactly, in one shot
Angledd rotations, depth 1each feature only statistically, via P(1) = sin2(xj/2)
Amplituden = log2NO(N) for a general vectorone index i per shot, drawn with probability xi2/‖x‖2

For the \"O(N)\" entry, the standard general construction by Möttönen, Vartiainen, Bergholm and Salomaa uses uniformly controlled rotations and needs 2n+2 − 4n − 4 CNOTs and 2n+2 − 5 one-qubit rotations to transform one arbitrary n-qubit state into another. A counting argument shows why nothing general can be much cheaper: an arbitrary real vector has N − 1 free directions after normalisation, and a circuit with G gates has only about G adjustable angles. Plugging in: n = 10 qubits (1,024 numbers) needs 4,052 CNOTs; n = 20 qubits (about a million numbers) needs 4,194,220 CNOTs. The qubit count shrank to 20, but the gate count is still of order N.

✅ VERIFIED

The CNOT and rotation counts are from M. Möttönen, J. J. Vartiainen, V. Bergholm, M. M. Salomaa, \"Transformation of quantum states using uniformly controlled rotations\", Quantum Information and Computation 5 (2005), arXiv:quant-ph/0407010 (arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/0407010). The quantum RAM proposal discussed below is V. Giovannetti, S. Lloyd, L. Maccone, \"Quantum random access memory\", Phys. Rev. Lett. 100, 160501 (2008). S. Aaronson's warning essay is \"Read the fine print\", Nature Physics 11, 291-293 (2015), nature.com/articles/nphys3272.

Checked 28 Sep 2026 by web search; the numbers 4,052 and 4,194,220 were computed from the published formula in Python.

4. Worked example: encoding one customer

Take one row from a customer table: age 34, monthly spend £120. Suppose age runs from 18 to 80 and spend from £0 to £400 in the training set. We angle-encode the two features on two qubits.

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE
  1. Scale each feature to [0, π] with min-max scaling, θ = π(x − min)/(max − min). Age: θ1 = π·(34 − 18)/(80 − 18) = π·16/62 = 0.8107 rad. Spend: θ2 = π·120/400 = 0.3π = 0.9425 rad. (Why [0, π]: the half-angle maps it onto the full sweep from |0⟩ to |1⟩ without wrapping.)
  2. Halve the angles (RY uses θ/2): θ1/2 = 0.4054, θ2/2 = 0.4712.
  3. Qubit 0 (age): RY(0.8107)|0⟩ = cos(0.4054)|0⟩ + sin(0.4054)|1⟩ = 0.9190|0⟩ + 0.3944|1⟩.
  4. Qubit 1 (spend): RY(0.9425)|0⟩ = cos(0.4712)|0⟩ + sin(0.4712)|1⟩ = 0.8910|0⟩ + 0.4540|1⟩.
  5. Tensor product |q0q1⟩ (big-endian): multiply amplitudes pairwise. |00⟩: 0.9190 × 0.8910 = 0.8188; |01⟩: 0.9190 × 0.4540 = 0.4172; |10⟩: 0.3944 × 0.8910 = 0.3514; |11⟩: 0.3944 × 0.4540 = 0.1790.
  6. Measurement probabilities (square each amplitude): 0.6704, 0.1741, 0.1235, 0.0321.

Answer: |φ(x)⟩ = 0.8188|00⟩ + 0.4172|01⟩ + 0.3514|10⟩ + 0.1790|11⟩. Sanity check: 0.6704 + 0.1741 + 0.1235 + 0.0321 = 1.0001, i.e. 1 up to rounding (numpy gives exactly 1.0).

Qiskit check (these lines run): qc = QuantumCircuit(2); qc.ry(0.8107335880, 0); qc.ry(0.9424777961, 1); Statevector(qc).probabilities_dict() returns 00: 0.6704, 01: 0.1235, 10: 0.1741, 11: 0.0321. The 0.1235 and 0.1741 look swapped only because Qiskit writes qubit 0 as the rightmost bit: Qiskit's \"01\" means q0 = 1, q1 = 0, which is our |10⟩.

A second, smaller example shows amplitude encoding. The 4-vector x = (2, 1, 0, 2) has ‖x‖ = √(4 + 1 + 0 + 4) = 3, so on two qubits it becomes |x⟩ = (2/3)|00⟩ + (1/3)|01⟩ + 0|10⟩ + (2/3)|11⟩ with probabilities 4/9 = 0.4444, 1/9 = 0.1111, 0, 4/9 = 0.4444 (sum 1). Qiskit's qc.initialize(x/3, [0, 1]) reproduces these probabilities. Notice what was lost: the overall scale ‖x‖ = 3 is not in the state at all, so if the norm matters for your model you must store it separately.

5. The data-loading bottleneck

Many proposed QML speed-ups (quantum linear-system solvers, quantum principal component analysis, quantum recommendation systems) run in time polylogarithmic in N, assuming the state |x⟩ is already available. If you have to build |x⟩ from a table with a general state-preparation circuit, you pay O(N) gates first and the exponential saving is gone before the algorithm starts. Two escape routes are proposed:

  • Structured data: if x comes from a formula (a smooth function, a sparse vector with few non-zeros, the output of another quantum process), it may be preparable with far fewer gates.
  • Quantum RAM (QRAM): a hypothetical memory that answers queries in superposition. Giovannetti, Lloyd and Maccone proposed a \"bucket-brigade\" architecture in which a query activates only O(log N) switches, but the memory still has O(N) physical cells and must be loaded, kept coherent and error-corrected. No large-scale QRAM has been built.

Aaronson's \"Read the fine print\" lists this as the first caveat to check on any exponential QML claim: how does the data get in, and how does the answer get out? Reading out is the mirror problem: a state with N amplitudes gives you one index per measurement, so recovering all N numbers to precision ε takes on the order of N/ε2 shots. Lesson 3 returns to this.

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE
  • Forgetting the half-angle. RY(θ)|0⟩ has amplitude sin(θ/2) on |1⟩, not sin θ. A feature scaled to π/2 gives P(1) = sin2(π/4) = 0.5, not 1.
  • Normalising by the sum instead of the root-sum-of-squares. Amplitude encoding divides by ‖x‖ = √(∑xi2); dividing (2,1,0,2) by 5 gives amplitudes whose squares sum to 9/25, which is not a quantum state.
  • \"20 qubits hold a million features, so loading is cheap.\" The qubit count is logarithmic; the gate count for a general vector is not.
  • Reading Qiskit bitstrings big-endian. In Qiskit output the rightmost character is qubit 0.
  • Scaling angles to [0, 2π]. Then the minimum and the maximum of a feature land on states that differ only by a sign and give identical measurement statistics.

6. How the choice looks to an analyst

Encoding is feature engineering. The same preprocessing questions you already ask apply: are features on comparable scales (min-max or standard scaling before choosing angles)? Are categorical columns one-hot or ordinal (basis encoding is natural for one-hot bits)? Are there outliers that would squash every other value into a tiny angle range? The difference is that on a quantum device every extra feature is a physical qubit or extra gates, and every number you want back costs repeated shots.

📊 FIGURE — One customer angle-encoded vs a 4-vector amplitude-encoded
Left: age and spend each drive one RY gate, giving the product state of the worked example. Right: four numbers fit in two qubits, but loading a general vector costs about N gates.
📊 YOUR DATA EDGE

Min-max scaling, outlier clipping and the difference between a sample estimate and the true value are everyday tools for you, and they are exactly what QML encoding needs. When a paper says \"we encode 4 features of the Iris dataset on 4 qubits\", ask what scaling was used, what range the angles cover, and how many shots stand behind each reported probability; a probability estimated from N shots has standard error √(p(1 − p)/N), so 1,000 shots gives roughly ±0.016 at p = 0.5.

Throughout this chapter, keep one question in mind: could a well-tuned classical model on the same preprocessed table do as well? Lesson 3 turns that question into a checklist.

7. What the exam asks

★ ON THE EXAM
  • Angle-encode a given feature value: scale, halve, take cos and sin, and give the state or P(1).
  • Amplitude-encode a short vector: compute the norm, write the normalised amplitudes, and give a measurement probability for a named basis state.
  • State the qubit count and the gate scaling of each encoding, and explain why log2N qubits does not mean log N preparation time.
  • Explain the data-loading (input) and read-out (output) caveats for exponential QML speed-up claims, and what QRAM would need to provide.
  • Translate between textbook |q0q1⟩ labels and Qiskit's little-endian bitstrings.

This lesson turns encoded states into models you can train. You will compute an entry of a quantum kernel matrix by hand and check it in Qiskit, build a small variational classifier, and compute its gradient with the parameter-shift rule, checking it against finite differences. These are the two workhorse QML models of the NISQ era (see the NISQ chapter for variational algorithms in general); the next lesson asks whether either beats classical machine learning.

1. The idea in plain words

You already know the kernel trick from support vector machines (SVMs): the SVM never needs the feature vectors themselves, only a similarity score k(x, x') for every pair of data points. A quantum kernel defines that similarity as \"how much do the two encoded quantum states overlap?\". The quantum computer only estimates the numbers in the kernel matrix; the SVM that uses them is ordinary classical software (scikit-learn's SVC(kernel=\"precomputed\")).

A variational classifier is closer to a small neural network. After encoding x, apply a circuit W(θ) with trainable angles θ, measure an observable such as Z on one qubit, and use the expectation value f(x; θ) ∈ [−1, 1] as the score, predicting the label sign(f). Training adjusts θ by gradient descent, with gradients measured on the quantum device itself.

2. The definitions

📘 DEFINITION

Quantum kernel. For a feature map x ↦ |φ(x)⟩ = U(x)|0…0⟩, the (fidelity) quantum kernel is k(x, x') = |⟨φ(x)|φ(x')⟩|2, a number between 0 (orthogonal states) and 1 (identical states up to phase).

Kernel (Gram) matrix. For training points x1, …, xm, the m × m matrix K with Kij = k(xi, xj). It is symmetric, has ones on the diagonal and is positive semidefinite (all eigenvalues ≥ 0).

Variational (parameterised) classifier. A model f(x; θ) = ⟨0…0|U(x)†W(θ)† O W(θ)U(x)|0…0⟩, where W(θ) is a circuit of rotation gates with trainable angles θ and O is a measured observable (here Z on one qubit). The prediction is sign f(x; θ).

3. The key equations

Estimating a kernel entry (compute-uncompute). Run U(x), then the inverse U(x')†, and measure every qubit. The probability of reading all zeros is

P(0…0) = |⟨0…0|U(x')†U(x)|0…0⟩|2 = |⟨φ(x')|φ(x)⟩|2 = k(x, x')

so with N shots you estimate k by the fraction of all-zero outcomes, with standard error √(k(1 − k)/N): a binomial proportion, exactly like a conversion rate.

Closed form for the angle-encoding map of Lesson 1. Because the state is a product, the overlap factorises: ⟨φ(x)|φ(x')⟩ = ∏j [cos(xj/2)cos(x'j/2) + sin(xj/2)sin(x'j/2)] = ∏j cos((xj − x'j)/2), hence

🧮 KEY EQUATION

k(x, x') = ∏j=1..d cos2((xj − x'j)/2) (product angle-encoding kernel)

∂f/∂θ = [ f(θ + π/2) − f(θ − π/2) ] / 2 (parameter-shift rule)

xj, x'j: the scaled angles of feature j for the two data points; d: number of features. f(θ): the measured expectation value as a function of one gate angle θ, all other angles held fixed. The shift rule holds exactly for any gate of the form exp(−iθP/2) with P a Pauli product (RX, RY, RZ, RZZ, …).

Why the shift rule is exact, not an approximation. If θ enters only through exp(−iθP/2) with P2 = I, then f(θ) = a cos θ + b sin θ + c for some constants a, b, c. Using cos(θ ± π/2) = ∓sin θ and sin(θ ± π/2) = ±cos θ:

f(θ+π/2) − f(θ−π/2) = a(−sin θ − sin θ) + b(cos θ + cos θ) = 2(−a sin θ + b cos θ) = 2 f'(θ)

Two circuit evaluations with a large shift (π/2) give the exact derivative, while finite differences use a tiny step and have a truncation error. The rule was introduced for quantum circuit learning by Mitarai et al. and generalised by Schuld et al.

✅ VERIFIED

Quantum kernels with a classically hard-looking feature map: V. Havlíček, A. D. Córcoles, K. Temme, A. W. Harrow, A. Kandala, J. M. Chow, J. M. Gambetta, \"Supervised learning with quantum-enhanced feature spaces\", Nature 567, 209-212 (2019) (pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30867609). Parameter-shift rule: K. Mitarai, M. Negoro, M. Kitagawa, K. Fujii, \"Quantum circuit learning\", Phys. Rev. A 98, 032309 (2018); M. Schuld, V. Bergholm, C. Gogolin, J. Izaac, N. Killoran, \"Evaluating analytic gradients on quantum hardware\", Phys. Rev. A 99, 032331 (2019) (arxiv.org/abs/1811.11184).

Checked 28 Sep 2026 by web search.

Havlíček et al. used an entangling feature map (the pattern behind Qiskit's ZZFeatureMap) precisely because the product map above has the closed form: anyone can compute it classically in O(d) arithmetic. Their map was chosen from a family of circuits believed, not proven, to be hard to simulate; a hard-to-simulate kernel is necessary for a quantum advantage but, as Lesson 3 shows, far from sufficient.

4. Worked example A: one quantum-kernel entry

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Customer A (age 34, spend £120) and customer B (age 52, spend £300), scaled to [0, π] as in Lesson 1 (age range 18-80, spend range £0-400).

📊 FIGURE — Kernel matrix of three customers and the parameter-shift rule
Left: each cell is k = overlap² of two encoded customers; A and C are similar, A and B are not. Right: two circuit runs shifted by ±π/2 give the exact slope of f(θ).
  1. Angles. A: (π·16/62, π·120/400) = (0.8107, 0.9425). B: (π·34/62, π·300/400) = (1.7228, 2.3562).
  2. Differences. Δ1 = 0.8107 − 1.7228 = −0.9121; Δ2 = 0.9425 − 2.3562 = −1.4137.
  3. Halve. Δ1/2 = −0.4560; Δ2/2 = −0.7069.
  4. Cosines. cos(−0.4560) = 0.8978; cos(−0.7069) = 0.7604 (cosine is even, so the sign of Δ does not matter).
  5. Square. 0.89782 = 0.8061; 0.76042 = 0.5782.
  6. Multiply. k(A, B) = 0.8061 × 0.5782 = 0.4661.
  7. Cross-check with state vectors. |φ(A)⟩ = (0.8188, 0.4172, 0.3514, 0.1790) and |φ(B)⟩ = (0.2493, 0.6018, 0.2904, 0.7010) in the order |00⟩, |01⟩, |10⟩, |11⟩. Their inner product is 0.6827 and 0.68272 = 0.4661.

Answer: k(A, B) = 0.4661. Sanity check: 0 ≤ k ≤ 1, and k(A, A) = ∏cos2(0) = 1.

Qiskit compute-uncompute check (runs as written; RY(−b)RY(a) = RY(a − b) on each qubit): qc = QuantumCircuit(2); qc.ry(0.8107336, 0); qc.ry(0.9424778, 1); qc.ry(-1.7228092, 0); qc.ry(-2.3561945, 1); Statevector(qc).probabilities_dict()[\"00\"] gives 0.4661. On hardware you would sample: one simulated run of 1,000 shots gave 469 all-zero outcomes, an estimate of 0.469, within one standard error √(0.4661 × 0.5339/1000) = 0.0158 of the true value.

Adding a third customer C (age 40, spend £150; angles 1.1148 and 1.1781) gives the kernel matrix below. Its eigenvalues are 0.0167, 0.5880 and 2.3953, all non-negative, as a valid kernel requires.

ABC
A10.46610.9636
B0.466110.6294
C0.96360.62941

A and C are similar customers (0.9636); A and B are not (0.4661). That smallest eigenvalue of 0.0167 is a warning: with shot noise of ±0.016 per entry, an estimated matrix can easily have a slightly negative eigenvalue, and practitioners then project it back onto the positive semidefinite matrices before training the SVM.

5. Worked example B: a variational classifier and its gradient

Circuit on two qubits for customer A (label y = −1), with one trainable angle θ, textbook order |q0q1⟩:

StepQubit 0Qubit 1
1 (encode)RY(x1 = 0.8107)RY(x2 = 0.9425)
2 (entangle)CNOT controlCNOT target
3 (train)(nothing)RY(θ)
4 (read out)(nothing)measure Z
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE
  1. After encoding: (0.8188, 0.4172, 0.3514, 0.1790) on |00⟩, |01⟩, |10⟩, |11⟩ (Lesson 1).
  2. After CNOT (flip q1 when q0 = 1, i.e. swap the |10⟩ and |11⟩ amplitudes): (0.8188, 0.4172, 0.1790, 0.3514).
  3. After RY(θ = 0.6) on q1: (0.6589, 0.6405, 0.0672, 0.3886); probabilities (0.4342, 0.4103, 0.0045, 0.1510).
  4. Expectation of Z on q1: P(q1 = 0) = 0.4342 + 0.0045 = 0.4387, P(q1 = 1) = 0.4103 + 0.1510 = 0.5613, so f = 0.4387 − 0.5613 = −0.1226. Prediction sign(f) = −1, correct but with low confidence. Squared loss L = (f − y)2 = (−0.1226 + 1)2 = 0.7699.
  5. Closed form (conjugating Z through the gates): f(θ) = cos θ cos x1 cos x2 − sin θ sin x2 = 0.8253 × 0.6890 × 0.5878 − 0.5646 × 0.8090 = −0.1226. It matches.
  6. Parameter shift: f(0.6 + π/2) = −0.8964 and f(0.6 − π/2) = +0.8964, so ∂f/∂θ = (−0.8964 − 0.8964)/2 = −0.8964 (exactly −0.8963707 to 7 places).
  7. Finite-difference check [f(θ + h) − f(θ − h)]/(2h): h = 0.1 gives −0.8949, h = 0.01 gives −0.8964 (−0.8963558), h = 0.0001 gives −0.8963707. The analytic derivative −sin θ cos x1 cos x2 − cos θ sin x2 is −0.8963707. All agree; only finite differences carry a step-size error.
  8. One gradient step with learning rate η = 0.5: ∂L/∂θ = 2(f − y)·∂f/∂θ = 2 × 0.8774 × (−0.8964) = −1.5730, so θ ← 0.6 + 0.5 × 1.5730 = 1.3865. Then f = −0.7211 and L = 0.0778.

Answer: f = −0.1226, ∂f/∂θ = −0.8964 by parameter shift, confirmed by finite differences; one step cuts the loss from 0.7699 to 0.0778. Sanity check: the four probabilities in step 3 sum to 1.0000. Here f(θ + π/2) = −f(θ − π/2) because this f has no constant term c; in general the two shifted values are not negatives of each other.

Qiskit check: qc = QuantumCircuit(2); qc.ry(0.8107336, 0); qc.ry(0.9424778, 1); qc.cx(0, 1); qc.ry(0.6, 1) then Statevector(qc).expectation_value(SparsePauliOp(\"ZI\")).real gives −0.1226. The Pauli label \"ZI\" puts Z on qubit 1 because Qiskit labels are little-endian too.

6. Why not just use finite differences? Shot noise

On hardware each f is an average of N shots of ±1 with variance (1 − f2)/N. We simulated 2,000 repetitions at N = 1,000 shots per circuit: the parameter-shift estimate had standard deviation 0.0099, while the finite difference with h = 0.01 had standard deviation 2.19, larger than the gradient itself. Dividing a noisy difference by a small 2h amplifies the noise by 1/(2h) = 50; the shift rule divides by 2. The cost is one pair of circuits per parameter, so a model with p parameters needs 2p circuits per gradient, each run for N shots.

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE
  • Forgetting to square the overlap. The kernel is |⟨φ(x)|φ(x')⟩|2 = 0.4661 in the example, not 0.6827.
  • Using the full angle difference. The product kernel uses cos2(Δ/2), a consequence of the half-angle in RY.
  • Dropping the /2 or the sign order in the shift rule: it is [f(θ + π/2) − f(θ − π/2)]/2.
  • Applying the ±π/2 shift to every gate. It is exact for exp(−iθP/2) with P a Pauli product. Controlled rotations and gates with other generator spectra need more shifted terms or a decomposition.
  • Thinking the quantum computer trains the SVM. In a quantum-kernel SVM only the kernel entries are quantum; the optimisation is classical.
★ ON THE EXAM
  • Compute a kernel entry for angle-encoded points (halve the differences, cos, square, multiply) and state why it lies in [0, 1].
  • Describe the compute-uncompute circuit and the shot count needed for a target standard error.
  • Evaluate a one-parameter circuit's expectation value and its parameter-shift derivative; show the two-line proof that the rule is exact.
  • Count circuits: m(m − 1)/2 distinct off-diagonal kernel entries for m training points; 2p circuits per gradient for p parameters.
  • Explain why parameter shift beats finite differences under shot noise.

This lesson is the reality check. After it you should be able to read a quantum machine-learning claim the way you would read a vendor's benchmark: find the assumptions, the baseline and the error bars, and say whether a speed-up is proven, conjectured or absent. It draws on complexity (Chapter \"Quantum Complexity and Quantum Advantage\") and on the two previous lessons, and it is where your analyst training matters most.

1. The idea in plain words

QML claims fall into three buckets, and they deserve very different levels of trust:

  1. Exponential speed-ups that assume fast quantum access to the data (QRAM-style input, Lesson 1). Several of the best known have been dequantized: a classical algorithm given comparable sampling access does almost as well.
  2. Provable advantages for specially built problems. These are rigorous but rely on structure such as the discrete logarithm (the problem Shor's algorithm breaks) or on data that are themselves quantum states from an experiment.
  3. Heuristic near-term models on ordinary classical data (the kernels and variational classifiers of Lesson 2). Here there is no demonstrated advantage: careful benchmarks find that tuned classical models usually do as well or better, and the models face trainability and measurement-cost problems that grow with qubit number.

None of this says QML is worthless. It says the burden of proof sits with the quantum claim, and the evidence to date supports advantages mainly for quantum data and for artificial problems, not for your company's churn table.

2. Definitions you need

📘 DEFINITION

Dequantization. Showing that a quantum algorithm's claimed exponential speed-up disappears by giving a classical algorithm that solves the same task, under a matching input model, with only polynomial slowdown.

Sample-and-query (ℓ2-norm sampling) access. A classical data structure that returns any entry Aij on request and can sample a row index i with probability ‖Ai‖2/‖A‖F2 (and an entry within a row with probability Aij2/‖Ai‖2). ‖Ai‖ is the Euclidean norm of row i and ‖A‖F the Frobenius norm (root of the sum of all squared entries). It is the classical counterpart of being able to prepare amplitude-encoded rows.

End-to-end advantage. A speed-up (or accuracy gain) that survives after counting data loading, read-out, shots, error correction and comparison with the best classical method for the same task, not a straw-man baseline.

Barren plateau. A training landscape whose gradients are exponentially small in the number of qubits for most parameter settings, so estimating them takes exponentially many shots.

3. Dequantization: the recommendation-system story

In a paper at ITCS 2017, Kerenidis and Prakash gave a quantum recommendation algorithm that samples good recommendations from a low-rank approximation of a user-product preference matrix in time polylogarithmic in the matrix dimensions, given a QRAM-like data structure. It was regarded as one of the strongest candidates for an exponential QML speed-up on a real task. In 2018 (arXiv; STOC 2019) Ewin Tang showed that a classical algorithm with ℓ2-norm sampling access to the same matrix can output a sample from a rank-k approximation in time polynomial in k and logarithmic in the dimensions, so the quantum algorithm is only polynomially faster, not exponentially. The key insight: the quantum input assumption (prepare any row as a state) quietly provides the same power as classical importance sampling by squared norms, and a low-rank matrix is well described by a few sampled rows and columns. Follow-up work extended this \"quantum-inspired\" technique to other low-rank linear-algebra QML proposals.

🧮 KEY EQUATION

P(row i) = ‖Ai‖2 / ‖A‖F2 (ℓ2-norm sampling, the classical analogue of measuring an amplitude-encoded state)

E[k] = (1/2 + 2/π2)d ≈ 0.7026d (mean product angle-encoding kernel, features uniform on [0, π])

N ≈ (1 − k) / (k r2) (shots to estimate a kernel value k with relative standard error r)

Ai: row i of the data matrix; d: number of features (qubits); k: a kernel value; r: target relative error (0.1 for 10%). The third line comes from the binomial standard error √(k(1 − k)/N) divided by k.

Notice that the row-sampling probability is exactly the Born rule for measuring the amplitude-encoded state of the vector of row norms. Whenever a QML paper assumes it can prepare |x⟩ cheaply, ask whether a classical algorithm with ℓ2-sampling access would do just as well; if the data are low rank, often it does.

✅ VERIFIED

I. Kerenidis, A. Prakash, \"Quantum Recommendation Systems\", ITCS 2017, LIPIcs 67, doi:10.4230/LIPIcs.ITCS.2017.49. E. Tang, \"A quantum-inspired classical algorithm for recommendation systems\", STOC 2019, doi:10.1145/3313276.3316310, arXiv:1807.04271 (arxiv.org/abs/1807.04271). Y. Liu, S. Arunachalam, K. Temme, \"A rigorous and robust quantum speed-up in supervised machine learning\", Nature Physics 17, 1013-1017 (2021) (nature.com/articles/s41567-021-01287-z). H.-Y. Huang et al., \"Power of data in quantum machine learning\", Nature Communications 12, 2631 (2021). H.-Y. Huang et al., \"Quantum advantage in learning from experiments\", Science 376, 1182-1186 (2022), doi:10.1126/science.abn7293.

J. R. McClean et al., \"Barren plateaus in quantum neural network training landscapes\", Nature Communications (2018), doi:10.1038/s41467-018-07090-4. S. Thanasilp, S. Wang, M. Cerezo, Z. Holmes, \"Exponential concentration in quantum kernel methods\", Nature Communications (2024), doi:10.1038/s41467-024-49287-w. M. Cerezo et al., \"Does provable absence of barren plateaus imply classical simulability?\", Nature Communications 16, 7907 (2025). J. Bowles, S. Ahmed, M. Schuld, \"Better than classical? The subtle art of benchmarking quantum machine learning models\", arXiv:2403.07059 (2024) (arxiv.org/abs/2403.07059).

All checked 28 Sep 2026 by web search.

4. When speed-ups can exist

  • Rigorous, but artificial. Liu, Arunachalam and Temme built a classification problem whose labels hide a discrete logarithm. A quantum kernel method learns it efficiently with only classical access to the data, while no efficient classical learner does better than random guessing, assuming discrete log is classically hard. It proves an end-to-end advantage is possible; it is not a dataset anyone has in practice.
  • Data change the game. Huang et al. (\"Power of data\") showed that a classical learner given training data can often predict functions that are hard to compute classically, so a hard-to-simulate kernel is not enough; they give a methodology, based on rigorous prediction-error bounds, for checking on the actual data whether a quantum model could beat classical ones before any advantage is claimed, and a \"projected\" quantum model with a provable speed-up for a problem in the fault-tolerant regime.
  • Quantum data. Huang et al. (Science 2022) proved exponential advantages for learning properties of quantum systems when the learner can store quantum states from an experiment in a quantum memory and process them jointly. This is the clearest case of a QML advantage, and it concerns data that are born quantum (sensors, quantum simulations), not rows of a CSV file.
  • Polynomial speed-ups from Grover-type search or amplitude estimation (Chapter \"Grover's Search\") can apply to some ML subroutines, but a quadratic gain needs fault-tolerant hardware and large problem sizes before it beats the constant-factor overheads of error correction.

On the heuristic side, two scaling problems appear. Barren plateaus (McClean et al.): for broad classes of random, deep parameterised circuits the gradient variance shrinks exponentially with qubit number. Exponential concentration (Thanasilp et al.): quantum kernel values for different inputs can crowd exponentially close to a fixed value, so a polynomial number of shots cannot tell data points apart and the trained model ignores its input. The standard cures (shallow circuits, local cost functions, small angle scales) tend to confine the computation to a small, structured part of the state space, and Cerezo et al. argue that many landscapes provably free of barren plateaus can then be simulated classically, or with a classical algorithm helped by a quantum device for data collection. Trainability and quantum advantage pull in opposite directions.

5. Worked example: how fast the product kernel concentrates

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Take the angle-encoding kernel of Lesson 2, k(x, x') = ∏cos2((xj − x'j)/2), and suppose each scaled feature of two random customers is independent and uniform on [0, π]. How big is a typical kernel value, and how many shots does estimating it take?

📊 FIGURE — How fast the product kernel concentrates as features grow
Each bar is one feature count d: the mean kernel value (grey row) shrinks as 0.7026ᵈ, and the shots needed to pin it to 10% grow from dozens to millions (log scale).
  1. Rewrite one factor. cos2(Δ/2) = (1 + cos Δ)/2 with Δ = x − x'.
  2. Expand. cos(x − x') = cos x cos x' + sin x sin x'.
  3. Average over [0, π]. E[cos x] = (1/π)∫0πcos x dx = 0 and E[sin x] = (1/π)∫0πsin x dx = 2/π. By independence E[cos Δ] = 0 · 0 + (2/π)(2/π) = 4/π2 = 0.4053.
  4. One factor. E[cos2(Δ/2)] = (1 + 0.4053)/2 = 1/2 + 2/π2 = 0.7026.
  5. d features. Features are independent, so E[k] = 0.7026d.
  6. Shots for 10% relative error: N ≈ 100(1 − k)/k.

d (qubits)E[k]shots for ±10%
10.702642
20.4937103
50.1713484
100.029333,309
208.60 × 10−4116,129
502.17 × 10−84.6 × 109
1004.71 × 10−162.1 × 1017

Answer: the mean kernel value falls as 0.7026d, and the shots per entry grow as roughly 1.42d; at 50 features one entry needs billions of shots. Sanity check: a Monte Carlo run in numpy with 200,000 random pairs gave a mean of 0.02936 at d = 10 (formula 0.02933); the median was only 0.00706, so typical values are even smaller than the mean.

And the twist: this particular kernel never needed a quantum computer. The closed form is d cosines and a product, O(d) classical arithmetic, and numpy reproduces the Lesson 2 entry 0.4661 in one line. A quantum kernel is only interesting if it is hard to compute classically, and then this lesson's other tests (the power of data, concentration, a tuned baseline) still apply.

Two more budget numbers make the point concrete. A training set of m = 1,000 points has 499,500 distinct kernel entries; at 1,000 shots each that is 499.5 million circuit executions before the SVM even starts, and reaching a standard error of 0.01 at k = 0.5 needs 2,500 shots per entry, 1.25 billion shots in all. Shrinking the angle scale (a \"bandwidth\", like γ in an RBF kernel) keeps kernel values away from zero and helps in practice; whether any quantum benefit is left once the bandwidth is tuned is an open question, not a known result.

6. Benchmarking against strong classical baselines

Bowles, Ahmed and Schuld ran a large open-source study: 12 popular QML models against classical models on 160 datasets drawn from 6 binary-classification tasks, using the same open-source pipeline for all of them. Out-of-the-box classical models generally beat the quantum classifiers, and removing the entanglement from the quantum models often did as well or better, suggesting that \"quantumness\" was not what made them work on these small problems. They also stress how much design choices (dataset, preprocessing, tuning budget, which baseline) change the verdict.

📊 YOUR DATA EDGE

Read a QML paper like a model-evaluation report. The checklist:

  • Baseline. Is the classical competitor tuned (RBF-SVM with a grid over C and γ, gradient boosting, a small MLP) with the same search budget as the quantum model? A linear model with default settings is a straw man.
  • Error bars and sample size. An accuracy of 0.84 on 100 test points has standard error √(0.84 × 0.16/100) = 0.037, so a 95% interval of about ±0.072; beating a classical 0.80 by 4 points on 100 points is noise. For two models on the same test set use a paired test (McNemar) rather than comparing intervals.
  • Simulated or hardware? Noise-free simulation of 8 qubits is not evidence about a noisy 100-qubit device, and a model small enough to simulate is, by definition, classically simulable.
  • Shots and wall-clock. Are the shots behind each kernel entry or gradient reported? What did training cost end to end, including data loading?
  • Leakage and selection. Were scaling, feature selection and hyperparameters fitted on the training fold only? Were only the datasets where quantum won reported?
  • Scaling claim vs measurement. Does the headline extrapolate an asymptotic speed-up from a toy size, and does the argument depend on QRAM or low rank that a dequantized algorithm could also exploit?
  • Ablation. Does performance survive if entanglement is removed or the quantum kernel is replaced by a classical one with the same bandwidth?
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE
  • \"Hard to simulate, therefore advantage.\" A classically hard kernel is necessary, not sufficient: with data, classical learners can often predict it well enough (Huang et al. 2021).
  • Quoting an asymptotic QRAM speed-up as a practical one. Without the input model, the exponential saving is gone; with it, dequantized classical algorithms may get the same.
  • Treating the discrete-log advantage as evidence for business data. It is a proof of possibility on a constructed dataset.
  • Reading \"outperforms classical\" without checking the baseline's tuning or the confidence intervals.
  • Believing more qubits always help. Wider product or random feature maps concentrate kernels and flatten gradients; the measurement budget explodes.
★ ON THE EXAM
  • Define dequantization and explain, using ℓ2-norm sampling and low rank, why Tang's result removed the exponential speed-up of the quantum recommendation algorithm.
  • Classify a claimed QML speed-up as proven (and under which assumption), conjectured or absent.
  • Compute a mean product-kernel value for d features and the shots needed for a target relative error.
  • Explain barren plateaus and exponential concentration and why their cures pull towards classical simulability.
  • Critique a benchmark: baseline, error bars, simulation versus hardware, shots, leakage.
