This lesson turns the pen-and-paper circuits of the earlier chapters into a program you can run. By the end you can write a Qiskit circuit, get its exact state vector, sample it like real hardware would, and read the counts dictionary without getting the qubit order backwards. Everything later in the chapter (transpiling, noise, other frameworks) builds on these three moves: build, simulate, read.

\n\n

The idea in plain words

\n

A quantum program in Qiskit is a data structure, not a running process. You create a QuantumCircuit object, append gates to it one by one (like appending rows to a table), and only then hand the finished object to something that executes it. There are two very different kinds of \"something\":

\n
    \n
  • An exact simulator that multiplies the 2n-entry state vector by each gate matrix. It returns amplitudes, which no real machine can give you. Qiskit's class for this is qiskit.quantum_info.Statevector.
    • \n
  • A sampler that behaves like hardware: it measures, collapses, repeats for a number of shots, and hands back only bitstrings and how often each appeared. Qiskit's built-in exact-sampling version is qiskit.primitives.StatevectorSampler.
    • \n
\n

The whole art of reading results is keeping those two apart: amplitudes are what the theory predicts, counts are a random sample from the probabilities |amplitude|2.

\n\n
📘 DEFINITION

Shot: one complete run of the circuit ending in measurement, producing one bitstring. Counts: a dictionary mapping each observed bitstring to the number of shots that produced it; the values add up to the number of shots.

Primitive: Qiskit's standard interface for executing circuits. The Sampler returns measurement outcomes (counts or bitstrings); the Estimator returns expectation values ⟨ψ|O|ψ⟩ of observables O such as Z⊗Z. The same interface is implemented by local simulators and by cloud hardware services.

\n\n

The objects you need and what each line means

\n

Installed here is Qiskit 2.5.2 (the 2.x series). Four imports cover nearly everything in this lesson:

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
ObjectWhere it livesWhat it is for
QuantumCircuitqiskitBuild the circuit: QuantumCircuit(2) makes qubits 0 and 1, all starting in |0⟩
Statevectorqiskit.quantum_infoExact amplitudes of a circuit without measurements
StatevectorSamplerqiskit.primitivesShot-based sampling of measured circuits, like hardware but noiseless
StatevectorEstimatorqiskit.primitivesExact expectation values of Pauli observables
\n

Gate methods read like the textbook: qc.h(0) appends a Hadamard on qubit 0, qc.cx(0, 1) appends a CNOT with control 0 and target 1 (control always first), qc.x(q), qc.ry(θ, q) and so on. qc.measure_all() adds a barrier, creates a classical register called meas with one bit per qubit, and measures qubit i into bit i.

\n\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

Qiskit labels the basis state of n qubits by the string bn−1 … b1 b0, so qubit 0 is the rightmost character (little-endian). The index into the state vector is

index = b0·20 + b1·21 + … + bn−1·2n−1

where bi ∈ {0, 1} is the value of qubit i. Example: qubit 1 = 1 and qubit 0 = 0 is the string '10' and the index 2. The textbook (big-endian) convention used in the rest of this course writes the same state as |q0q1⟩ = |01⟩. Same physics, reversed label.

\n\n

Worked example: a Bell-state program, line by line

\n

Goal: prepare (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2, check it exactly, then sample it 1,000 times. Every line below was run on Qiskit 2.5.2 and the output shown is the real output.

\n

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from qiskit.quantum_info import Statevector
from qiskit.primitives import StatevectorSampler

qc = QuantumCircuit(2)
qc.h(0)
qc.cx(0, 1)
sv = Statevector.from_instruction(qc)
print(sv.data.round(4))
print({str(k): round(float(v), 4) for k, v in sv.probabilities_dict().items()})

qc.measure_all()
sampler = StatevectorSampler(seed=42)
job = sampler.run([qc], shots=1000)
result = job.result()
counts = result[0].data.meas.get_counts()
print(counts)

\n

Real output:

\n

[0.7071+0.j 0. +0.j 0. +0.j 0.7071+0.j]
{'00': 0.5, '11': 0.5}
{'11': 497, '00': 503}

\n\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE
    \n
  1. Start: QuantumCircuit(2) means the state is |00⟩, vector (1, 0, 0, 0). Both qubits start in |0⟩, no initialisation line needed.
    2. \n
  2. qc.h(0): qubit 0 becomes (|0⟩ + |1⟩)/√2. In Qiskit labels the state is (|'00'⟩ + |'01'⟩)/√2, amplitudes 0.7071 at indices 0 and 1 (index 1 because b0 = 1 gives 20 = 1).
    3. \n
  3. qc.cx(0, 1): where qubit 0 is 1, flip qubit 1. The index-1 component '01' becomes '11' (index 3). Result: 0.7071 at indices 0 and 3, which is exactly the first printed line.
    4. \n
  4. Probabilities: |0.7071|2 = 0.5 for '00' and for '11'; '01' and '10' have amplitude 0 so they never appear. Sanity check: 0.5 + 0.5 = 1.
    5. \n
  5. Why measure_all comes after Statevector: Statevector.from_instruction needs a circuit with no measurements, because measurement is not a unitary. So we took the exact state first, then appended measurements for the sampler.
    6. \n
  6. Sampling: sampler.run([qc], shots=1000) takes a list of circuits (each is a \"pub\", primitive unified bloc) and returns a job. job.result() is a list-like object with one entry per pub, so result[0] is our circuit's result.
    7. \n
  7. Reaching the counts: result[0].data.meas is the bit array for the register named meas (the name measure_all chose). .get_counts() turns it into a dictionary. We got {'11': 497, '00': 503}: never '01' or '10', and roughly 50/50. Sanity check: 497 + 503 = 1000 shots.
    8. \n
\n\n

The seed makes the sample reproducible: running the script again gives exactly 497 and 503. Without seed=42 you would get a different split each time, typically within a few percent of 500.

\n\n

Reading counts when the qubits differ

\n

The Bell example hides the bit-ordering trap because '00' and '11' read the same both ways. This one does not. Same sampler object, run on:

📊 FIGURE — Qiskit's build-run-read workflow and little-endian counts
Top: the circuit is a data structure that is built, optionally transpiled, run for shots and read as counts. Bottom: in '01' the rightmost character is qubit 0.
\n

qc2 = QuantumCircuit(2)
qc2.x(0)
qc2.h(1)
qc2.measure_all()
counts2 = sampler.run([qc2], shots=2000).result()[0].data.meas.get_counts()
print(counts2)

\n

Real output: {'11': 992, '01': 1008}

\n\n\n\n\n\n
BitstringQubit 1 (left char)Qubit 0 (right char)ShotsFrequency
'01'0110080.504
'11'119920.496
\n

Qubit 0 was flipped by X, so it is 1 in every shot: that is the rightmost character, always '1'. Qubit 1 went through H, so it is the random one: the leftmost character. If you read the strings left-to-right as q0q1 you would wrongly conclude that qubit 0 is random and qubit 1 is fixed.

\n\n

Expectation values with the Estimator

\n

Many algorithms (VQE, QAOA, the machine-learning chapter) need ⟨O⟩ rather than counts. The Estimator takes (circuit, observable) pairs; the circuit must have no measurements:

\n

from qiskit.quantum_info import SparsePauliOp
from qiskit.primitives import StatevectorEstimator
bell = QuantumCircuit(2)
bell.h(0)
bell.cx(0, 1)
obs = [SparsePauliOp(\"ZZ\"), SparsePauliOp(\"ZI\"), SparsePauliOp(\"XX\")]
print(StatevectorEstimator().run([(bell, obs)]).result()[0].data.evs)

\n

Real output: [1. 0. 1.]

\n

Read the Pauli strings little-endian too: in \"ZI\" the Z sits on qubit 1 and the identity on qubit 0. ⟨Z⊗Z⟩ = +1 because the two bits always agree; ⟨Z on one qubit⟩ = 0 because each qubit alone is a fair coin; ⟨X⊗X⟩ = +1 because the Bell state is also a +1 eigenstate of XX. These are exact values, not estimates from shots.

\n\n

The traps

\n
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE
    \n
  • Reversing the bitstring. In Qiskit '01' means qubit 0 = 1, qubit 1 = 0. In the textbook |q0q1⟩ notation that same state is |10⟩. Always say which convention you are using before you write an answer.
    • \n
  • Treating counts as probabilities. 497/1000 is an estimate of 0.5, not a sign that the circuit is biased. Its standard error is √(0.5·0.5/1000) ≈ 0.0158, so anything from about 0.47 to 0.53 is unremarkable.
    • \n
  • Asking a Statevector of a measured circuit. Statevector.from_instruction raises an error on a circuit containing measure. Take the state before you call measure_all(), or build two circuits.
    • \n
  • Old tutorials. Code with from qiskit import execute, Aer is from before Qiskit 1.0. execute() was removed in Qiskit 1.0, and Aer is a separate package (qiskit-aer, not installed here). Use primitives instead.
    • \n
  • Wrong register name. measure_all() names the register meas; a circuit built as QuantumCircuit(2, 2) with explicit measure calls has a register named c, reached as result[0].data.c.
    • \n
\n\n
✅ VERIFIED

qiskit.execute() was deprecated in Qiskit 0.46 and removed in Qiskit 1.0; the replacement is transpile followed by a primitive or backend.run(). Qiskit 2.0 then removed the old BackendV1 interface. Sources: IBM Quantum documentation, \"Qiskit 1.0 feature changes\" (quantum.cloud.ibm.com/docs/en/guides/qiskit-1.0-features); Qiskit 2.0.0 release notes (github.com/Qiskit/qiskit/releases/tag/2.0.0).

The Qiskit README describes Qiskit as an SDK for circuits, operators and the Sampler and Estimator primitives, with hardware-optimised primitives in the separate qiskit-ibm-runtime package (github.com/Qiskit/qiskit). Checked 28 Sep 2026.

\n\n
📊 YOUR DATA EDGE

A counts dictionary is a GROUP BY bitstring, COUNT(*) over a table of shots, and the sampler can give you that raw table too: result[0].data.meas.get_bitstrings() returns one string per shot. Everything you know about sampling error applies. With N shots the estimate p̂ of an outcome probability p has standard error √(p(1−p)/N): 0.0158 at N = 1,000 and p = 0.5, halving to 0.0079 at N = 4,000. Quadrupling the shots only halves the error.

When a paper reports \"fidelity 0.97 from 1,000 shots\", ask for the error bar before you compare it with another result.

\n\n

What the exam asks

\n
★ ON THE EXAM
    \n
  • Given a short Qiskit program, write down the state vector (with the index of each non-zero amplitude) or the counts keys you expect. Show the bit order you used.
    • \n
  • Convert between Qiskit strings and textbook kets: Qiskit '110' on three qubits means q2 = 1, q1 = 1, q0 = 0, which is the textbook |q0q1q2⟩ = |011⟩, index 6.
    • \n
  • Explain the difference between an exact simulation (amplitudes, including phases) and sampling (counts only; phases invisible unless you change basis before measuring).
    • \n
  • Decide whether an observed count split is consistent with a predicted probability, using the binomial standard error.
    • \n
\n

One habit pays off in every later chapter: before trusting a sampled result, run the same circuit through Statevector and check that the counts are close to N·|amplitude|2 for every key. If they are not, the bug is in your reading of the output, not in the physics.

The circuits you wrote in the last lesson assume any gate on any pair of qubits, with no errors. Real processors offer a handful of native gates, connect each qubit to only a few neighbours, and make mistakes at every step. This lesson shows what the transpiler does to bridge that gap, how to measure the cost it adds, how noise changes your counts, and how to read a device's calibration data so you can predict, before you spend queue time, whether a run is worth doing. It links the software of this chapter to the hardware chapter and the error-mitigation ideas of the NISQ chapter.

\n\n

The idea in plain words

\n

Think of the transpiler as a compiler for a very picky machine. You hand it a circuit written in textbook gates (H, CNOT, Toffoli...). It hands back an equivalent circuit that the device can execute directly, called an ISA circuit (instruction set architecture circuit). To get there it does four jobs:

\n
    \n
  1. Layout: choose which physical qubit on the chip plays the role of each of your logical qubits.
    2. \n
  2. Routing: where two qubits that must interact are not physically connected, insert SWAP gates to move quantum states next to each other.
    3. \n
  3. Translation: rewrite every gate in the device's native gate set (the basis gates).
    4. \n
  4. Optimisation: cancel and merge gates to shorten the result.
    5. \n
\n

Each of these can make the circuit longer, and on a noisy device longer means worse. So a good programmer checks the transpiled circuit, not only the one they wrote.

\n\n
📘 DEFINITION

Basis (native) gates: the gates the hardware implements directly with calibrated control pulses, e.g. {RZ(θ), SX = √X, X, CX} on the simulated device below. Coupling map: a graph whose nodes are physical qubits and whose edges are the pairs on which a two-qubit gate is available.

Depth: the number of time steps (layers) when every gate is placed as early as its qubits allow. Two-qubit gate count: the number of CX/CZ-type gates, usually the dominant error source.

T1 (relaxation time): the time scale on which |1⟩ decays to |0⟩. T2 (dephasing time): the time scale on which a superposition loses its relative phase; physically T2 ≤ 2T1.

\n\n

The key equations: what a gate costs

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

H = eiπ/4 · RZ(π/2) · SX · RZ(π/2) (as operators, the rightmost acts first; the phase eiπ/4 is global and unobservable)

SWAP = CX(a→b) · CX(b→a) · CX(a→b), so each inserted SWAP costs three two-qubit gates.

ESP ≈ ∏g (1 − εg), the estimated success probability: the product over every gate and measurement g of one minus its reported error rate εg. It is a crude model (it ignores idle decoherence and correlated errors) but ranks candidate circuits well.

P(|1⟩ survives time t) = e−t/T1, where t is the time the qubit spends in |1⟩ and T1 the relaxation time. With t = 20 μs and T1 = 100 μs this is e−0.2 ≈ 0.8187.

\n\n

Translation: the Hadamard in native gates

\n

Real output from Qiskit 2.5.2:

\n

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit, transpile
from qiskit.transpiler import CouplingMap
from qiskit.quantum_info import Operator

h = QuantumCircuit(1)
h.h(0)
th = transpile(h, basis_gates=[\"rz\", \"sx\", \"x\", \"cx\"], optimization_level=1)
print([(i.operation.name, [round(float(p), 4) for p in i.operation.params]) for i in th.data])
print(th.global_phase, Operator(th).equiv(Operator(h)))

\n

[('rz', [1.5708]), ('sx', []), ('rz', [1.5708])]
0.7853981633974483 True

\n

So one H became three native gates, with global phase π/4 ≈ 0.7854 recorded on the circuit. Operator.equiv confirms the two are the same unitary up to global phase. RZ is usually implemented \"virtually\" in software by changing the phase of later pulses, so on superconducting devices it takes no time and adds almost no error; SX and CX are the real physical pulses.

\n\n

Worked example: routing on a line of three qubits

\n

Suppose the chip is a line 0 — 1 — 2 (edges 0–1 and 1–2 only) and your circuit is H on qubit 0, then CX(0, 2). Qubits 0 and 2 are not neighbours.

📊 FIGURE — Routing H + CX(0, 2) onto a 3-qubit line: SWAP vs a better layout
Circles are physical qubits P0–P2 joined by coupling-map edges; the label inside is the logical qubit placed there. A poor layout forces a SWAP (3 extra CX); a better layout needs none.
\n

line = CouplingMap.from_line(3)
qc = QuantumCircuit(3)
qc.h(0)
qc.cx(0, 2)
t0 = transpile(qc, coupling_map=line, basis_gates=[\"rz\", \"sx\", \"x\", \"cx\"], initial_layout=[0, 1, 2], optimization_level=0, seed_transpiler=1)
print(t0.depth(), dict(t0.count_ops()))
t3 = transpile(qc, coupling_map=line, basis_gates=[\"rz\", \"sx\", \"x\", \"cx\"], optimization_level=3, seed_transpiler=1)
print(t3.depth(), dict(t3.count_ops()))

\n

Real output:

\n

7 {'cx': 4, 'rz': 2, 'sx': 1}
4 {'rz': 2, 'sx': 1, 'cx': 1}

\n\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE
    \n
  1. Forced layout (t0): initial_layout=[0, 1, 2] pins logical qubit i to physical qubit i, so the CX must span physical 0 and 2.
    2. \n
  2. Routing: the router inserts one SWAP on edge 0–1, moving logical qubit 0 to physical 1, which is next to physical 2. Cost: 3 CX.
    3. \n
  3. The real CX: now CX(physical 1, physical 2) is legal. Total two-qubit gates: 3 + 1 = 4, matching 'cx': 4.
    4. \n
  4. Depth: H becomes RZ·SX·RZ (3 layers), the SWAP adds 3 layers, the final CX 1 more: 3 + 3 + 1 = 7.
    5. \n
  5. Free layout (t3): at optimisation level 3 the layout pass chose initial layout [0, 2, 1], i.e. logical 2 sits on physical 1, right next to logical 0. No SWAP is needed: 1 CX, depth 4.
    6. \n
  6. Sanity check: the two-qubit gate count fell from 4 to 1 without changing what the circuit computes. With a 1% error per CX that is roughly 0.994 ≈ 0.961 versus 0.99, a four-fold cut in the CX error budget.
    7. \n
\n\n

Reading calibration data

\n

Every backend publishes a Target: which gates exist on which qubits, with an error rate and duration for each, plus T1 and T2 per qubit. Real devices refresh these numbers regularly. Here we use Qiskit's GenericBackendV2, a synthetic backend whose numbers are random but realistic in size (seeded, so reproducible). It is not a model of any real chip.

\n

from qiskit.providers.fake_provider import GenericBackendV2
backend = GenericBackendV2(num_qubits=5, coupling_map=CouplingMap.from_line(5), seed=42)
target = backend.target
print(backend.operation_names)
for q in range(5):
    props = target.qubit_properties[q]
    print(q, f\"T1={props.t1*1e6:.1f} us\", f\"T2={props.t2*1e6:.1f} us\", f\"readout_err={target['measure'][(q,)].error:.4f}\")
for edge in [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4)]:
    print(edge, f\"cx_err={target['cx'][edge].error:.4f}\", f\"cx_time={target['cx'][edge].duration*1e9:.0f} ns\")

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
QubitT1 (μs)T2 (μs)Readout error
0177.4143.90.0028
1169.7109.40.0032
2176.1178.60.0028
3145.0137.10.0002
4164.4182.30.0011
\n

The native operations printed were ['cx', 'id', 'rz', 'sx', 'x', 'reset', 'delay', 'measure']. CX errors on edges 0–1, 1–2, 2–3, 3–4 were 0.0028, 0.0038, 0.0039, 0.0008, with durations 266, 598, 812 and 116 ns. Edge 3–4 is the best pair on this chip; edge 2–3 the worst.

\n\n

Same state, two circuits: why structure matters

\n

A 5-qubit GHZ state (|00000⟩ + |11111⟩)/√2 can be made with CXs all from qubit 0 (a \"star\") or as a chain 0→1→2→3→4. On a line-shaped chip they transpile very differently. Using the ESP function (product of 1 − error over every gate and measurement in the transpiled circuit, barriers skipped), with transpile(ghz, backend=backend, optimization_level=1, seed_transpiler=7), the real output was:

\n\n\n\n\n\n
VersionDepthCX countESP
Star (CX from qubit 0 to each)11100.957
Chain (CX i → i+1)840.979
\n

The chain matches the hardware graph, so no SWAPs are needed; the star forces six extra CXs of routing. Same ideal output, noticeably different expected quality.

\n\n

Noise models: predicting what hardware will do

\n

A noise model attaches an error channel to each gate or measurement. The standard toy channel is the single-qubit depolarizing channel with Kraus operators √(1−3p/4)·I, √(p/4)·X, √(p/4)·Y, √(p/4)·Z. You can build it with core Qiskit's qiskit.quantum_info and apply it to a density matrix:

\n

import numpy as np
from qiskit.quantum_info import DensityMatrix, Kraus, Statevector, state_fidelity
p = 0.05
I2 = np.eye(2)
X = np.array([[0, 1], [1, 0]])
Y = np.array([[0, -1j], [1j, 0]])
Z = np.diag([1, -1])
dep = Kraus([np.sqrt(1 - 3*p/4)*I2, np.sqrt(p/4)*X, np.sqrt(p/4)*Y, np.sqrt(p/4)*Z])
bell = QuantumCircuit(2)
bell.h(0)
bell.cx(0, 1)
rho = DensityMatrix(bell).evolve(dep, qargs=[0]).evolve(dep, qargs=[1])
print({str(k): round(float(v), 6) for k, v in rho.probabilities_dict().items()})
print(round(state_fidelity(rho, Statevector(bell)), 4))

\n

{'00': 0.475625, '01': 0.024375, '10': 0.024375, '11': 0.475625}
0.9269

\n

Check by hand: in the Z basis only the X and Y parts flip a bit, so each qubit flips with probability p/2 = 0.025. The Bell outcomes become \"wrong parity\" when exactly one qubit flips: 2 × 0.025 × 0.975 = 0.04875, split equally over '01' and '10' (0.024375 each). Sanity check: 0.475625 × 2 + 0.024375 × 2 = 1. The fidelity 0.9269 is lower than 1 − 0.04875 because phase errors (Z) are invisible in counts but still damage the state.

\n

For larger circuits the usual tool is the separate qiskit-aer package, whose noise module can build a noise model from a backend's calibration data (gate errors, readout errors and thermal relaxation). It is not installed in this course's environment, so no Aer code is shown here.

\n\n

Running on real hardware

\n

The modern workflow on IBM hardware, via the separate qiskit-ibm-runtime package, is: pick a backend; transpile to an ISA circuit with generate_preset_pass_manager(optimization_level=..., backend=backend); create a Sampler or Estimator in that backend's mode; submit; wait in the queue; fetch the result. The first two steps run here on the generic backend exactly as they would for a real one:

\n

from qiskit.transpiler import generate_preset_pass_manager
pm = generate_preset_pass_manager(optimization_level=1, backend=backend, seed_transpiler=7)
isa = pm.run(bell)
print(dict(isa.count_ops()))

\n

Real output: {'rz': 2, 'sx': 1, 'cx': 1}. Jobs on shared devices wait in a queue with other users' jobs, so plan for delays from minutes to much longer, batch many circuits into one submission, and save the job ID so you can collect results later. Calibration data changes between runs: record the backend name and the calibration timestamp with your results.

\n\n
✅ VERIFIED
    \n
  • IBM's Open Plan gives free QPU time of up to 10 minutes per 28-day rolling window (IBM Quantum documentation, \"Plans overview\", source at github.com/Qiskit/documentation; page quantum.cloud.ibm.com/docs/en/guides/plans-overview).
    • \n
  • With qiskit-ibm-runtime's SamplerV2 in backend mode, circuits must first be transpiled to ISA circuits for that backend (IBM \"Sampler quickstart\", quantum.cloud.ibm.com/docs/en/guides/get-started-with-sampler).
    • \n
  • Qiskit Aer's NoiseModel.from_backend includes gate, readout and thermal-relaxation errors by default (qiskit.github.io/qiskit-aer/apidocs/aer_noise.html).
    • \n
  • IBM's Heron processors use a CZ two-qubit gate via tunable couplers, with RZ, SX and X single-qubit gates (postquantum.com, Heron R2; review in J. Supercomputing, link.springer.com). Checked 28 Sep 2026.
    • \n
\n\n
❓ NOT VERIFIED

Secondary sources say newer Heron revisions also offer \"fractional\" RZZ(θ) and RX(θ) gates, and that the free plan reaches systems of more than 100 qubits. Plan terms, device lists and gate sets change often; confirm before you rely on this by reading the backend's own Target (backend.operation_names) at the time you run.

\n\n

The traps

\n
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE
    \n
  • Judging a circuit by the logical depth. The GHZ star has logical depth 5 but 10 CXs after routing on a line. Always inspect count_ops() and depth() of the transpiled circuit.
    • \n
  • Forgetting the seed. Layout and routing use randomised heuristics. Without seed_transpiler two runs of the same script can produce different circuits (the forced-layout example above gave depth 4 on one unseeded run and 7 on the seeded one). Seed it for reproducible research.
    • \n
  • Reading bits on the wrong qubits. After layout, logical qubit 0 may sit on physical qubit 3; the counts are still reported per classical bit, which follow your logical qubits. Use transpiled.layout when you need to know which physical qubit was used.
    • \n
  • Trusting old calibration. Error rates drift. An ESP computed from last week's data is only a rough guide today.
    • \n
  • Submitting non-ISA circuits. Hardware primitives reject circuits containing gates the device does not support; transpile against the same backend you run on.
    • \n
\n\n

What the exam asks

\n
★ ON THE EXAM
    \n
  • Count the CX gates added by routing: each SWAP is 3 CX; a CX between qubits at distance d on a line needs d − 1 SWAPs if you swap one qubit along.
    • \n
  • Estimate success probability as a product of (1 − error) terms, e.g. 10 CXs at 0.5% each: 0.99510 ≈ 0.9511; three readouts at 2% each: 0.983 ≈ 0.9412.
    • \n
  • Explain T1 versus T2, and compute a decay factor e−t/T.
    • \n
  • Given a coupling map and two equivalent circuits, choose the one that needs fewer SWAPs and justify it.
    • \n
  • List what you must record to make a hardware run reproducible: backend, calibration time, transpiled circuit, seeds, shots, software versions.
    • \n
"}, "QUANTUM/programming/s3": {"body": "

Qiskit is one stack among several. Research papers, job adverts and cloud services also use Cirq, PennyLane, Q# and a shared text format, OpenQASM. This lesson lets you read code from any of them, move a circuit between tools without scrambling the qubit order, and choose a stack for a project with reasons you can defend. It closes the programming chapter and prepares the capstone project, where you will have to make exactly this choice and make your results reproducible.

\n\n

The idea in plain words

\n

Every quantum SDK does the same three things you met in this chapter: build a circuit, compile it for a target, execute it on a simulator or device. They differ in what they optimise for and whose hardware they reach first. A useful analogy from data work: Qiskit, Cirq and PennyLane are like pandas, Polars and a deep-learning framework; they overlap, but each was designed around a different main job. OpenQASM plays the role that SQL or CSV plays: a common language that lets tools exchange work.

\n\n
📘 DEFINITION

OpenQASM (Open Quantum Assembly Language) is a text language for quantum circuits. Version 2 describes gates and measurements; version 3 adds classical types, control flow (if, while, for) that can depend on mid-circuit measurements, subroutines, and timing instructions for scheduling gates.

Interchange format: a representation that different tools can all write and read, so a circuit made in one can be run or analysed in another. Reproducibility: someone else, later, can rerun your code and get the same result, or a result within the stated statistical error.

\n\n

The four tools side by side

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
ToolMade byLanguageMain strengthBit order in outputs
QiskitIBM and communityPython (core partly Rust)Full stack: circuits, transpiler, primitives, IBM hardwareLittle-endian (qubit 0 rightmost)
CirqGoogle Quantum AIPythonFine control of circuits as time slices (\"moments\") for NISQ devices; Google hardwareBig-endian (first qubit is the most significant bit)
PennyLaneXanadu (PennyLaneAI)PythonDifferentiable programming: gradients of circuits inside PyTorch, JAX or TensorFlow modelsBig-endian: wire 0 is the most significant bit (checked with PennyLane 0.45.1)
Q#MicrosoftQ# (own language) with a Python packageAlgorithm-level programming, resource estimation for fault-tolerant machinesDepends on how results are returned; check the docs
\n

Cirq's documentation states that when it lays out a state vector, \"the first qubit's computational basis values are looped over in the outermost loop\", which makes the first qubit the most significant bit. That is the textbook convention of this course and the opposite of Qiskit's.

\n\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

For n qubits with values b0, b1, …, bn−1:

Qiskit index = ∑i bi · 2i Cirq / textbook index = ∑i bi · 2n−1−i

To convert a bitstring from one convention to the other, reverse the string; to convert a state vector, reverse the order of the qubit axes (for two qubits this swaps the entries at indices 1 and 2). In Qiskit, QuantumCircuit.reverse_bits() and Statevector.reverse_qargs() do this for you.

\n\n

Worked example: one circuit, two frameworks

\n

Circuit: X on qubit 0, H on qubit 1. In Qiskit 2.5.2 (Python 3.11):

📊 FIGURE — The same 2-qubit state indexed by Qiskit and by Cirq
Both rows hold the same state: 0.7071 on (q0, q1) = (1, 0) and (1, 1). Qiskit puts qubit 0 last, so the entries sit at indices 1 and 3; Cirq puts it first, giving 2 and 3.
\n

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit, qasm2, qasm3
from qiskit.quantum_info import Statevector
qc = QuantumCircuit(2)
qc.x(0)
qc.h(1)
print(Statevector(qc).data.real.round(4))

\n

Real output: [ 0. 0.7071 -0. 0.7071]

\n

The same circuit in Cirq 1.7.0 (installed in a separate environment for this check):

\n

import cirq
q0, q1 = cirq.LineQubit.range(2)
circuit = cirq.Circuit(cirq.X(q0), cirq.H(q1), cirq.measure(q0, q1, key=\"m\"))
state = cirq.Simulator().simulate(circuit[:-1]).final_state_vector
print(state.round(4))
result = cirq.Simulator(seed=1).run(circuit, repetitions=1000)
print(result.histogram(key=\"m\"))

\n

Real output:

\n

[0. +0.j 0. +0.j 0.7071+0.j 0.7071+0.j]
Counter({3: 506, 2: 494})

\n\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE
    \n
  1. Physics: qubit 0 is certainly 1; qubit 1 is (|0⟩ + |1⟩)/√2. The two basis states present are (q0, q1) = (1, 0) and (1, 1), each with amplitude 1/√2 ≈ 0.7071.
    2. \n
  2. Qiskit indices: index = b0 + 2b1. (1, 0) gives 1, (1, 1) gives 3. Non-zero entries at 1 and 3, as printed (the \"-0.\" is a harmless negative zero from floating point).
    3. \n
  3. Cirq indices: index = 2b0 + b1. (1, 0) gives 2, (1, 1) gives 3. Non-zero entries at 2 and 3, as printed.
    4. \n
  4. Counts: Cirq's histogram reports integers built the same big-endian way: 2 = binary 10 and 3 = binary 11, where the first digit is q0. Qiskit would report '01' and '11', where the last digit is q0.
    5. \n
  5. Sanity check: both vectors have two entries of 0.7071, so probabilities 0.5 + 0.5 = 1; reversing the 2-bit labels maps Qiskit {1, 3} onto Cirq {2, 3}. Same state, different filing system.
    6. \n
\n\n

OpenQASM 3 as the go-between

\n

Qiskit writes OpenQASM 3 with qasm3.dumps:

\n

bell = QuantumCircuit(2, 2)
bell.h(0)
bell.cx(0, 1)
bell.measure([0, 1], [0, 1])
print(qasm3.dumps(bell))

\n

Real output, line by line:

\n

OPENQASM 3.0;
include \"stdgates.inc\";
bit[2] c;
qubit[2] q;
h q[0];
cx q[0], q[1];
c[0] = measure q[0];
c[1] = measure q[1];

\n

Read it like a tiny program: a version line; an include of the standard gate library (h, cx, and friends); declarations of a 2-bit classical register and a 2-qubit register; two gates; and measurements written as assignments, which is new in version 3 (version 2 wrote measure q[0] -> c[0];). Because the text names qubits and bits by index, it carries no endianness at all: each tool applies its own display convention when it prints results.

\n

Reading OpenQASM 3 back into Qiskit needs the optional qiskit_qasm3_import package, which is not installed here (Qiskit raises a MissingOptionalLibraryError that says so). The OpenQASM 2 round trip works with core Qiskit:

\n

text2 = qasm2.dumps(bell)
back = qasm2.loads(text2)
print(dict(back.count_ops()))

\n

Real output: {'measure': 2, 'h': 1, 'cx': 1}

\n\n

What makes PennyLane different: gradients

\n

Variational algorithms need the derivative of an expectation value with respect to a gate angle. For gates generated by a Pauli (RX, RY, RZ) the parameter-shift rule gives it exactly from two more circuit runs: ∂⟨O⟩/∂θ = [⟨O⟩(θ + π/2) − ⟨O⟩(θ − π/2)] / 2. PennyLane automates this and plugs the result into PyTorch or JAX training loops. You can check the rule with Qiskit's Estimator for RY(θ)|0⟩ and O = Z, where ⟨Z⟩ = cos θ:

\n

import numpy as np
from qiskit.circuit import Parameter
from qiskit.quantum_info import SparsePauliOp
from qiskit.primitives import StatevectorEstimator
theta = Parameter(\"θ\")
c = QuantumCircuit(1)
c.ry(theta, 0)
t0 = np.pi / 3
evs = StatevectorEstimator().run([(c, SparsePauliOp(\"Z\"), [[t0 + np.pi/2], [t0 - np.pi/2], [t0]])]).result()[0].data.evs
print(evs.round(4), round(float((evs[0] - evs[1]) / 2), 4))

\n

Real output: [-0.866 0.866 0.5 ] -0.866. The value at θ = π/3 is cos(π/3) = 0.5 and the shift-rule gradient is −0.866 = −sin(π/3), the exact derivative. The same computation in PennyLane 0.45.1, with @qml.qnode(dev, diff_method=\"parameter-shift\") around qml.RY(theta, wires=0) and qml.expval(qml.PauliZ(0)), printed 0.5000000000000002 -0.8660254037844387 for the value and qml.grad.

\n\n

Choosing a stack and keeping results reproducible

\n
    \n
  • Learning, IBM hardware, broad tutorials: Qiskit.
    • \n
  • Google hardware or very fine control of when gates happen: Cirq.
    • \n
  • Hybrid quantum machine learning, gradients inside a classical model: PennyLane (it has plugins that run on other vendors' devices and simulators).
    • \n
  • Estimating resources for fault-tolerant algorithms, strongly typed algorithm code: Q# and Microsoft's Quantum Development Kit.
    • \n
  • Moving circuits between any of these or to a cloud service: export OpenQASM, and test the round trip on a small circuit first.
    • \n
\n

For reproducibility, record: exact package versions (pip freeze), random seeds for samplers and the transpiler, the transpiled circuit (save it as OpenQASM), shots, backend name and calibration time for hardware runs, and the bit-ordering convention of every table you publish.

\n\n
✅ VERIFIED
    \n
  • OpenQASM 3 is described in Cross et al., \"OpenQASM 3: A Broader and Deeper Quantum Assembly Language\", ACM Transactions on Quantum Computing 3(3), article 12, 2022 (doi.org/10.1145/3505636). The language is governed by a Technical Steering Committee; the repository lists the current version as 3.1 (github.com/openqasm/openqasm).
    • \n
  • Cirq was developed by Google's quantum team, announced in public alpha on 18 July 2018, reached version 1.0 in July 2022, and represents circuits as sequences of Moments (Google Open Source Blog; Wikipedia, Cirq; github.com/quantumlib/Cirq). Qubit-order quote from Cirq's simulation docs (github.com/quantumlib/Cirq).
    • \n
  • PennyLane: Bergholm et al., \"PennyLane: Automatic differentiation of hybrid quantum-classical computations\" (arXiv:1811.04968); open source under Apache 2.0 with PyTorch, TensorFlow and JAX interfaces (github.com/PennyLaneAI/pennylane).
    • \n
  • Microsoft rewrote its Quantum Development Kit mostly in Rust (runs in VS Code and the browser; pip install qsharp for Python) and released QDK 1.0 in January 2024; the repository includes the Q# compiler and a resource estimator (Microsoft Quantum blog; InfoQ; github.com/microsoft/qdk).
    • \n
  • Cloud access: Amazon Braket accepts OpenQASM 3.0 programs for gate-based devices and simulators (announced March 2022, aws.amazon.com); Azure Quantum's hardware providers include IonQ, Pasqal, Quantinuum and Rigetti (learn.microsoft.com). Checked 28 Sep 2026.
    • \n
\n\n
❓ NOT VERIFIED

Exactly which QPUs each cloud currently offers, and whether a given vendor accepts every OpenQASM 3 feature (loops, subroutines, timing) rather than a subset, change often and were not confirmed here. Confirm before you rely on this by checking the provider's device page on the day you submit.

\n\n

The traps

\n
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE
    \n
  • Comparing outputs across tools without flipping bits. Qiskit '01' and Cirq's 2 (binary 10) describe the same outcome for the circuit above. Convert before you compare or merge result tables.
    • \n
  • Assuming OpenQASM 3 is fully supported everywhere. A tool can write version 3 syntax that another tool or device only partly accepts. Test with a small circuit and read the error message.
    • \n
  • Confusing \"differentiable\" with \"faster\". PennyLane's gradients still cost circuit runs: the parameter-shift rule needs two evaluations per parameter, so a 100-parameter model needs 200 circuits per gradient on hardware.
    • \n
  • Treating a framework as a speed-up. No SDK makes a quantum algorithm faster than its theory allows; they differ in convenience, compilation quality and hardware access.
    • \n
  • Unpinned versions. Quantum SDKs change APIs quickly (Qiskit removed execute() in 1.0). An unpinned notebook may not run next year.
    • \n
\n\n

What the exam asks

\n
★ ON THE EXAM
    \n
  • Convert a state vector index or bitstring between Qiskit's little-endian and the big-endian convention of Cirq and the textbook.
    • \n
  • Read a short OpenQASM 3 program and state the circuit, the classical register and the counts keys you expect.
    • \n
  • Apply the parameter-shift rule to a given expectation function and compare with the analytic derivative.
    • \n
  • Recommend a stack for a scenario (hybrid ML model, Google device, resource estimation, cross-vendor benchmark) and justify it in two sentences.
    • \n
  • List the items that make a quantum experiment reproducible.
    • \n
"}, "QUANTUM/security/s1": {"body": "

This lesson lets you explain, in the language of both a physicist and a security engineer, why Shor's algorithm forces a change of public-key cryptography, which NIST standards replace what, and how an organisation (including a plant, a substation or a pipeline) actually plans the migration. It sits near the end of the degree because it pulls together the Shor and Grover chapters with real-world engineering; it is also the part of quantum computing you are most likely to be paid for, and it maps directly onto Security+ topics: key exchange versus signatures, PKI, crypto-agility, asset inventory and risk management.

\n\n

The idea in plain words

\n

Almost every secure connection uses two kinds of cryptography. Public-key (asymmetric) cryptography does two jobs: it lets two strangers agree a secret key (key establishment: RSA key transport, Diffie-Hellman, ECDH) and it proves who sent something (signatures: RSA, ECDSA, EdDSA). Symmetric cryptography (AES, SHA-2/SHA-3, HMAC) then does the bulk encryption and integrity with that shared key.

\n

Shor's algorithm solves factoring and discrete logarithms in polynomial time on a fault-tolerant quantum computer. Those two problems are the entire foundation of RSA, DH and elliptic-curve cryptography, so a large enough machine breaks all of them outright. Grover's algorithm gives only a square-root speed-up for brute-force search, which halves the effective bit-strength of a symmetric key; doubling the key length (AES-256) restores the margin. So the problem is concentrated in public-key cryptography, and the fix is to replace it with algorithms built on problems for which no efficient quantum algorithm is known: lattices, hash functions, error-correcting codes.

\n

Two threats make this urgent before any such machine exists:

\n
    \n
  • Harvest now, decrypt later: an adversary records encrypted traffic today and decrypts it once a quantum computer arrives. Anything that must stay secret for years is already exposed.
    • \n
  • Forge later: once signatures can be forged, an attacker can sign malicious firmware or a fake certificate. For devices that verify firmware with a key burned into hardware, the root of trust must be replaced before that day, because it cannot be patched afterwards.
    • \n
\n\n
📘 DEFINITION

Post-quantum cryptography (PQC): classical algorithms, run on ordinary computers, whose security rests on problems believed hard for both classical and quantum computers. PQC needs no quantum hardware at all.

CRQC (cryptographically relevant quantum computer): a fault-tolerant machine large enough to run Shor against real key sizes such as RSA-2048 or P-256. None exists today, and nobody can give a verified arrival date.

KEM (key-encapsulation mechanism): one party publishes an encapsulation key; the other uses it to produce a ciphertext and a shared secret; the first decapsulates the ciphertext to get the same secret. It replaces ECDH-style key agreement.

Crypto-agility: the ability to swap algorithms, key sizes and parameters through configuration and updates, without redesigning the system or replacing hardware.

\n\n

The NIST standards and what they replace

\n\n\n\n\n\n
StandardAlgorithm (origin)JobHard problemReplaces
FIPS 203ML-KEM (CRYSTALS-Kyber)Key establishmentModule learning with errors (lattice)RSA key transport, DH, ECDH
FIPS 204ML-DSA (CRYSTALS-Dilithium)General-purpose signaturesModule latticesRSA, ECDSA, EdDSA signatures
FIPS 205SLH-DSA (SPHINCS+)Conservative backup signaturesOnly the security of hash functionsSame, where large signatures are acceptable
Selected 2025HQCBackup KEMError-correcting codes (not lattices)A fallback if lattice KEMs are ever weakened
\n

The design logic is diversity: two of the three finished standards are lattice-based, so NIST added a hash-based signature (SLH-DSA) and a code-based KEM (HQC) so that a single mathematical breakthrough against lattices would not leave the world without an option. The numbers after the names are parameter sets: ML-KEM-512/768/1024 and ML-DSA-44/65/87 trade size for security category.

\n\n
✅ VERIFIED

FIPS 203 (ML-KEM), FIPS 204 (ML-DSA) and FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA) were approved by NIST on 13 August 2024; issuance was announced in the Federal Register on 14 August 2024: Federal Register 2024-17956.

NIST announced HQC as the fifth algorithm selected for standardization on 11 March 2025, as a code-based backup to ML-KEM (which stays the primary recommendation): NIST news release.

Sizes used below: ML-KEM-768 encapsulation key 1,184 B, ciphertext 1,088 B (FIPS 203); ML-DSA-65 public key 1,952 B, signature 3,309 B (FIPS 204); SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s public key 32 B, signature 7,856 B, 128f signature 17,088 B (OpenSSL SLH-DSA docs). Checked 28 Sep 2026.

\n\n
❓ NOT VERIFIED

Reports say NIST planned a draft HQC standard (possibly numbered FIPS 207) for 2026 and a final in 2027, and that FIPS 206 (FN-DSA, from Falcon) was submitted for approval in August 2025. I could not confirm whether either is final as of 28 Sep 2026: confirm before you rely on this, on NIST CSRC.

\n\n

The key equations: Mosca's inequality and Grover's discount

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

Mosca: if x + y > z, data protected today is at risk

x = how many years the data (or the trust in a signature) must stay secure; y = how many years your migration takes; z = years until a CRQC exists. The exposure is x + y − z years of secrets readable by an adversary who harvested them.

Grover cost ≈ (π/4)·√N = (π/4)·2k/2 for a k-bit key

N = 2k keys. For AES-128: (π/4)·264 ≈ 1.4488 × 1019 ≈ 263.65 sequential oracle calls, each a full reversible AES circuit. For AES-256: ≈ 2127.65. Grover parallelises badly (splitting over M machines only gains √M), which is why symmetric crypto survives with larger keys.

\n\n

Worked example: a substation gateway

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

A utility's substation gateway protects grid topology and protection-relay settings that remain sensitive for x = 25 years. Replacing gateways across 400 sites, with testing and outage windows, takes y = 10 years. Nobody knows z, so we tabulate it (computed in Python).

  1. Compute x + y = 25 + 10 = 35 years.
  2. Compare with each scenario for z and take x + y − z (floored at 0).
z (years to CRQC)x + yAt risk?Exposure (years)
1035yes25
1535yes20
2035yes15
3035yes5
4035no0

Now the bandwidth cost. The gateway authenticates a TLS-style session with a two-certificate chain (leaf + intermediate, each carrying a public key and its CA's signature) plus one handshake signature:

  1. ML-DSA-65: 2 × (1,952 + 3,309) + 3,309 = 13,831 bytes.
  2. ECDSA P-256 (65 B uncompressed key, 64 B raw signature): 2 × (65 + 64) + 64 = 322 bytes. Ratio 13,831 / 322 ≈ 42.95.
  3. Hybrid key exchange X25519 + ML-KEM-768: client share 32 + 1,184 = 1,216 B; server share 32 + 1,088 = 1,120 B.
  4. On a 9,600 baud serial link (8N1 framing = 10 bits per byte): 13,831 × 10 / 9,600 = 14.41 s for authentication alone, versus 0.34 s classically; adding both key shares gives 16,167 B, 16.84 s. At 115,200 baud: 1.20 s and 1.40 s.

Answer: the gateway is already at risk for any z below 35 years, and a naive PQC swap adds about 16 s of handshake on a legacy serial link, so the design must reuse sessions, terminate PQC at a network gateway, or upgrade the link. Sanity check: 1,216 + 1,120 + 13,831 = 16,167 bytes, as used.

\n\n

Planning the migration

📊 FIGURE — PQC standard dates and the Mosca test for a substation gateway
Top: only the dates the lesson gives; hollow dashed marks are reports it could not confirm. Bottom: each red bar is x + y − z, the years of harvested data exposed if a CRQC arrives in z years.
\n
    \n
  1. Inventory: find every place cryptography is used (protocols, certificates, libraries, HSMs, firmware signing keys, VPNs, embedded devices, vendor cloud links). The result is often called a cryptographic bill of materials (CBOM).
    2. \n
  2. Prioritise by Mosca: long-lived secrets and long-lived trust anchors first (firmware roots of trust, long-term PKI, VPN key exchange carrying sensitive data).
    3. \n
  3. Go hybrid during the transition: combine a classical and a PQC algorithm so the session is safe if either holds. Hybrid X25519+ML-KEM-768 key exchange is already widely deployed in TLS.
    4. \n
  4. Build crypto-agility: algorithms negotiated and configurable, keys and certificates rotated by automation, not by hand.
    5. \n
  5. Test for message size, fragmentation, latency, CPU and memory, then engage vendors: most OT cryptography lives in products you do not control.
    6. \n
\n\n
✅ VERIFIED

NSM-10 (May 2022) directs US federal agencies to migrate to quantum-resistant cryptography with a 2035 goal. NSA's CNSA 2.0 suite for national security systems specifies ML-KEM-1024, ML-DSA-87, AES-256, SHA-384/512, and LMS or XMSS (SP 800-208) for software and firmware signing, with timelines: software/firmware signing support-and-prefer by 2025, exclusive by 2030; traditional networking equipment (VPNs, routers) 2026 / 2030; web browsers, servers and cloud services 2025 / 2033; operating systems 2027 / 2033; all NSS quantum-resistant by 2035 (NSA CNSA 2.0 FAQ, summary of the updated FAQ).

NIST IR 8547 (initial public draft, Nov 2024) proposes deprecating 112-bit quantum-vulnerable algorithms such as RSA-2048 and P-256 after 2030 and disallowing RSA/ECC entirely after 2035 (NIST IR 8547 ipd).

CISA, NSA and NIST's joint factsheet \"Quantum-Readiness: Migration to Post-Quantum Cryptography\" (21 Aug 2023) tells critical-infrastructure owners to build a roadmap, a cryptographic inventory spanning IT and OT, and to engage vendors (CISA). Checked 28 Sep 2026.

\n\n
❓ NOT VERIFIED

Search snippets report a June 2026 US executive order (numbered 14412 in one source and 14409 in another) setting end-2030 deadlines for post-quantum key establishment in high-value federal systems and end-2031 for authentication, implemented by OMB memo M-26-15 (M-26-15). The sources disagree on details: confirm before you rely on this.

\n\n

Where OT/ICS makes it harder

\n
    \n
  • Lifetimes: PLCs, RTUs, relays and safety systems stay in service for decades, so x and y in Mosca are both large. A device bought today without crypto-agility may still be running when a CRQC appears.
    • \n
  • Availability first: OT ranks availability and safety above confidentiality. A larger handshake that times out a control loop is a safety problem, not an inconvenience, so every change goes through change management and test benches.
    • \n
  • Constrained hardware and links: small microcontrollers, little RAM, serial and radio links (the worked example). ML-KEM is fast; the pain is size, especially signatures and certificate chains.
    • \n
  • Firmware signing is the first deadline: secure boot keys are often fused into silicon. Stateful hash-based signatures (LMS, XMSS) are approved for this, but they must never reuse a one-time key index, so the signing HSM's state is itself a critical asset to back up correctly.
    • \n
  • Architecture helps: IEC 62443 zones and conduits let you put PQC-capable VPN gateways on conduits between zones, protecting legacy devices that cannot be upgraded (compensating controls, in Security+ language).
    • \n
\n\n
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE
  • \"Post-quantum means we need quantum hardware.\" No: PQC is ordinary software; quantum hardware is QKD, a different thing (next lesson).
  • \"Quantum computers break AES.\" Grover only halves the bit strength; AES-256 remains the recommendation. The emergency is RSA/ECC/DH.
  • \"Wait until a CRQC exists.\" Harvested data and fused-in roots of trust are already exposed; Mosca says act when x + y exceeds z.
  • Replacing the key exchange but forgetting signatures, or forgetting that certificates, firmware images and vendor update servers all carry signatures.
\n\n
📊 YOUR DATA EDGE

A cryptographic inventory is a data-engineering job: join a certificate scan, network flow logs and the asset register, then rank. For example:

SELECT site, asset, algorithm, secrecy_years + migration_years AS x_plus_y FROM crypto_inventory WHERE algorithm IN ('RSA','ECDSA','ECDH') ORDER BY x_plus_y DESC;

Deduplicating assets, handling missing firmware versions, and quantifying uncertainty in z (a distribution, not a date) are exactly the skills that make such an inventory trustworthy.

\n\n
★ ON THE EXAM
  • Match FIPS 203/204/205 to ML-KEM/ML-DSA/SLH-DSA and to their jobs; know HQC is a backup code-based KEM.
  • Explain why Shor breaks public-key crypto but Grover only weakens symmetric crypto; compute Grover's (π/4)·2k/2.
  • Apply Mosca's inequality to a scenario and state the exposure in years.
  • Describe harvest-now-decrypt-later, hybrid key exchange and crypto-agility, and give one OT-specific constraint.

This lesson lets you run the BB84 quantum key distribution protocol by hand and in Python, turn an observed error rate into a secret-key length, and explain honestly what QKD does and does not guarantee. It uses the measurement postulate and the Hadamard basis change from the early chapters, the no-cloning theorem, and the CHSH inequality from the protocols chapter. In security terms, QKD is a different answer to the same key-establishment problem that ML-KEM solves in the previous lesson: it rests on physics rather than on a hard maths problem, but it pays for that with special hardware and short distances.

\n\n

The idea in plain words

\n

Alice sends single photons, each carrying one bit encoded in one of two bases that Bob cannot tell apart. If Bob happens to measure in the same basis he reads the bit perfectly; if not, he gets a coin flip. Afterwards they announce the bases (never the bits) over a public channel and keep only the rounds where the bases matched. An eavesdropper, Eve, cannot copy the photons (no-cloning) and does not know the basis, so any attempt to measure them disturbs some of them. Alice and Bob compare a random sample of their key: a low error rate bounds how much Eve can know, and they then shrink the key until her knowledge is negligible.

\n\n
📘 DEFINITION

BB84 (Bennett and Brassard, 1984): a prepare-and-measure QKD protocol with four states. Convention used here: Z basis encodes 0 → |0⟩, 1 → |1⟩; X basis encodes 0 → |+⟩ = (|0⟩ + |1⟩)/√2, 1 → |−⟩ = (|0⟩ − |1⟩)/√2. Preparation is Xbit then H if the basis is X; measuring in X means applying H and then measuring in Z.

Sifting: discarding rounds where Alice's and Bob's bases differ; about half survive. QBER (quantum bit error rate): the fraction of compared sifted bits that disagree.

Error correction (information reconciliation, e.g. Cascade or LDPC codes) makes Bob's key equal Alice's, leaking some parity bits publicly. Privacy amplification hashes the corrected key with a randomly chosen universal hash (e.g. a Toeplitz matrix) into a shorter key about which Eve knows essentially nothing.

\n\n

The key equations

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

h(Q) = −Q·log2Q − (1 − Q)·log2(1 − Q)

r = 1 − 2h(Q) (secret bits per sifted bit, asymptotic, one-way post-processing)

Q is the QBER, h is the binary entropy (bits). One h(Q) pays for the parity bits leaked during error correction (Shannon limit); the other h(Q) is removed by privacy amplification because Eve's information is bounded by the phase-error rate, which for BB84 equals Q. If r ≤ 0, abort.

Setting 1 − 2h(Q) = 0 and solving numerically (bisection in Python) gives Q = 0.1100: the 11% threshold.

Intercept-resend QBER = P(Eve's basis wrong) × P(Bob's bit wrong | wrong basis) = ½ × ½ = ¼

\n\n
✅ VERIFIED

Shor and Preskill, \"Simple proof of security of the BB84 quantum key distribution protocol\", Physical Review Letters, July 2000, proved BB84 secure against all attacks for bit error rates up to about 11% with one-way post-processing (paper PDF; context in arXiv quant-ph/0510041). Checked 28 Sep 2026. The threshold depends on the protocol and on post-processing: protocols using two-way classical communication tolerate higher error rates, so \"11%\" is the one-way BB84 number, not a law of nature.

\n\n

Worked example: a simulated BB84 run

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Simulated with Qiskit 2.5 (Statevector for each photon, numpy random generator seed 7): Alice's random bits and bases, Bob's random bases, Bob's outcome drawn with the Born-rule probability P(1) = |⟨1|ψ'⟩|2 after his basis change. No Eve, no noise.

📊 FIGURE — BB84 by hand: bits, bases and the sifted key
Each column is one photon. Shaded columns are rounds where Alice and Bob chose the same basis; only those bits form the sifted key, and there they agree exactly.
\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n

  1. Why P = 1.0 in round 2: Alice sends |−⟩ = H|1⟩; Bob applies H, and H·H|1⟩ = |1⟩, so he reads 1 with certainty.
  2. Why P = 0.5 in round 1: Alice sends |1⟩; Bob applies H and gets |−⟩ = (|0⟩ − |1⟩)/√2, so P(1) = |−1/√2|2 = 0.5; his bit is useless.
  3. Sifting: bases match in rounds 2, 5, 7, 10, 11, 12, 14, i.e. 7 of 16 (expected 8).
  4. Sifted keys: Alice 1110010, Bob 1110010, 0 errors.

Scaled up (20,000 photons, seed 2026, half of the sifted bits sacrificed to estimate the QBER):

\n\n\n\n

Eve intercept-resend on every photon9,9664,9831,1980.24040.7957−0.59150 (abort)

Result: with 2.93% QBER, 4,983 untested sifted bits distil to 3,080 secret bits (asymptotic formula, ignoring finite-size corrections); Eve's full intercept-resend shows up as 24.04% QBER, close to the predicted 25%, and the run aborts. Sanity check: sifted/sent = 9,966/20,000 = 0.498 ≈ ½, and 4,983 × 0.61827 = 3,080.8, rounded down to 3,080 whole bits.

\n\n

E91: the entanglement version

\n

In Ekert's 1991 protocol a source (which may even be Eve's) emits pairs in |Φ+⟩ = (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2. Alice and Bob each measure along randomly chosen directions. Rounds with compatible directions give correlated key bits; the rest are used to evaluate the CHSH combination S. Measuring the observable cos θ·Z + sin θ·X at Alice angles 0, π/2 and Bob angles π/4, −π/4, the correlations are E(a, b) = cos(a − b):

\n

S = E(0,π/4) + E(0,−π/4) + E(π/2,π/4) − E(π/2,−π/4) = 0.7071 + 0.7071 + 0.7071 + 0.7071 = 2.8284 = 2√2

\n

Any local-hidden-variable (and hence any pre-programmed, Eve-controlled) model gives |S| ≤ 2. Observing S near 2√2 certifies that the pairs are close to maximally entangled, and monogamy of entanglement then limits what Eve can hold. For white noise with visibility V, S = 2√2·V and the QBER is (1 − V)/2, so the 11% threshold corresponds to V = 0.78 and S = 2.2062. This idea is the seed of device-independent QKD, where security is certified from the observed statistics rather than trusted hardware models.

\n\n

Practical limits and attacks on real systems

\n
    \n
  • Authentication is not included. The public channel must be authenticated or Eve simply impersonates Bob. That needs a pre-shared key or a (post-quantum) signature, so QKD is really key growing, not key establishment from nothing.
    • \n
  • Multi-photon pulses. Practical sources are attenuated lasers; a pulse sometimes carries two photons, and Eve can split one off and wait for the basis announcement (photon-number splitting). Decoy states (randomly varying the intensity) detect this.
    • \n
  • Detectors are the soft target. Side channels such as blinding detectors with bright light let Eve control the clicks without raising the QBER. Measurement-device-independent QKD removes all detector side channels by moving the measurement to an untrusted relay.
    • \n
  • Distance and cost: point-to-point links over fibre, a few hundred km at most (next lesson), special hardware per link, and an easy denial of service: Eve can always force an abort by adding noise.
    • \n
\n\n
✅ VERIFIED

The NSA states that it does not support QKD or quantum cryptography for national security systems, citing: only a partial solution (no built-in authentication), special-purpose equipment, higher infrastructure cost and insider risk, difficulty of securing and validating implementations, and increased denial-of-service risk; it prefers post-quantum cryptography (NSA QKD page). Checked 28 Sep 2026.

\n\n
❓ NOT VERIFIED

The first well-known demonstration of detector blinding against commercial QKD systems is usually credited to Lydersen and colleagues around 2010, and decoy states and MDI-QKD to papers from the mid-2000s and 2012. My searches could not confirm the citations: confirm before you rely on this.

\n\n
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE
  • Announcing the bits instead of the bases during sifting: bases are public, bits never are (except the sacrificed test sample).
  • Thinking intercept-resend gives 50% QBER: Eve guesses right half the time, and even when wrong Bob is correct half the time, so ¼.
  • Keeping the test bits in the key: once compared publicly they are known to Eve and must be discarded.
  • Saying QKD is \"unconditionally secure\" full stop: the proofs assume an authenticated channel and devices that match their models; real devices have side channels.
  • Treating 11% as universal: it is the asymptotic one-way BB84 threshold, and finite-size effects lower the usable QBER in practice.
\n\n
★ ON THE EXAM
  • Given bits and bases for Alice and Bob, perform sifting and compute the sifted key and QBER.
  • Derive the 25% intercept-resend QBER, or the QBER when Eve attacks a fraction f of photons (f/4).
  • Evaluate r = 1 − 2h(Q) for a given QBER and turn it into a number of secret bits; state the 11% threshold.
  • Explain why QKD still needs authentication and name one implementation attack and its countermeasure.
  • Compute S = 2√2 for E91 and say what S ≤ 2 would mean.

This lesson lets you predict how far a QKD link can reach, explain why the fix used for classical fibre (amplifiers) is forbidden for qubits, and describe the machinery that replaces it: entanglement swapping, quantum repeaters, trusted nodes and satellites. It rounds off the applied part of the degree by linking the no-cloning theorem and Bell states from the early chapters, the error-correction chapter, and the security picture of this chapter. For an OT/ICS engineer the practical question is simple: over what distances, at what key rate, and with which nodes you must trust.

\n\n

The idea in plain words: photons get lost

\n

Optical fibre absorbs and scatters light, and the loss is exponential in length: every extra 15 km of typical fibre at 0.2 dB/km removes another half of the photons. Classical networks solve this with amplifiers every 50-100 km that boost the signal. A quantum signal cannot be amplified, because an amplifier that produced extra copies of an unknown qubit would be a cloning machine. So in fibre the key rate falls exponentially with distance until detector noise wins and the error rate crosses the security threshold. There are three ways out: trust intermediate nodes, go through space where most of the path is vacuum, or build quantum repeaters that extend entanglement instead of copying states.

\n\n
📘 DEFINITION

Transmittance η: the probability that a photon entering a channel comes out. Attenuation α: loss in decibels per kilometre.

Entanglement swapping: a Bell-state measurement on one half of each of two entangled pairs, which leaves the two far halves entangled although they never interacted.

Quantum repeater: a chain of nodes that create entanglement over short links, store it in quantum memories, purify it and swap it to span the whole distance.

Trusted node: a relay that runs ordinary QKD with each neighbour and passes keys on by combining them classically; the node knows the keys, so it must be physically secured. A trusted node is not a repeater.

\n\n

The key equations

\n
🧮 KEY EQUATION

ηch = 10−αL/10 (L in km, α in dB/km; the loss in dB is αL)

Y = ηch·ηd + 2pd, Q = (eopt·ηchηd + pd)/Y, R = f·½·Y·[1 − 2h(Q)]

Y = probability Bob gets a click per pulse; ηd = detector efficiency; pd = dark-count probability per detector per pulse (two detectors; a dark click is wrong half the time); eopt = optical misalignment error; f = pulse rate; ½ = sifting; h = binary entropy from the previous lesson.

Repeaterless bound: R/f ≤ −log2(1 − ηch) ≈ 1.44·ηch for small ηch: no point-to-point protocol, however clever, beats a rate linear in the transmittance.

\n\n

Worked example: key rate versus distance

\n
✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Assumptions (idealised, stated so you can change them): a true single-photon BB84 source at f = 1 GHz, α = 0.2 dB/km, detector efficiency ηd = 0.8, dark-count probability pd = 10−8 per pulse per detector, eopt = 1%. Computed in Python.

📊 FIGURE — QKD key rate falls with distance; swapping extends entanglement
Top (log scale): the modelled BB84 rate drops tenfold every 50 km, then collapses at 350.6 km; the dashed bound caps any repeaterless link. Bottom: a Bell measurement in the middle joins two short links.
  1. At L = 100 km: loss = 0.2 × 100 = 20 dB, so ηch = 10−2 = 0.01.
  2. Y = 0.01 × 0.8 + 2 × 10−8 = 8.000 × 10−3.
  3. Q = (0.01 × 0.008 + 10−8)/0.008 = 0.0100; h(0.01) = 0.0808, so 1 − 2h = 0.8384.
  4. R = 109 × 0.5 × 0.008 × 0.8384 = 3.354 × 106 bit/s; a 256-bit AES key takes 76 µs.
  5. Repeat for each distance:
\n\n\n\n\n\n\n

(The bound column uses the exact −log2(1 − ηch), which is 1.520 rather than 1.443 × 108 at 50 km where ηch is not small.)

  1. Where does it stop? Bisection on R(L) = 0 gives L = 350.6 km, exactly where Q reaches 0.1100: dark counts (2 × 10−8 per pulse) become comparable to signal clicks and push the QBER over the 11% threshold.
  2. At 1,000 km even a perfect link delivers 109 × 10−20 = 10−11 photons per second: one photon every 1011 s ≈ 3,169 years.

Answer: in this model the rate falls by 10× every 50 km while dark counts are negligible (to about 200 km), then faster: 3.354 × 106 bit/s at 100 km, 285 bit/s at 300 km, and zero beyond about 351 km. Sanity check: every row stays below the repeaterless bound, as it must.

\n\n

Why amplifiers cannot help: no-cloning

\n

Suppose a unitary U amplified qubits: U|0⟩|0⟩ = |0⟩|0⟩ and U|1⟩|0⟩ = |1⟩|1⟩. Linearity then forces U|+⟩|0⟩ = (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2, which is entangled, not the wanted |+⟩|+⟩ = (|00⟩ + |01⟩ + |10⟩ + |11⟩)/2. Their overlap is ⟨++|Φ+⟩ = (1/2)(1/√2)(1 + 1) = 0.7071, fidelity 0.5. Any device that copies the Z basis destroys the X basis, which is exactly what BB84 relies on; an eavesdropper and an amplifier are the same thing to the physics.

\n\n

Entanglement swapping and repeaters

\n

Take two pairs, qubits (1,2) and (3,4), each in |Φ+⟩. A node holding qubits 2 and 3 performs a Bell measurement. Computed with numpy by projecting the 16-amplitude state onto each Bell state of qubits 2 and 3:

\n\n\n\n\n\n
Bell outcome on (2,3)ProbabilityState of (1,4)Correction on qubit 4
Φ+0.25(|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2none
Φ−0.25(|00⟩ − |11⟩)/√2Z
Ψ+0.25(|01⟩ + |10⟩)/√2X
Ψ−0.25(|01⟩ − |10⟩)/√2X then Z (up to a global phase)
\n

Probabilities sum to 1, and after the two-bit classical message and Pauli correction qubits 1 and 4 hold |Φ+⟩ with fidelity 1.0000. This is teleportation of an entangled half. A repeater chain splits 1,000 km into, say, 10 links of 100 km, each with η = 10−2 instead of 10−20 end to end. Each link retries until it heralds success, stores the pair in a quantum memory, and the nodes swap once neighbours are ready; purification (distillation) trades several noisy pairs for fewer better ones. In the ideal limit the rate then scales with the single-link transmittance, not the total; real memories decohere and swaps fail, so practical long-distance repeater networks remain a research goal.

\n\n

Satellites and records

\n
✅ VERIFIED
  • Micius (QUESS) launched 16 August 2016 into an orbit of about 500 km (QUESS summary; Micius review, arXiv 2208.10236).
  • 2017: satellite-to-ground QKD over about 1,200 km (Nature) and entanglement distribution to ground stations about 1,200 km apart (Science, \"Satellite-based entanglement distribution over 1200 kilometers\").
  • Intercontinental QKD via Micius between Xinglong (China) and Graz (Austria), 7,600 km apart, securing a 75-minute Beijing-Vienna videoconference; here the satellite is a trusted relay (CNSA).
  • 2020: entanglement-based QKD over 1,120 km (Delingha-Nanshan) at 0.12 bit/s without trusting the satellite (Nature 582, 501).
  • Jinan-1 microsatellite, launched 27 July 2022, gave a 12,900 km China-South Africa link with real-time QKD and ~100 kg ground stations, published in Nature in March 2025 (CAS news).

Fibre record: twin-field QKD over 1,002 km, 9.53 × 10−12 secret bits per pulse, Physical Review Letters, May 2023 (arXiv 2303.15795). Checked 28 Sep 2026.

\n

Why space works: most of a downlink passes through vacuum, and the loss grows with the square of distance (beam spreading) rather than exponentially, but it works mostly at night, in clear weather, during passes of a few minutes. Twin-field QKD beats the linear repeaterless scaling (its rate goes as √η) because each party sends to a central station and only one photon has to survive half the distance, yet it too is limited to one link.

\n\n

The quantum-internet roadmap

\n

A useful way to read claims is as a ladder of capability: (1) trusted-node networks, which exist today; (2) end-to-end prepare-and-measure links, where any two users can run QKD through untrusted relays; (3) entanglement-distribution networks, which also enable device-independent protocols; (4) networks with quantum memories, for repeaters and blind computing; (5) networks of fault-tolerant processors, i.e. distributed quantum computing. Each rung needs a new hardware ability, and today's long-distance links sit on the first two.

\n\n
❓ NOT VERIFIED

The staged roadmap above is usually attributed to Wehner, Elkouss and Hanson (Science, 2018); the repeaterless bound to Pirandola, Laurenza, Ottaviani and Banchi (2017); reports say Micius has since re-entered the atmosphere; and large trusted-node fibre backbones are reported in China. I could not check these citations and dates: confirm before you rely on this.

\n\n
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE
  • Treating dB as linear: 40 dB is not twice 20 dB of loss, it is 100 times more (10−4 versus 10−2).
  • Calling a trusted node a repeater: a trusted node sees the key; a repeater never does.
  • Believing entanglement swapping sends information faster than light: qubit 4's local state is maximally mixed until the classical Bell result arrives.
  • Quoting a satellite distance record as if it were a continuous network: passes last minutes and the intercontinental key relied on a trusted satellite.
\n\n
★ ON THE EXAM
  • Convert distance and dB/km into η, and into photons or key bits per second.
  • Explain, with the linearity argument, why no-cloning rules out amplifiers.
  • Carry out entanglement swapping for a given Bell outcome and name the correction.
  • Distinguish trusted nodes, repeaters, twin-field QKD and satellite links, and name one verified milestone with its caveat.

This lesson lets you say precisely what \"a quantum computer can solve a problem efficiently\" means, place that class of problems (BQP) among the classical classes you met in the classical-computing chapter, and separate the three kinds of statement people mix up: what is proven, what is believed for good reasons, and what is simply unknown. It is the theory that sits under every algorithm chapter (Shor, Grover, simulation) and under every \"quantum advantage\" headline in the next two lessons.

The idea in plain words

A complexity class is a set of yes/no problems (decision problems, or \"languages\") grouped by how the cost of solving them grows with the input length n. We do not care about one input; we care about the scaling. \"Efficient\" means the cost grows at most polynomially: n, n², n³ log n, and so on. Exponential growth such as 2n is \"inefficient\", however fast one run might be for small n.

A classical computer that may flip fair coins and is allowed to be wrong with probability at most 1/3 on every input defines the class BPP. Replace the coin-flipping computer by a quantum circuit that is measured at the end and you get BQP (bounded-error quantum polynomial time). The 1/3 is not special: repeat the algorithm and take a majority vote and the error falls exponentially fast, as the worked example below shows.

The definition

📘 DEFINITION

A language L (a set of bit strings) is in BQP if there is a family of quantum circuits {Cn} such that: (1) a classical deterministic machine can write down Cn in time polynomial in n (the family is uniform); (2) Cn has poly(n) gates drawn from a fixed universal gate set such as {H, T, CNOT}; (3) on input x of length n the circuit starts in |x⟩|0…0⟩, runs, and measures its first qubit; (4) if x ∈ L the outcome is 1 with probability ≥ 2/3, and if x ∉ L the outcome is 1 with probability ≤ 1/3.

BPP is the same with a polynomial-time classical randomized algorithm in place of the circuit. P: deterministic polynomial time, no error. NP: yes-instances have a certificate a polynomial-time verifier can check. PP: randomized polynomial time where the answer only has to be right with probability strictly above 1/2 (the gap may be exponentially small). PSPACE: anything solvable with polynomial memory, however long it runs.

Two details of the definition carry weight. Uniformity stops us from \"hiding\" the answer to a hard problem in the choice of circuit for each n. And the fixed gate set matters only up to polynomial factors: the Solovay–Kitaev theorem (from the universality chapter) says any other finite universal set can approximate these gates with only polylogarithmic overhead, so BQP does not depend on which reasonable universal set you pick.

The key inclusions, and which ones are theorems

🧮 KEY EQUATION

P ⊆ BPP ⊆ BQP ⊆ PP ⊆ PSPACE ⊆ EXP

📊 FIGURE — Where BQP sits among P, BPP, NP, PP, PSPACE and EXP
Solid nested outlines are proven inclusions. The dashed NP outline only partly overlaps BQP because NP ⊄ BQP is believed, not proven; factoring sits in NP and BQP but, it is believed, outside BPP.

Every ⊆ in this chain is a proven theorem. P ⊆ BPP is trivial (ignore the coins). BPP ⊆ BQP: a quantum circuit can make a fair coin (apply H to |0⟩ and measure) and can run any classical gate reversibly with Toffoli gates. BQP ⊆ PSPACE was proven by Bernstein and Vazirani (1997); BQP ⊆ PP by Adleman, DeMarrais and Huang (1997). PSPACE ⊆ EXP because a machine with polynomial memory has only exponentially many configurations.

What is not known: whether any single ⊆ here is strict, except that P ≠ EXP (the time hierarchy theorem) so at least one link is strict. Nobody has proven BPP ≠ BQP, and nobody can do so without also proving P ≠ PSPACE, a famous open problem.

Why would a proof of BPP ≠ BQP imply P ≠ PSPACE? Because if P = PSPACE, the whole chain from P to PSPACE collapses into one class, and BPP = BQP along with it. So a separation of BPP from BQP is at least as hard as one of the biggest open problems in computer science. That is why every statement of the form \"quantum computers are exponentially faster\" is, strictly, a belief supported by evidence, not a theorem about unrestricted computation.

StatementStatusEvidence
BPP ⊆ BQP ⊆ PP ⊆ PSPACEProvenTheorems above
Factoring ∈ BQPProvenShor (1994): a polynomial-time quantum algorithm
Factoring ∉ BPPBelieved, unprovenDecades of failed attempts; the best known classical algorithm (number field sieve) is super-polynomial
BPP ≠ BQPBelieved, unprovenFactoring, discrete log, simulation of quantum systems; oracle separations (next lesson)
BPP = PBelieved, unprovenDerandomization results under circuit lower-bound assumptions
NP ⊄ BQPBelieved, unprovenSearch lower bound Ω(√N); no structure to exploit in NP-complete problems
BQP ⊄ NP (and ⊄ PH)Unknown; true relative to an oracleRaz–Tal (2019) oracle separation using a Forrelation variant

Why NP-complete problems are not expected to become easy

Factoring is in NP (a factor is a certificate you can check), but it is not believed to be NP-complete: it also lies in co-NP, and if an NP-complete problem were in NP ∩ co-NP then NP = co-NP, which almost nobody believes. So Shor's algorithm tells you nothing about NP-complete problems such as 3-SAT or the travelling salesperson decision problem.

The natural quantum attack on 3-SAT is to search the 2n assignments. Bennett, Bernstein, Brassard and Vazirani (1997) proved that any quantum algorithm that treats the checker as a black box needs Ω(√N) queries to find a marked item among N, so Grover's search is optimal. With N = 2n that is still about 2n/2 steps: a quadratic improvement on an exponential, which remains exponential. Beating this would require exploiting structure in the problem, and Shor-style structure (hidden periodicity, group structure) is exactly what NP-complete problems do not seem to have. This is a belief backed by evidence, not a theorem: nobody has proven NP ⊄ BQP, since that would in particular prove P ≠ NP.

Worked example: why BQP fits in polynomial space

The proof of BQP ⊆ PSPACE is a path sum (Feynman's sum over histories). An output amplitude of a circuit Um…U1 is

⟨x|Um⋯U1|0⟩ = ∑y1,…,ym−1 ⟨x|Um|ym−1⟩ ⋯ ⟨y1|U1|0⟩

where each yk runs over basis states. There are exponentially many paths, but you can visit them one at a time, keeping only a running total and a counter: polynomial memory, exponential time. That is exactly what PSPACE allows.

✏️ WORKED EXAMPLE

Compute P(0) and P(1) for the one-qubit circuit H, then T, then H, starting from |0⟩, by summing paths. Convention: |0⟩ = (1,0)ᵀ, H = (1/√2)[[1,1],[1,−1]], T = diag(1, eiπ/4). Checked in numpy and with Qiskit's Statevector.

  1. Because T is diagonal, a path is fixed by the middle basis state m ∈ {0,1}: amplitude(x) = ∑m Hxm · Tmm · Hm0.
  2. For x = 0, path m = 0: (1/√2)(1)(1/√2) = 0.5. Path m = 1: (1/√2)(eiπ/4)(1/√2) = 0.5eiπ/4 = 0.3536 + 0.3536i.
  3. Add the amplitudes (not the probabilities): amplitude(0) = 0.8536 + 0.3536i. So P(0) = 0.8536² + 0.3536² = 0.8536, which is exactly (2 + √2)/4.
  4. For x = 1, path m = 0 gives 0.5 and path m = 1 gives (1/√2)(eiπ/4)(−1/√2) = −0.3536 − 0.3536i. Sum: 0.1464 − 0.3536i, so P(1) = 0.1464 = (2 − √2)/4.
  5. Sanity check: 0.8536 + 0.1464 = 1. Memory used: one running sum and one bit for m, however many paths there are.

Contrast that with the obvious simulation, which stores all 2n complex amplitudes. In double precision each amplitude takes 16 bytes (two 8-byte floats), so the state vector needs 16 · 2n bytes:

n qubitsamplitudes 2nmemory at 16 bytes each
301,073,741,82416 GiB (a good laptop)
40≈ 1.0995 × 101216 TiB ≈ 17.6 TB
50≈ 1.1259 × 1015≈ 18.0 PB
53≈ 9.0072 × 1015≈ 144.1 PB

Each extra qubit doubles the memory. The path sum trades that memory for time, and real simulators (tensor networks, the subject of lesson 3) sit in between.

Finally, amplification. If one run is right with probability 2/3, run it k times (k odd) and take the majority. The majority is wrong only if at most (k−1)/2 runs are right. Summing the binomial tail in Python with p = 2/3 gives error 0.3333 for k = 1, 0.2099 for k = 5, 0.1221 for k = 11, 0.0557 for k = 21 and 0.0003 for k = 101. The error falls exponentially in k (a Chernoff bound), so the constant 2/3 in the definition is a convention: any fixed gap above 1/2 gives the same class.

The traps

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE
  • \"A quantum computer tries all 2n answers in parallel, so it solves NP-complete problems.\" Measurement returns one outcome; useful algorithms need interference that concentrates amplitude on the answer, and for unstructured search the proven limit is Ω(√N) queries.
  • \"BQP ⊆ PSPACE shows quantum computers are no more powerful than classical ones.\" PSPACE allows exponential time; the inclusion is an upper bound, not a statement about speed.
  • \"It has been proven that BQP is strictly bigger than BPP.\" It has not; such a proof would also prove P ≠ PSPACE.
  • \"Factoring is NP-complete, so Shor breaks NP.\" Factoring is in NP ∩ co-NP and is not believed to be NP-complete.
  • Exponential memory to store a state is not the same as exponential speed-up for a task: 2n amplitudes cannot be read out, and Holevo's bound limits n qubits to n bits of retrievable classical information.
✅ VERIFIED

Bernstein and Vazirani proved BPP ⊆ BQP ⊆ PSPACE (\"Quantum complexity theory\", SIAM J. Comput. 1997; author copy); Adleman, DeMarrais and Huang improved the upper bound to BQP ⊆ PP (summarised in Aaronson, arXiv:quant-ph/0412187).

Raz and Tal, \"Oracle separation of BQP and PH\", STOC 2019, journal version J. ACM 69(4), 2022: dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3530258. Both checked 28 Sep 2026.

What the exam asks

★ ON THE EXAM

Expect: (1) state the definition of BQP with the 2/3 and 1/3 thresholds and the uniformity condition; (2) write the chain P ⊆ BPP ⊆ BQP ⊆ PP ⊆ PSPACE and say which parts are theorems; (3) explain why proving BPP ≠ BQP would prove P ≠ PSPACE; (4) explain why Shor does not put NP-complete problems in BQP and why Grover gives only a quadratic speed-up for brute-force search; (5) a calculation: state-vector memory for n qubits, a path-sum amplitude, or the majority-vote error after k repetitions.

Marks are lost for writing \"=\" or \"⊊\" where only \"⊆\" is known, and for calling beliefs theorems.
